questions.stem: A company has been using predictive methods for a very long time and is trying to implement a few iterative initiatives within its project framework. A project manager has been appointed to lead the first project in this hybrid environment. How should the project manager build awareness of the hybrid approach within the organization?

options.text: Meet with the project team in order to define roles and responsibilities.
options.rationale: Defining roles inside one team is project set-up, not organisational awareness. The question asks how awareness spreads across the organization, and a team meeting reaches nobody outside the team.

options.text: Build the project schedule with iterative sessions and communicate this to stakeholders.
options.rationale: Showing iterations on a schedule tells stakeholders what is happening but not why the approach differs or what it requires of them. Exposure to an artefact is not the same as understanding the method behind it.

options.text: Invite key stakeholders to the daily stand-ups and project review meetings.
options.rationale: Observing ceremonies without grounding leaves stakeholders to infer the method from what they see, and daily attendance is a heavy ask for senior people. It also reaches only those already close to this one project.

options.text: Recommend iterative methodology training for senior managers.
options.rationale: Training the senior layer gives the people who set direction a real understanding of what iterative delivery offers and how it improves delivery overall. Awareness that starts at that level carries into the wider organization rather than staying inside one project.

questions.explanation: When an organization is adopting a new delivery method, awareness has to be built where authority sits, because the layer that approves budgets and interprets results shapes whether the method survives past the pilot. Actions confined to a single team or its immediate stakeholders change nothing organisationally, however well executed.
questions.mindset: To change how an organization works, build understanding at the level that sets its direction.

questions.stem: A project is nearing completion and a stakeholder wants to know how the project outcomes will impact the organization. What should the project manager review with the stakeholder?

options.text: Business case
options.rationale: The business case sets out why the investment was justified, not when value arrives or how it is measured once the work is done. It answers whether the project should have started, which is a different question.

options.text: Benefits management plan
options.rationale: This is the artefact that describes how and when benefits are delivered and what the outcome means for the organization. It is the only document that maps outcomes to organisational impact over time.

options.text: Project charter
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project and names its high-level objectives, but it does not track or describe realised impact. Reaching for it here confuses authorisation with outcome measurement.

options.text: Assumption log
options.rationale: The assumption log records what was taken as true and what remains unverified. It has no bearing on what the delivered outcome will do for the organization.

questions.explanation: A question about organisational impact routes to the artefact that defines when value lands and how it is measured, not to the documents that authorised or justified the work. Charters and business cases look backwards to the decision to invest; impact questions look forward to realisation.
questions.mindset: Match the question to the artefact built to answer it, not to the one that started the project.

questions.stem: At the beginning of a project, a stakeholder is concerned that the initiative may not deliver value to the organization. What should the project manager do first to increase the chances of project success?

options.text: Review the business case and benefits management plan with the stakeholder.
options.rationale: Together these documents show the project has a clear purpose, defined goals and a plan for measuring and realising what it promises. Going through them with the stakeholder answers the doubt directly and builds confidence at the point it matters.

options.text: Provide continual communication of the project status to stakeholders.
options.rationale: Regular status keeps stakeholders informed but never addresses a fundamental doubt about whether the work is worth doing. Frequency of contact is not a substitute for answering the question asked.

options.text: Schedule training for everyone on the use of the new product.
options.rationale: Training addresses the skills needed to use the product, which is a later concern and a different one. The stakeholder is questioning the project's value, not their ability to operate its output.

options.text: Perform an audit to make sure the benefits are realized.
options.rationale: An audit assesses whether objectives were achieved and belongs after completion, not at the start. There is nothing yet to audit when the project has only just begun.

questions.explanation: A doubt about whether an initiative is worth doing is answered with the artefacts that set out its justification and how its worth will be measured, and answered early rather than deferred. Communication cadence, user readiness and after-the-fact assurance all sidestep the substance of the concern.
questions.mindset: Answer a doubt about value with the evidence for it, at the moment it is raised.

questions.stem: A project manager is building a project team. All of the project team members have worked together on previous projects. One of the team members is known for challenging most organizational procedures and processes. What should the project manager do first to ensure a smooth project initiation?

options.text: Review the organizational process assets (OPAs) with all team members and establish ground rules.
options.rationale: OPAs carry the organization's processes, policies and accumulated lessons, and reviewing them with the whole team sets a shared basis for how work will be done. Ground rules agreed on that basis give the team an agreed standard rather than one person's preference.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to define the ground rules and share them with the team members.
options.rationale: Ground rules imposed from outside carry no ownership and invite exactly the challenge the scenario describes. Setting the team's working agreements is the project manager's job, not something to pass upward.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to replace or remove the troubled team member.
options.rationale: Removing someone for questioning process punishes a behaviour that has caused no harm yet and discards an experienced team member. It also hands a team-management problem to the sponsor rather than addressing it.

options.text: Set up a meeting with the team members to review the project management plan.
options.rationale: Reviewing the plan is useful but comes after the team has agreed how it will work together. Walking into that meeting without ground rules leaves the same disagreements unresolved.

questions.explanation: A team that is likely to argue over process needs an agreed standard established before the work starts, and the organization's own documented practice is what that standard rests on. Escalating a personality concern or jumping to content review both skip the step that would have prevented the friction.
questions.mindset: Set the terms of how a team will work together before you ask it to work.

questions.stem: A lengthy upgrade project is being delivered in a series of phased outputs. The end users will face some level of disruption during each phase prior to the outputs being achieved. What should the project manager do to ensure that the intended value is being delivered at each phase?

options.text: Gather feedback using surveys of the end user experience and analyze the results.
options.rationale: Survey feedback captures how disruptive users found the phase, which is sentiment rather than value. A phase can be well received and still deliver none of the benefits it was meant to.

options.text: Review the actual costs incurred to ensure that the project remains on budget.
options.rationale: Cost performance shows what the phase consumed, not what it returned. Staying on budget while delivering nothing of worth is entirely possible.

options.text: Validate the scope to ensure that the required quality of outputs is being met.
options.rationale: Scope validation confirms the outputs match what was specified, which is conformance rather than value. Meeting the specification does not establish that the specified thing was worth having.

options.text: Track progress toward each benefit, based on the benefits management plan.
options.rationale: Benefits have to be identified and given measures before progress towards them can be seen, and the plan holds both. Tracking against it is the only option that tests value rather than conformance or spend.

questions.explanation: Cost, scope and satisfaction measure whether the work was done as agreed; none of them tests whether the agreed thing is producing the worth it promised. Value questions need measures defined in advance and tracked against, which is why they route to the artefact that holds those measures.
questions.mindset: Delivering what was specified is not the same as delivering what it was for.

questions.stem: A project manager in a quickly growing hybrid organization is becoming increasingly frustrated at the rapid amount of change in daily operations. Several newer team members have already left the team or have been promoted to other roles in the organization. What should the project manager do to ensure the project governance remains stable?

options.text: Work with leadership to update the organizational process assets (OPAs).
options.rationale: Updating the OPAs with leadership gives the organization a clear and consistent account of how work should be done as it grows. That consistency is what holds governance steady while people and operations keep changing.

options.text: Develop a new social contract to empower the team.
options.rationale: A social contract sets expectations for behaviour within the team and can improve the working environment. It operates at the wrong level to keep governance stable across a rapidly changing organization.

options.text: Update the team charter with the newer team members.
options.rationale: Refreshing the charter as people join is good practice but only records the current team's purpose and roles. It does nothing about the instability in how the organization works.

options.text: Update the project management plan on a regular basis.
options.rationale: Keeping the plan current matters, but it describes the approach to one project rather than the rules the organization runs by. Repeatedly revising it chases the change instead of settling it.

questions.explanation: Stability under constant change comes from the organisation-level record of how work is done, because that is the one thing new arrivals and departing staff do not carry away with them. Team-level agreements and project-level documents adapt to churn rather than insulating governance from it.
questions.mindset: When people keep changing, anchor the rules somewhere the people are not.

questions.stem: A project manager was recently assigned to an information technology project. The project is in the initiation stage, and the team found a compatibility issue in the technical infrastructure used by the vendor and the organization. What initial step should the project manager take to address this issue effectively?

options.text: Examine if there is an alternate solution.
options.rationale: Designing an alternative before checking the record risks rebuilding a solution the organization has already tried and rejected. This is the right next step only once the lessons learned turn up nothing.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the technical infrastructure team.
options.rationale: Escalating before assessing hands someone else a problem the project manager cannot yet describe. An issue has to be understood before it can usefully be passed on.

options.text: Check the lessons learned database.
options.rationale: Lessons learned from earlier projects are there to be retrieved during initiation, and the first question is whether this compatibility problem has arisen before. The record may name solutions already tried or disqualified, saving the project the time of rediscovering them.

options.text: Consult the project sponsor about the issue.
options.rationale: A technical compatibility problem is not a sponsor-level decision, even where the sponsor happens to have the expertise. Going there first misuses the sponsor and skips the project manager's own assessment.

questions.explanation: Before designing a response to a newly surfaced problem, find out what the organization already knows about it, because a documented history can rule out dead ends and point at answers that worked. Escalating or inventing a fix first both spend effort that the record might have made unnecessary.
questions.mindset: Check what the organisation already knows before designing a solution.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to an existing agile team and is preparing for an upcoming project. The last project that the team worked on was so successful that a senior stakeholder requested that the team use the same governance structure for the new project. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Consult with the project management office (PMO) to gain their insight on governance for the project.
options.rationale: PMO input may well be useful, but seeking it before speaking to the team and the stakeholder who raised the request is premature. It brings in a third party before the immediate parties have discussed the question.

options.text: Collaborate with the team and the senior stakeholder to discuss tailoring the existing governance.
options.rationale: Tailoring means deliberately analysing and modifying governance so it fits the environment and the work at hand, which keeps what worked before without assuming it transfers wholesale. Involving both the team and the stakeholder makes the resulting structure workable and supported.

options.text: Inform senior management that the same project governance can be used for the new project.
options.rationale: This accepts the request without testing it against the new project's characteristics, which may differ in ways that make the old structure a poor fit. Agreeing to a structure before examining it is not governance, it is deference.

options.text: Request that the senior stakeholder discuss all governance-related concerns with the product owner.
options.rationale: Redirecting the stakeholder removes the project manager from a discussion they should be leading. Governance for the project is squarely within the project manager's remit.

questions.explanation: Practice that succeeded on one project is a starting point, not a template, and the correct response to a request to reuse it is a deliberate fit assessment with the people affected. Accepting or deflecting the request both skip the analysis that makes a structure suit the work in front of it.
questions.mindset: What worked last time is a candidate for reuse, not a reason to skip the fit test.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a virtual project with a global team for the first time and encounters an issue with stakeholder participation in team meetings. Some stakeholders do not participate, others complain about scheduling, and others do not acknowledge meeting invitations. What should the project manager do to address these issues and ensure smoother meetings?

options.text: Allow the stakeholders to participate in asynchronous meetings using written communication.
options.rationale: Moving to written exchange sidesteps the symptoms without touching the causes of disengagement, scheduling complaints or ignored invitations. Stakeholders who do not respond to invitations are unlikely to respond to documents.

options.text: Inform the project sponsor of the situation and ask for support in enforcing meeting attendance.
options.rationale: Compelled attendance is a last resort and is reached only after the project manager has tried and failed to resolve the problem directly. Going there first converts an engagement problem into a compliance one.

options.text: Review the organizational culture and structure to properly coordinate meetings.
options.rationale: Understanding the cultures and structures the participants work within reveals why the current format produces discomfort and avoidance. That understanding is what lets the project manager design a schedule and format people will actually use.

options.text: Reschedule meetings for different times and dates according to time zones.
options.rationale: Time zones address only the scheduling complaint and guarantee nothing about attendance, while constant rescheduling is disruptive and time-consuming. It treats one visible symptom as though it were the whole problem.

questions.explanation: Several unrelated-looking complaints from a dispersed group usually share a cause in how people from different cultures and structures expect to be convened, so the move is to understand that context before redesigning anything. Fixing one surface symptom, switching medium, or invoking authority all act before the cause is known.
questions.mindset: When a group behaves in ways you did not expect, understand its context before changing its arrangements.

questions.stem: During the final stage of a project, one of the key stakeholders asks the project manager to brief the executive board about the return on investment (ROI) and any relevant new commercial value identified during project implementation. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Present the cost-benefit analysis.
options.rationale: A cost-benefit analysis is a forecast made to justify the investment, not a record of what the investment returned. At the final stage the board wants realised results, not the projection that preceded them.

options.text: Present the achieved benefits.
options.rationale: What the board needs is evidence of the value the project actually delivered, framed in the terms that matter to them such as revenue gained, cost reduced or customers better served. That directly answers both the return and the new commercial value the stakeholder asked about.

options.text: Present the cost management plan.
options.rationale: The cost management plan describes how money was to be planned and controlled, which is process detail rather than outcome. It says nothing about what the organization got back.

options.text: Present the financial success factors.
options.rationale: Success factors define what would count as a good result; they do not report whether the result was reached. The board is asking for the outcome, not the criteria.

questions.explanation: At the close of a project an executive audience wants realised outcomes, so the answer is whatever records what the organization has gained, not the plans, criteria or forecasts produced earlier to justify or control the work. Those artefacts describe intent; a closing brief has to describe result.
questions.mindset: When the work is done, report what was gained, not what was planned.

questions.stem: A project manager has completed the project deliverable and has passed the acceptance criteria. Which statement confirms that project benefits have been achieved?

options.text: The deliverable has been approved and the value has been confirmed.
options.rationale: Benefits are achieved only when the output is formally accepted and the worth it was meant to produce has been verified. This is the one statement containing both the formal approval and the confirmation of value.

options.text: The deliverable solved all of the issues specified by the project sponsors.
options.rationale: Solving the stated issues describes what the deliverable does, with no formal validation and no confirmation that the expected value followed. Problem resolution and benefit realisation are not the same test.

options.text: The project has seen some improvements in the ability to make decisions.
options.rationale: An unquantified improvement observed somewhere in the project is not a measured benefit against a defined target. Nothing here has been formally validated.

options.text: The project was completed on schedule, without any complaints from end users
options.rationale: Time performance and an absence of complaints say the project ran smoothly, not that it produced worth. A project can hit every date and return nothing.

questions.explanation: Confirming benefit realisation needs two things present together: a formal acceptance of the output, and a verified measure that the intended worth materialised. Statements offering good delivery performance, satisfied users or problems solved supply neither of those and describe the project rather than its return.
questions.mindset: A benefit is realised when someone has formally confirmed the value, not when the work looks successful.

questions.stem: As a project is nearing completion, a struggle between the product owner and the project sponsor regarding who owns the benefits derived from the deliverable becomes a matter of litigation. What should the project manager have done to prevent this conflict from occurring?

options.text: Identified the project sponsor as a stakeholder at the beginning of the project.
options.rationale: Naming someone on a register records that they matter but settles nothing about what they are owed. Identification is not agreement.

options.text: Developed and approved the business case jointly with the product owner and the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Joint development and approval forces both parties to agree on the benefits, and on whose they are, before any work begins. That agreement is what removes the ambiguity the dispute later grew out of.

options.text: Identified and captured any potential issues in the issue log and monitored them frequently.
options.rationale: The issue log tracks problems once they surface; it does not prevent a disagreement over entitlement from forming. Monitoring an ambiguity is not the same as resolving it.

options.text: Created a detailed work breakdown structure (WBS) and implemented systematic tracking.
options.rationale: A WBS decomposes the work to be done and says nothing about who owns what the work produces. Tracking execution in detail leaves the ownership question entirely untouched.

questions.explanation: A dispute over entitlement to project outcomes is prevented by securing written agreement from both claimants at the point the outcomes are defined, not by any amount of tracking or logging afterwards. Artefacts that record work or surface problems cannot settle a question of who is owed the return.
questions.mindset: Settle who owns the value before the work that creates it begins.

questions.stem: A company is transitioning from using a predictive approach to a hybrid predictive-agile project implementation. The leadership team is concerned about benefits realization and is closely following up on one of the project iterations with the project manager. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Update the leadership team with a quantifiable value report for each iteration.
options.rationale: A report describes value at a remove rather than putting the working increment in front of leadership. It substitutes a document for the demonstration that would actually build their confidence.

options.text: Demonstrate the business value to the leadership team and get their buy-in.
options.rationale: A one-off demonstration seeking approval treats benefits realisation as a single event to be signed off. In this environment value accrues across iterations, so a single buy-in moment misses how it is produced.

options.text: Keep delivering iterations of the solution and show the benefit increments to the leadership team.
options.rationale: In this environment the team produces value collaboratively and incrementally, so continued delivery with visible increments is what evidences realisation. The historical record that builds also improves leadership's forecasting and decisions.

options.text: Wait for the leadership team to share the benefits realization updates for each iteration with management.
options.rationale: This inverts the responsibility, leaving leadership to source information the project team holds. Waiting while leadership is already anxious will deepen the concern rather than answer it.

questions.explanation: Where delivery is iterative, worth is evidenced by a steady run of working increments rather than by a report or a single approval event, and the accumulating record gives leadership better data for forecasting. Responsibility for surfacing that evidence sits with the delivery team, not with the audience asking for it.
questions.mindset: In incremental delivery, show the value accruing rather than describing it.

questions.stem: A newly hired project manager is assigned to a school construction project. The school serves students from surrounding neighborhoods and must be completely energy efficient. The project manager must provide a final report. How can the project manager determine whether the planned business value was delivered?

options.text: Inspect the approved technical specifications to confirm that they match the final product deliverables.
options.rationale: Matching the build to its specification confirms conformance, not worth. A building can meet every specification and still fail to produce the benefits that justified it.

options.text: Consult with the team and confirm that the customer was satisfied with the construction of the school.
options.rationale: Satisfaction is subjective feedback and does not measure delivered business value. A pleased customer is not evidence that the intended benefits materialised.

options.text: Review the project charter and business case to determine if the deliverables achieved the intended benefits.
options.rationale: These documents set out the goals, objectives and intended benefits the project was authorised to produce, which is the standard the result has to be measured against. Comparing outcome to that standard is what establishes whether planned value was delivered.

options.text: Demonstrate that the school construction project was delivered on schedule and within budget.
options.rationale: Time and cost performance describe how efficiently the work was executed, not what it returned. Hitting both targets says nothing about whether the intended benefits arrived.

questions.explanation: Judging delivered value means comparing the result against the benefits the project was authorised to produce, which is why closure routes back to the documents that stated those intentions. Conformance to specification, delivery performance and customer sentiment each measure something real but none of them measures return.
questions.mindset: Measure the result against what the project promised, not against how well it ran.

questions.stem: A project manager conducted an analysis with relevant stakeholders to validate project alignment with organizational strategy and expected business value. Several key stakeholders missed the analysis session and their input was not included in the analysis. What is the main consequence of stakeholders missing the analysis session?

options.text: Formal approval of project change requests is delayed.
options.rationale: This assumes change requests exist that need approving, which the scenario does not establish. It is a possible downstream effect rather than the direct consequence of the missing input.

options.text: Stakeholder dissatisfaction with key project deliverables.
options.rationale: Dissatisfaction may or may not follow, and it describes a reaction rather than the defect the absence created. The gap is in the analysis itself, not in how people feel about the outputs.

options.text: Conflict in subsequent phases of the project may result.
options.rationale: Conflict is a possible later symptom and is not certain to occur. Naming a downstream risk does not identify what the session actually failed to produce.

options.text: Inconsistent input on benefits from key stakeholders.
options.rationale: The session existed to establish agreed measures of value, and without the key stakeholders present that input is incomplete and inconsistent. The result is ambiguity and misalignment between project goals and what those stakeholders expect.

questions.explanation: When people whose agreement the exercise depended on are absent, the direct consequence is a defect in the output of that exercise, not the disputes or delays it might cause later. Candidates go wrong by picking a plausible downstream symptom over the gap that was created at the moment of the absence.
questions.mindset: Name the damage an omission does immediately, not the trouble it may cause later.

questions.stem: A hybrid project involving many stakeholders is underway. As requested by the project management office (PMO), the project status reports, as well as other project documents, are being stored in a central repository. When reviewing the documents stored in the repository, the project manager discovered that documents were either not updated or were missing. What should the project manager do in this situation?

options.text: Discuss the situation with the project sponsor to reduce the level of documentation.
options.rationale: Reducing a PMO requirement because the team is not meeting it treats the standard as the problem rather than the compliance gap. Remedying this sits within the project manager's own authority and needs no sponsor involvement.

options.text: Work with the team leaders to update the required project reports.
options.rationale: The first move is to correct the deficiency by getting the required reports brought up to date. Working through the team leaders also re-establishes the documentation procedures so the gap does not simply reopen.

options.text: Stop all project activities until the project documents are updated and uploaded.
options.rationale: Halting the whole project is disproportionate to a documentation lapse that can be fixed alongside continuing work. The cost of the stoppage would far exceed the problem being solved.

options.text: Schedule a knowledge transfer session at the final stage of the project.
options.rationale: Deferring to the end leaves the repository unreliable for everyone who needs it in the meantime. Documentation and knowledge transfer belong throughout the project, not only at its close.

questions.explanation: A lapse in required records is fixed by bringing the records current and reinforcing the procedure with the people responsible, both of which sit inside the project manager's authority. Escalating, halting the work, or deferring the remedy to the end each respond to a routine correction as though it were something larger.
questions.mindset: Fix what is within your authority to fix, at the scale the problem deserves.

questions.stem: An oil refinery project is in the middle of the execution phase. The project team found that the project is delayed because of an environmental regulation change, procurement delays, and a change in government. However, the project deliverable is still urgently needed. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Terminate the project immediately, avoid further loss through more expenditure, and absorb the current loss.
options.rationale: Termination discards a deliverable the scenario says is still urgently needed, on the basis of delays that have not yet been assessed. It is the most drastic response available and nothing supports reaching for it.

options.text: Review the impact of the changes, comply with the new regulations, and then propose a realistic plan.
options.rationale: Regulatory changes have to be reviewed and the project realigned to them, since compliance is not optional. Assessing first and then proposing a revised plan addresses the delays while keeping the still-needed deliverable in play.

options.text: Make the necessary arrangements for the procurement materials, and continue the project as planned.
options.rationale: This fixes one of the three causes and ignores the regulatory change entirely, leaving the project heading for non-compliance. Continuing to the existing plan assumes conditions that no longer hold.

options.text: Stop the project and negotiate with the new government to pay the invoices for work done up to that point.
options.rationale: Stopping work to pursue payment abandons an urgently needed deliverable and treats a political change as a reason to exit. It is premature, and no assessment supports it.

questions.explanation: When external conditions shift under a project, the sequence is assess the impact, satisfy any mandatory requirements, then put a revised plan to the decision-makers. Drastic exits and business-as-usual continuation are both decisions taken before anyone knows the size of the problem.
questions.mindset: Size the change before you decide how far to move.

questions.stem: A project manager noticed that one team member is frequently absent from project team meetings. Instead of working on the current project, the team member has been working on a task assigned by their functional manager. What should the project manager do to resolve this issue?

options.text: Discuss the resource allocation with the team member's functional manager.
options.rationale: The functional manager is the person assigning the competing work and therefore the stakeholder who can resolve the allocation. Taking the issue to them addresses the cause rather than its visible effect.

options.text: Remove the team member from the project team due to their continued absences.
options.rationale: This penalises someone who is following instructions from their own manager and loses the project a resource it needs. The competing demand would still be there for whoever replaced them.

options.text: Record the absences in the team member's performance appraisal.
options.rationale: Documenting the absences marks the symptom on someone's record without changing the allocation that caused them. It punishes an individual for a conflict between two managers.

options.text: Ask another team member for input regarding the issue.
options.rationale: Asking a colleague deflects rather than resolves, and gathers hearsay about a situation whose cause is already known. The person who can fix it has not been approached.

questions.explanation: When a team member's availability is being consumed elsewhere, the resolution lies with whoever controls that competing demand, so the project manager goes to them directly. Options that document, penalise or canvass opinion all leave the underlying allocation untouched.
questions.mindset: Take a resource conflict to the person who controls the resource.

questions.stem: After the transition and completion of a large equipment installation project, the project manager receives a request from the customer to add some operational cost to the project budget for team-building activities. The project was completed under budget, project contingency reserves were not spent, and the team-building activities will ensure the operational team's optimal performance. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reject the request and close the project financials.
options.rationale: The project is complete and has been transitioned, and contingency reserves are not available for operational items unrelated to the project's success. The financials should be closed so the unspent budget returns to the organization for other opportunities.

options.text: Perform the integrated change control process.
options.rationale: Change control governs changes to a project that is still running; there is no live scope or baseline here to change. Running the process would lend legitimacy to a request that falls outside the project altogether.

options.text: Approve the expenditure to ensure customer satisfaction.
options.rationale: Spending project funds on operational activity because the customer asked misapplies money held for project purposes. Satisfaction does not create an entitlement to funds set aside for something else.

options.text: Document the request in the lessons learned repository.
options.rationale: The lessons learned repository records insight for future work, not requests requiring a decision now. Filing it there leaves the customer without an answer.

questions.explanation: Money held against project risk belongs to the project and to the organization once the work transitions, and it cannot be redirected to operational spending however worthwhile. A request that arrives after handover falls outside the project entirely, so the answer is a clear refusal and a clean financial close rather than any process designed for live work.
questions.mindset: Once the work has transitioned, its money goes back to the organisation, not to new requests.

questions.stem: In a company that recently adopted hybrid practices, a project is struggling to perform as expected. Neither the project manager nor the team members have previous experience with this new approach to project management. The project manager wants to ensure the transition to hybrid practices is producing the desired results. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take an active role in assigning tasks to team members and follow up with their results.
options.rationale: Directive task assignment works around the capability gap rather than closing it and pulls against the way hybrid delivery is meant to run. The team remains inexperienced the moment the project manager steps back.

options.text: Arrange for basic hybrid training for team members and ensure the team performs coordination meetings.
options.rationale: Training in the methods actually being used strengthens commitment and improves the flow of work, which is what the inexperience is costing. Regular coordination meetings then give the team a structure in which to apply what it has learned.

options.text: Issue performance reports to all team members so they can review and act on them.
options.rationale: Reports tell the team it is underperforming without giving it the knowledge to perform differently. Measurement is not a remedy for not knowing how.

options.text: Build a WBS and RACI chart to ensure all aspects of the project are owned and tasks are clear.
options.rationale: Clarifying ownership and tasks addresses confusion about who does what, which is not the stated problem. The team's difficulty is unfamiliarity with the approach, and no chart teaches it.

questions.explanation: Where a team underperforms because it has never worked this way before, the remedy has to close the knowledge gap rather than manage around it, and a supporting routine then embeds the new practice. Tighter control, clearer artefacts and more reporting all assume a capability the team does not yet have.
questions.mindset: When people underperform because they do not know how, teach them rather than steer them.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to a project in a country where the company has not previously done business. At the beginning of the project, the project manager realizes that there are certain regulatory requirements for which the project team has no experience. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Assign sufficient budget in case such requirements have to be met.
options.rationale: Setting money aside before anyone knows whether the requirements apply or what they demand is guesswork dressed as prudence. The amount cannot be estimated until the obligation is understood.

options.text: Consult with a subject matter expert on how to avoid such requirements.
options.rationale: Regulatory requirements are not optional and the project must comply with those that apply to it. Engaging an expert to find a way around them misdirects the expertise and exposes the organization.

options.text: Engage a subject matter expert to check if the requirements are relevant to the project.
options.rationale: Expert judgment is the means of establishing which requirements actually bear on this project in an unfamiliar jurisdiction. Knowing what applies is the prerequisite for every decision that follows.

options.text: Escalate concerns about the requirements to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Raising a concern with the sponsor before making any attempt to resolve it is poor practice. The project manager can obtain the missing knowledge without involving the sponsor at all.

questions.explanation: Where a team lacks knowledge the work depends on, the move is to bring in expertise to establish what actually applies, before budgeting, escalating or looking for exemptions. Funding an unquantified obligation and seeking to dodge a mandatory one are both decisions taken in the absence of the facts.
questions.mindset: Establish what applies to you before deciding what to do about it.

questions.stem: A company has launched a new strategic project. The goal and scope of the project were loosely defined at the executive committee meeting, and the stakeholders have been appointed. The project manager needs to hold the kickoff meeting. However, most of the stakeholders are in different locations and some are on vacation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold the kickoff meeting with the available stakeholders and update others later.
options.rationale: Briefing part of the group and catching the rest up afterwards produces uneven understanding and costs more effort overall. Those updated second-hand miss the discussion that gave the first group its alignment.

options.text: Postpone the kickoff meeting until the stakeholders have returned.
options.rationale: Waiting delays the start of the project and may be impossible against a tight deadline. It treats physical availability as a constraint that cannot be worked around, which is no longer true.

options.text: Schedule one-on-one sessions with the stakeholders before they leave.
options.rationale: Individual sessions are useful for gathering input but give none of the shared understanding a group kickoff creates. Stakeholders never hear each other's questions or assumptions.

options.text: Arrange a virtual team kickoff meeting with the stakeholders.
options.rationale: A virtual meeting reaches everyone regardless of location or leave, so all stakeholders receive the same information and can ask questions together. It can also be recorded and shared with anyone genuinely unable to attend live.

questions.explanation: A launch event exists to give every stakeholder the same picture at the same moment, so dispersion is solved by changing the medium rather than by splitting the audience or delaying the project. Serial briefings and one-to-one sessions both deliver information without delivering common ground.
questions.mindset: When people cannot be in one room, change the room rather than the meeting.

questions.stem: During a predictive project, the project manager is in the process of finalizing the exit criteria for a significant system development project. At this stage, a stakeholder responsible for risk and compliance informs the project manager that an additional deliverable must be completed due to recently passed legislation by the local government. This requested change is expected to have an impact on the scheduled release date of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Meet with the stakeholders and advise them that the request was not part of the exit criteria.
options.rationale: Pointing out that the deliverable was not in the exit criteria does not dispose of it, because the legislation requires it regardless. Declining on procedural grounds leaves the project heading for non-compliance.

options.text: Collaborate with the stakeholder and submit a change request to the Change Control Board (CCB).
options.rationale: Working with the stakeholder establishes the nature and implications of what the legislation demands, and the formal request then puts it before the body empowered to decide. That route gets the impact assessed and the consequences made visible to everyone affected.

options.text: Escalate the issue to the sponsor to avoid delaying the project release date.
options.rationale: The CCB is already empowered to approve this, so involving the sponsor first is unnecessary. Sponsor involvement belongs after assessment and formal submission, not instead of them.

options.text: Add this new risk to the risk register and monitor because changes are outside the project scope.
options.rationale: A mandatory legislative deliverable is a change to be approved, not an uncertainty to be watched. Treating it as a risk leaves the required work unauthorised and undone.

questions.explanation: A legally mandated addition still enters the project through the formal approval route, with the requester engaged first so the submission describes the obligation accurately. Refusing on scope grounds, escalating past the change authority, or logging it for monitoring each fail to get the work authorised.
questions.mindset: An obligation you cannot refuse still has to be approved through the proper route.

questions.stem: An urban hotel design project has an international, multidisciplinary, and cross-cultural team. The project manager is in the process of developing the first version of the project management plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use a waterfall approach to project management.
options.rationale: Choosing a method by default rather than by fit ignores the complex dependencies and cross-functional working the scenario describes. The team's composition is the planning problem, and the choice of life cycle does not address it.

options.text: Delegate most tasks to team members based in their same timezone.
options.rationale: Allocating work by proximity rather than by skill wastes the expertise the team was assembled for. It is neither fair nor practical as a basis for assignment.

options.text: Use a single communication channel for the entire project team.
options.rationale: One channel imposed across an international team may suit nobody and may not even be available in every location. Uniformity is not the same as effectiveness.

options.text: Incorporate cultural considerations into the project management plan.
options.rationale: Building cultural and communication considerations into the plan is what makes it intelligible and usable by every member regardless of background or working style. A plan the team cannot follow is not a plan.

questions.explanation: The composition of a team is an input to planning, not an obstacle to be routed around, so differences in culture and communication style belong inside the plan itself. Standardising the method, the channel or the allocation each impose uniformity where the situation calls for accommodation.
questions.mindset: Plan for the team you have, not for a team without differences.

questions.stem: A project manager is managing an upgrade from an older system to a new version. Halfway through the upgrade, the older system failed to upgrade and could not be restored. What should the project manager do to manage this situation?

options.text: Abandon the old system and tell the team to speed up work on other deliverables.
options.rationale: Abandonment may not be possible and can generate further issues and impacts nobody has looked at. Accelerating other work is activity chosen in place of understanding the problem.

options.text: Ask for more time to restore the old system while continuing with the project.
options.rationale: The scenario states the system could not be restored, so requesting time for it pursues an option already ruled out. It also commits to a schedule change before the impact is known.

options.text: Assess the impacts of the failure and communicate them with relevant stakeholders.
options.rationale: Understanding the consequences has to come before any other action, and stakeholders need that understanding to work through mitigation with the project manager. Without it both sides are acting on an unclear picture of what has happened.

options.text: Tell the team to continue working as they are not responsible for the old system.
options.rationale: Ownership of the old system is beside the point when the current project depends on it. Disclaiming responsibility leaves a live dependency unmanaged.

questions.explanation: A failure that the project depends on is assessed for consequence and then shared with the people who will help respond, before any remedy is chosen. Acting first, whether by pressing on, reversing course or disclaiming ownership, commits the project without anyone knowing the size of what has gone wrong.
questions.mindset: Understand the damage before you choose the response.

questions.stem: A major change in a government policy may cause a project's completion date to be delayed. The project is 90% complete. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Suspend the project until the issue with the government policy is resolved.
options.rationale: Suspension is costly and time-consuming and may prove wholly unnecessary if the policy turns out to have little effect. It commits to the most disruptive response before the impact has been assessed.

options.text: Engage the change control board (CCB) to assess possible impacts to the project.
options.rationale: The CCB is the body that evaluates and approves changes, and engaging it gets the policy change properly assessed. A mitigation plan can then be developed on the basis of that assessment.

options.text: Move forward with the project since it is near completion.
options.rationale: Being 90% complete does not make the project immune to a policy change that may still affect its outcome. Pressing on regardless risks the success of work nearly finished.

options.text: Assign a new completion date for the project and inform stakeholders.
options.rationale: Announcing a new date presumes an impact that has not been evaluated and a remedy that has not been agreed. This step belongs after the assessment, not instead of it.

questions.explanation: An external change that may move a baseline goes to the body empowered to evaluate it, whatever proportion of the work is already done. Suspending, continuing or re-dating the project are all responses selected before the magnitude of the change is known, and one of them will be right only by accident.
questions.mindset: Route a potential baseline change to the authority that evaluates it, not to your own judgement.

questions.stem: Organizations face different challenges within their operational areas due to external factors. This has required companies to develop formal engagement documents to guide their various operations. How should a project manager make their team members and stakeholders aware of the uniqueness of the organizational standards?

options.text: The various external factors of the project will be an input to the project management plan and will form part of the briefing at the kick-off meeting.
options.rationale: The project environment, covering the organization, government and other external factors, is a ground rule that has to be communicated at the outset. Feeding it into the plan and briefing it at kickoff puts it in front of everyone before the work starts.

options.text: The various external factors should already be understood by team members and stakeholders and including them is optional.
options.rationale: Prior knowledge cannot be assumed, and treating the briefing as optional leaves awareness to chance. The project has an obligation to ensure it explicitly.

options.text: Anyone who is involved in the project must understand these various external factors and make an effort to research them.
options.rationale: Pushing the research onto individuals produces inconsistent understanding and no assurance anyone has done it. Establishing shared ground rules is the project manager's job, not homework for participants.

options.text: The team members and stakeholders will be informed about these various external factors through the official organizational communications channel.
options.rationale: A general corporate channel carries no guarantee that project participants read or connect the material to this project. It substitutes broadcast for a project briefing.

questions.explanation: The environment a project operates within is a ground rule, which means it is stated deliberately at the start and built into the plan rather than assumed, delegated or broadcast. Anything that leaves understanding to individual initiative produces a team working to different assumptions.
questions.mindset: Never assume shared understanding of the rules you are working under; establish it.

questions.stem: A project was undertaken to set up a new business function in the company. Several months after completion, the project manager is still handling business operations for the project while working on another project. What should the project manager have done at the beginning of the project to prevent this?

options.text: Ensured that the revision to the organizational structure was a deliverable.
options.rationale: Restructuring may be needed to stand up a new function but it is not a project deliverable in the proper sense. It also does nothing to define who takes the running of the function when the project ends.

options.text: Included the transition plan as a deliverable in the project closing process.
options.rationale: A transition plan sets out how the outputs pass to the operations team, which is exactly what was missing here. Making it a deliverable forces the handover to be planned rather than left to drift onto the project manager.

options.text: Clarified the RACI chart with the project sponsor at the project's onset.
options.rationale: A RACI assigns responsibility for project work, not for the ongoing operation of what the project produced. It stops being relevant at the point the handover problem arises.

options.text: Ensured that the recruitment process was included in the project management plan.
options.rationale: Recruiting may be a necessary step in establishing the function but it is not a project deliverable. Having people in post does not by itself transfer the work to them.

questions.explanation: A project that creates something operational is not finished when the thing exists; it is finished when responsibility for running it has formally moved. Planning that transfer as a deliverable is what prevents the project manager from becoming the permanent operator by default.
questions.mindset: Plan how the work leaves you, not just how it gets built.

questions.stem: A company that has traditionally used predictive approaches has been experimenting with the use of agile in portions of a project. Because the company has been pleased with the results, the project sponsor now requests that the entire project be converted to agile. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Propose that the approach change to agile take effect for new projects.
options.rationale: Deferring the request to future projects declines it without evaluation and leaves the sponsor's request unanswered. Whether this project can convert is a question for the approval body, not for a counter-proposal.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Switching the delivery approach of a live project is a change that must be approved before it is incorporated. The CCB is the body that gives that approval, so the request goes there first.

options.text: Consult the product owner as they may have reasons to continue using a predictive approach.
options.rationale: Canvassing another party's preference is not required here and does not substitute for approval. The decision rests with the change authority regardless of what the product owner prefers.

options.text: Convert the project deliverables to user stories and inform the team.
options.rationale: This implements the change before it has been approved, which is the error the scenario is testing. Informing the team afterwards does not make an unapproved change legitimate.

questions.explanation: Changing how a running project is delivered is as much a change as altering its scope, so it goes through the approval route before anything is reworked. A sponsor's enthusiasm is a request, not an authorisation, and acting on it directly bypasses the control the organization has put in place.
questions.mindset: A request from a senior figure still needs approval from the body that grants it.

questions.stem: A junior project manager approaches a senior project manager and asks for assistance in initiating the final closeout process for a project. Before offering guidance, the senior project manager requires additional information. What should the senior project manager do first?

options.text: Ask if the acceptance criteria for all deliverables have been met.
options.rationale: Meeting the acceptance criteria is what establishes that the project is genuinely complete and the customer is satisfied with what was produced. Without that, closeout cannot properly begin.

options.text: Ask if the deliverables were completed within budget and on time.
options.rationale: Time and cost performance describe how the project ran, not whether its outputs are finished and accepted. A project can overrun both and still be complete.

options.text: Ask if the customer has paid for all product development expenses.
options.rationale: Payment status is a commercial matter that does not have to be settled before closeout is initiated. It says nothing about whether the work is done.

options.text: Ask if quality assurance activities were conducted.
options.rationale: Quality assurance concerns the processes used during delivery rather than the completeness of the outputs. It is not a precondition for starting closeout.

questions.explanation: Closure begins from a test of completeness against the agreed standard for the outputs, because everything else in closeout assumes the work is genuinely finished. Performance data, payment and process assurance each describe something real about the project without answering the only question that gates the decision.
questions.mindset: Before closing anything out, confirm it is actually finished by the agreed standard.

questions.stem: In the middle of executing an IT project, two project team members discover a new feature that will change the appearance of the product and make it more aesthetically appealing. Excited about the opportunity to add this feature, they approach the project manager to approve this addition to the deliverables, which will increase client satisfaction and possibly increase the company's chances of receiving additional project contracts from the client. How should the project manager respond?

options.text: Approve the idea in order to achieve the projected expectations of the team members.
options.rationale: The project manager cannot authorise an addition to approved deliverables on their own, however enthusiastic the team. Meeting the team's expectations is not a basis for bypassing change management.

options.text: Remind team members that, without an approved change request, the focus should be on the agreed scope.
options.rationale: Changes to an approved plan go through change management before any work is done, and adding unrequested features is gold plating, which is not acceptable practice. Redirecting the team to the agreed scope holds that line without dismissing the idea.

options.text: Get the buy-in of the remaining team members and implement the feature once the team members give their consent.
options.rationale: Team consensus is not an approval authority and cannot substitute for a change request. Widening the circle of agreement does not make an unapproved change permissible.

options.text: Implement the change as soon as possible to improve the possibility for future revenue.
options.rationale: Potential future business does not authorise altering contracted deliverables. Acting first and seeking approval later puts the contract requirements at risk.

questions.explanation: Adding value the customer did not ask for is not a favour, it is an unapproved change, and the route for any change to approved deliverables runs through the formal process whatever its merits. Neither the project manager's judgement nor the team's agreement is a substitute for that authorisation.
questions.mindset: Extra that nobody approved is still a change, not a gift.

questions.stem: A project manager has been informed that the first of several major deliveries from another country will be delayed. These deliveries are on the critical path, and the delay will result in a missed milestone. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Update the project's lessons learned register and project management plan.
options.rationale: Both matter, but they follow the logging of the issue and the immediate response. Recording insight while a live milestone is slipping puts reflection ahead of action.

options.text: Revise the project schedule and notify the stakeholders of the delay.
options.rationale: Reworking the schedule commits to an outcome before any attempt has been made to contain the delay. This comes after the issue is logged and an action plan exists.

options.text: Register the delay in the issue log and develop an immediate action plan.
options.rationale: The issue log is the central record for project issues, and entering the delay there makes it tracked and visible. An immediate action plan, built from the root cause, is what limits the damage to the milestone.

options.text: Identify the parties responsible for the delay to issue back charges for their portion.
options.rationale: Recovering costs does nothing to protect the milestone and belongs well after the delay has been managed. Pursuing liability first prioritises blame over delivery.

questions.explanation: A live problem is first recorded where the project tracks problems and then met with a plan to contain it; every other response either documents history or accepts the consequence. Rescheduling and cost recovery are the actions of someone who has already concluded the delay cannot be mitigated.
questions.mindset: Log a live problem and act on it before you adjust plans around it.

questions.stem: A project manager works at a construction company. The current project is a three year, multimillion-dollar initiative to rebuild a stadium. The first phase of the project has been completed within the three month timeframe and within budget. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Move on to the next phase.
options.rationale: Starting the next phase without closing the previous one leaves obligations from that phase unresolved. It is not good practice regardless of how well the phase performed.

options.text: Secure approval from the program manager.
options.rationale: Phase completion is not approved by the program manager, so this seeks authorisation from the wrong place. It also skips the closure activities the phase requires.

options.text: Proceed with the contractual closure of the phase.
options.rationale: Contractual closure finalises all activities for the phase or contract, which is what the end of a phase calls for. Once closure is received the next phase can start as planned and budgeted.

options.text: Begin the administrative closure process.
options.rationale: Administrative closure belongs to final project closure, not to the completion of one phase of a three-year initiative. Applying it here treats a phase boundary as the end of the project.

questions.explanation: A phase boundary is a closure point with its own obligations to finalise, and clearing them is what authorises the next phase to begin. Candidates go wrong by either treating the boundary as nothing at all or by reaching for the process reserved for the end of the whole project.
questions.mindset: Close each phase properly before opening the next.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a project that has been ongoing for some time and is currently at the 70% completion mark. The development team has been diligently following the project management plan and scope defined in the project charter. During a product review meeting, a stakeholder complains that additional features should be included. These features were not initially part of the project scope but have now become a pressing concern for the stakeholder. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Analyze changes with the team and go through the formal change control process.
options.rationale: Analysing with the team first produces a real understanding of what the features would take and whether they are feasible this late. The formal process then evaluates the effect on schedule, budget and scope, assesses risk and obtains the necessary approvals.

options.text: Inform the stakeholder that the changes will be applied later as product fixes.
options.rationale: Promising later delivery commits to something that may not be achievable without harming schedule or budget. It also decides the request without any analysis of it.

options.text: Update the project management plan with the requested changes and inform relevant stakeholders.
options.rationale: Amending the plan enacts the change before it has been through the process that authorises it. Informing people afterwards does not supply the missing approval.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board and inform the sponsor about the changes.
options.rationale: Submitting straight away sends the board a request nobody has yet assessed, leaving it to decide without the information it needs. The analysis with the team is what makes the submission worth considering.

questions.explanation: A late scope request is understood with the people who would build it before it is put to the approval body, so that the decision rests on real feasibility and real cost. Going to the board unprepared is a subtler error than acting unilaterally, but it still asks someone to decide on an impact nobody has measured.
questions.mindset: Understand what a request would cost before asking anyone to approve it.

questions.stem: During a project closing review meeting, the project manager notes that a software development task took longer to complete than was planned. Which action should the project manager take for continuous project improvement?

options.text: Update the performance data in the lessons learned register.
options.rationale: At closing, the place for an observation about how the work actually performed is the lessons learned register. That is what carries the insight forward to future projects.

options.text: Update the risk register so the problem will not happen in the future.
options.rationale: The risk register serves a project that is still running and has no function once this one is closing. Recording a past event as a future risk also misuses the artefact.

options.text: Update the problem in the issue log and distribute it to the project team.
options.rationale: The issue log is used during execution to track problems needing resolution, not at closing to record what happened. There is nothing left for the team to act on.

options.text: Update the communications management plan with details of the problem.
options.rationale: The communications plan governs how information flows during the project and is not a repository for performance observations. It has no bearing on future improvement.

questions.explanation: Where the project sits in its life cycle decides which artefact an observation belongs in, and at closing the only one still doing useful work is the one that carries knowledge to the next project. Registers and logs used to steer live work have no purpose once there is no live work left to steer.
questions.mindset: Record an observation where the project's current stage says it belongs.

questions.stem: Halfway through implementation, the project co-sponsor, who is contributing a significant amount of capital to the project, informs the project team of an additional feature to the project deliverable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess the impact of the new requirement and update the risk register.
options.rationale: Updating the risk register comes after a change has been approved, not in place of processing the request. It responds to a scope change as though it were an uncertainty to monitor.

options.text: Complete the current project as planned and update it later with the new requirements.
options.rationale: Deferring a key stakeholder's requirement without their agreement disregards a legitimate request from someone central to the project. It damages the prospects for project success.

options.text: Collect the co-sponsor's requirements and perform the integrated change control process.
options.rationale: The co-sponsor is a key stakeholder whose requirements need to be taken seriously and captured properly. Running them through integrated change control is how a mid-implementation addition is evaluated and decided.

options.text: Convince the co-sponsor to maintain the current scope and complete the project as planned.
options.rationale: Talking a key stakeholder out of a requirement dismisses it without evaluation. Persuasion is not an assessment and negatively affects the project's standing with its funders.

questions.explanation: A new requirement from a key stakeholder is captured and put through the formal evaluation route, rather than deferred, argued away or logged as an uncertainty. Each of those alternatives reaches a verdict on the request without the analysis that would justify one.
questions.mindset: Take a requirement seriously enough to evaluate it properly, whoever it comes from.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a project to modernize a bank's information technology (IT) infrastructure. The project manager recently received approval of the project's change management plan from the project sponsor. The project sponsor now requests that the project manager implement a new piece of technology in the solution. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Add the new technology as a risk in the risk register.
options.rationale: A sponsor's request to change the solution is a change, not an uncertainty to be logged and watched. Recording it as a risk leaves the request itself unprocessed.

options.text: Submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: A proposed change to the solution is formally documented, evaluated and approved or rejected through change control. The CCB weighs its effect on project objectives and decides.

options.text: Update the schedule and cost baselines with the new technology.
options.rationale: Baselines are updated only once a change has been approved, never in anticipation of approval. Doing it now rewrites the plan on the strength of a request.

options.text: Request the project sponsor to procure the new technology.
options.rationale: Procuring the technology starts implementing the change before it has been authorised. No action towards the new solution is warranted until the change request is decided.

questions.explanation: The sponsor approving a change management plan does not exempt the sponsor from it, so a request to alter the solution enters the same formal route as any other. Updating baselines or beginning procurement both act on an approval that does not yet exist.
questions.mindset: The people who approve the process are also bound by it.

questions.stem: During the planning phase of a project, the project manager is having trouble identifying stakeholders. Without input from the correct stakeholders, getting user feedback will be challenging. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: The engagement plan is not usually created until stakeholders have been identified and analysed, so it cannot be the source of the identification. Consulting it here assumes the output of a step not yet performed.

options.text: Inform the project sponsors.
options.rationale: Telling the sponsor about the difficulty is neither comprehensive nor efficient and passes on a task the project manager can do. The information needed is already available in the project's own documents.

options.text: Refer to the project charter to identify stakeholders.
options.rationale: The charter records the project's purpose, objectives and stakeholders, making it the most direct source when identification stalls. Those named there can then be carried into analysis and engagement planning.

options.text: Review the project scope document.
options.rationale: The scope document defines what the project will produce rather than who has an interest in it. It is less comprehensive than the charter and is not normally used for identification.

questions.explanation: The document that authorised the project is the earliest record of who has an interest in it, which makes it the starting point when identification is incomplete. Artefacts produced later in the sequence cannot supply an input that their own creation depends on.
questions.mindset: When a step stalls, look to the artefact that precedes it rather than the one that follows.

questions.stem: During project closure, the team considers that the final sprint retrospective is not necessary because there are no remaining sprints. What could be a potentially beneficial outcome of conducting this sprint retrospective?

options.text: Improvement in velocity if the same team is formed in the future
options.rationale: This depends on the same people being reassembled, which nothing guarantees, and narrows the benefit to a single metric. It is not the outcome a final retrospective is held for.

options.text: Promotion opportunities for the team members
options.rationale: A retrospective examines how the team worked, not how individuals should be rewarded. Individual advancement is unconnected to the purpose of the event.

options.text: Information that could be useful for future projects
options.rationale: Reflecting on overall performance captures knowledge that applies to similar work and to continuous improvement generally. It also lets the team mark what went well and settle anything still outstanding.

options.text: Tips for adapting to working together if that happens in the near future
options.rationale: Interpersonal adaptation for a hypothetical future grouping is not the main objective of the event. It reduces a knowledge-capture exercise to social preparation.

questions.explanation: The value of reflecting at the end of work lies in what it releases to the organization rather than in what it returns to this particular team, which is why the absence of further iterations does not remove the reason to do it. Answers tied to the same people regrouping miss that the knowledge travels further than they do.
questions.mindset: Reflect for whoever comes next, not only for the people in the room.

questions.stem: A project manager has just finished a project charter and received approval from the project sponsor. The project manager then presented the project charter to the stakeholders and noticed a lack of participation from some of them during this meeting. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Include this in the risk register because the Project Manager is uncertain that the stakeholders understood their responsibilities in this project.
options.rationale: This is a present problem for the project manager to resolve, not a future uncertainty to record and watch. Logging it as a risk defers action on something already happening.

options.text: Hold one-on-one meetings with these stakeholders to ensure their understanding of key deliverables and their responsibilities.
options.rationale: Every stakeholder needs to understand the deliverables and what is expected of them, and individual meetings establish that directly. Addressing it immediately prevents the disengagement from hardening.

options.text: Report the concerns about the stakeholders' lack of involvement to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Reporting the concern upward does not resolve it and leaves the stakeholders no more engaged. Securing engagement is the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Ask the project team to monitor these stakeholders and their involvement.
options.rationale: Monitoring observes the problem without addressing it, and the task is not the project team's to carry. Engagement belongs to the project manager.

questions.explanation: Disengagement observed now is an issue to be worked, not a risk to be logged or a matter to be passed on, and it is resolved by going to the people directly. Delegating the problem or escalating it leaves the understanding gap exactly where it was.
questions.mindset: An engagement problem you can see is yours to address, in person.

questions.stem: A project manager for a new project is tasked with applying agile practices to improve team performance. Which approach should the project manager take?

options.text: Utilize active listening techniques to address the needs of the team.
options.rationale: Active listening is a valuable skill for any project manager but is not an agile practice and does not by itself lift team performance. The question asks which agile practice to apply, and this is a general communication technique.

options.text: Request a budget from finance for training the team members.
options.rationale: Training may help the team in time but it is an external intervention rather than an agile practice the team runs itself. It also does nothing about how the team inspects and adjusts its own working.

options.text: Assign a budget for team activities during the planning phase of the project.
options.rationale: Funding team activities may improve morale without changing how the team examines its performance. Spending on the team is not the same as building a practice of improvement into its rhythm.

options.text: Ensure team retrospectives are done regularly.
options.rationale: Retrospectives are a core agile practice in which the team reflects on its own performance and identifies where to improve. Holding them regularly is what turns improvement into a habit rather than a one-off effort.

questions.explanation: Improving how an agile team performs comes from the recurring practice by which the team inspects its own working and adjusts, not from skills the project manager brings or resources spent on the team. Useful interventions from outside are not the same as a mechanism the team operates on itself.
questions.mindset: Build improvement into the team's routine rather than supplying it from outside.
