questions.stem: During a retrospective meeting, project team members complain that open issues that were not fixed during the iteration are impacting their velocity. What should the project manager do to improve productivity?

options.text: Ensure team members attend daily standup meetings to discuss the impediments.
options.rationale: The standup is where impediments surface daily so they can be cleared before they accumulate across an iteration. Facilitating and removing those blockers is the servant leadership the situation calls for.

options.text: Document the issues in the issue log and wait to solve them at another time.
options.rationale: Recording the issues and deferring them is what allowed them to build up and drag on velocity in the first place. Documentation without resolution changes nothing about productivity.

options.text: Extend the daily standup meetings to discuss the issues in more detail.
options.rationale: Lengthening the standup consumes the team's time and works against the purpose of a short, focused event. Detailed problem-solving belongs in separate sessions with the people concerned.

options.text: Escalate the issues to the project sponsor to get them solved immediately.
options.rationale: Handing team-level impediments to the sponsor deflects responsibility the project manager holds. Most of these blockers can be cleared without involving anyone outside the team.

questions.explanation: Blockers that go unresolved within an iteration are handled by using the routine built for surfacing them daily, so they are cleared while they are still small. Logging them for later, lengthening the routine, or passing them upward each let the accumulation continue.
questions.mindset: Clear blockers at the cadence they appear, not after they have piled up.

questions.stem: A project manager has a newly formed team that includes junior members who have not worked on agile projects before. The product owner wants to ensure that the team performs as expected in the sprint. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Allocate time to mentor team members on agile processes.
options.rationale: Developing the team's capability is what closes the gap between inexperienced members and what the sprint expects of them. Mentoring makes clear both the expectations and which items they should be working on, which is the servant leadership agile requires.

options.text: Emphasize the importance of sprint backlog prioritization.
options.rationale: Stressing why prioritisation matters does not teach people who have never worked this way how to operate within it. It addresses one topic rather than the underlying inexperience.

options.text: Improve productivity through the use of Scrum techniques.
options.rationale: Applying techniques to a team that does not yet understand them is unlikely to raise performance. The constraint is knowledge, and technique alone does not supply it.

options.text: Communicate project information and updates effectively.
options.rationale: Good information flow is necessary on any project but does not develop capability in people new to the approach. Being well informed is not the same as knowing how to work.

questions.explanation: When a team includes people who have not worked this way before, performance is secured by investing in their development rather than by applying technique, emphasis or information to them. Recognising which activities actually build capability is what separates the right answer from three plausible good practices.
questions.mindset: Build the team's capability before expecting the team's output.

questions.stem: An agile project is in its first of ten iterations. After the iteration review, the team receives stakeholder feedback that the first deliverable is not aligned with the project objectives. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the team to meet with stakeholders to understand their needs.
options.rationale: Gathering more detail from stakeholders matters but is not the first move when the backlog itself may be misaligned. It also routes around the person accountable for what the backlog contains.

options.text: Ask the product owner to review the product backlog and its priorities.
options.rationale: The product owner owns the backlog and its priorities, so misalignment with objectives is theirs to examine and correct. They may need to reprioritise or remove items so the work serves what stakeholders actually need.

options.text: Ask stakeholders to prioritize their needs.
options.rationale: Stakeholders supply input but do not set backlog priority, which is the product owner's accountability. Asking them to prioritise bypasses the role that exists to reconcile competing needs.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to define the stakeholders' priorities.
options.rationale: The sponsor does not determine stakeholder priorities or backlog order. Escalating to them puts the decision with someone who holds neither the accountability nor the detail.

questions.explanation: When delivered work turns out not to serve the objectives, the correction is made where the ordering of work is owned, by the role accountable for it. Going to stakeholders or the sponsor gathers opinion while leaving the mechanism that actually determines what gets built untouched.
questions.mindset: Take a problem about what is being built to whoever owns the order of the work.

questions.stem: A Scrum team is halfway to its release. During the sprint demo, new software is selected by one of the developers and presented to the team. The new software was not planned work but meets the date for the release. Several prioritized features for the next two sprints are disrupted. What actions should the team do to minimize the disruption?

options.text: Work with the product owner on the backlog to introduce the new software.
options.rationale: The backlog is the only source of work for a Scrum team, and only the product owner may reprioritise it. Introducing the new software through the backlog with the product owner is what keeps the disrupted features properly ordered.

options.text: The scrum team makes the decisions themselves as a self-organized team and presents the change during the demo.
options.rationale: Self-organisation governs how the team does its work, not whether it can unilaterally change the product. Presenting a change already decided leaves the product owner with no say over their own backlog.

options.text: The developers reach out to the scrum master regarding the change to determine where and when the change can be discussed.
options.rationale: Involving the scrum master is only partly right, since they facilitate rather than decide product content. The change still has to reach the backlog through the product owner.

options.text: The scrum team evaluates the new software and informs the client about the impact to the release plan
options.rationale: Telling the client about a release impact before the product owner has considered the change presents it as settled. The product owner may well reject the software, making the communication premature and damaging.

questions.explanation: A team's freedom to organise its own work does not extend to deciding what the product contains, which is held by a single accountable role and expressed through one ordered list. Every route that reaches the team, the facilitator or the client without passing through that role changes the product without authority.
questions.mindset: Deciding how you work is not the same as deciding what you build.

questions.stem: During a Scrum board review for a hybrid project, a team member suggests adding a task that is outside of the baseline scope. This task could reduce risk to the project. The team member raises it in the review. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assess the feasibility and impact of including the task and incorporate it into future sprints if appropriate.
options.rationale: A suggestion falling outside the baseline is analysed for what including it would take and what it would affect. Where it proves feasible and beneficial it is folded into later sprints, which keeps the project adaptable without accepting work blindly.

options.text: Instruct the product owner to assess the benefit of the activity toward meeting the project's initial requirements.
options.rationale: Directing the product owner misreads the relationship, since they own backlog content rather than take instruction on it. It also narrows the test to the initial requirements when the value offered is risk reduction.

options.text: Direct the team toward the critical path activity and include the task in the backlog column for later review.
options.rationale: Parking the task without assessment defers a possible risk reduction indefinitely. Redirecting the team treats a useful suggestion as a distraction rather than something to evaluate.

options.text: Document the task in the project documentation, noting may reduce risk but it is outside of the baseline scope.
options.rationale: Recording the idea alongside the observation that it sits outside the baseline effectively declines it while appearing to act. The potential benefit is noted and then never pursued.

questions.explanation: Work proposed from outside an agreed baseline is neither accepted nor dismissed on the spot; it is tested for feasibility and effect, and taken forward into later cycles if it stands up. Parking, documenting or redirecting all reach a verdict by omission on something that has never been examined.
questions.mindset: Evaluate a good idea that arrives late rather than filing it away.

questions.stem: During an iteration, the team spent twice as much time as expected because one of the product backlog items was complex and could not be split into smaller items. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Incorporate an adaptive approach for the rest of the project.
options.rationale: The project is already running iteratively, so this offers a broad change of approach in place of dealing with the specific item. It does not touch the backlog problem that caused the overrun.

options.text: Incorporate a predictive approach for the rest of the project.
options.rationale: Predictive planning leans on historical estimates that this project has just shown to be unreliable. Switching to forecasts would compound the problem rather than contain it.

options.text: Develop a risk management plan for this sprint.
options.rationale: Planning for risk within a sprint that has already overrun addresses an uncertainty after it has materialised. What is needed is a change to how the remaining work is ordered.

options.text: Have the product owner reprioritize the product backlog.
options.rationale: Reprioritising with the product owner addresses the complexity directly and puts the team's remaining effort where it counts most. It is the adaptive, improvement-focused response to an item that consumed twice its estimate.

questions.explanation: A single item that blows its estimate is answered by reordering the work that remains, not by changing the delivery approach or writing a plan for a risk that has already landed. The specific problem gets a specific remedy before anything broader is considered.
questions.mindset: Fix the problem in front of you before reconsidering the whole method.

questions.stem: A project manager receives an email shortly after the beginning of a sprint. It is from a key stakeholder who is unfamiliar with agile methodologies and has a serious complaint about the work that was just started. The stakeholder insists that one deliverable should be changed. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Address the request at the daily standup and ask for the project team's opinion.
options.rationale: The standup exists to check sprint progress and surface the team's own impediments, not to process stakeholder change requests. Putting it there misuses the event and asks the team to weigh something outside its remit.

options.text: Modify the backlog to accommodate the change, and tell the team to start the requested deliverable immediately.
options.rationale: Only the product owner is authorised to change the backlog, so this acts without the necessary authority. It also commits the team mid-sprint on the strength of one email.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the stakeholder and product owner to discuss the request.
options.rationale: Bringing the stakeholder together with the product owner puts the concern in front of the person accountable for the backlog. The discussion both addresses the complaint and gives the stakeholder the context they lack about how the work is ordered.

options.text: Cancel the current sprint, schedule a priority retrospective, and invite the stakeholder to discuss the request.
options.rationale: Cancelling a sprint is a drastic step reserved as a last resort, and nothing here approaches that threshold. It discards committed work over a request that has not yet been discussed.

questions.explanation: A change pressed by a stakeholder is taken to the role accountable for deciding it, with the stakeholder present so the reasoning is heard rather than relayed. Acting on the request directly, routing it to the team, or tearing up the current cycle all respond before the right people have spoken.
questions.mindset: Put the person asking and the person who decides in the same room.

questions.stem: A project manager has been asked to manage an existing complex project. Some goals have already been delivered by the previous project manager. While reviewing the project management plan, the project manager realizes that one of the key deliverables is missing from the project goal. What should the project manager do next to ensure the expected project value is delivered?

options.text: Escalate the issue about the deliverable to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalation is a last resort and creates tension before the project manager has attempted a resolution. The team and other stakeholders should be engaged first.

options.text: Confirm the expected deliverables and rebaseline the project.
options.rationale: Confirming what is genuinely expected and then rebaselining brings the plan back into line with the value the project is meant to deliver. Acting proactively here also builds stakeholder confidence in the new project manager.

options.text: Track the deliverable by reviewing the requirements traceability matrix.
options.rationale: The traceability matrix is useful for tracking but tracking alone does not get a missing deliverable produced. Visibility is not the same as action.

options.text: Use the contingency fund for more resources to complete the missing deliverable.
options.rationale: Committing contingency assumes the scale of the gap before it has been confirmed with anyone. Funding a remedy precedes establishing what the remedy needs to be.

questions.explanation: A gap discovered between what a plan says and what the project is meant to produce is closed by establishing the true set of deliverables and resetting the plan to match. Tracking the gap, funding it or escalating it each leave the plan saying something the project manager already knows to be wrong.
questions.mindset: When the plan and the expectation diverge, correct the plan rather than working around it.

questions.stem: During the final sprint review, the product owner stated that the product does not deliver any value. The project manager believes that the product meets all the provided specifications. The team is confused by the product owner's statement. What should the project manager do when using a hybrid approach?

options.text: Review the project's benefits management plan with the product owner.
options.rationale: That plan sets out how and when the project's benefits arrive and how they are measured, which is the standard the product owner's claim has to be tested against. Reviewing it together establishes whether value is genuinely absent or simply not yet visible.

options.text: Escalate the matter to the executive board so they can decide on next steps.
options.rationale: Taking the dispute upward before examining the agreed measures of value asks the board to adjudicate without evidence. The project manager has not yet done the work that would inform a decision.

options.text: Prioritize the project backlog and ask the development team to fix the issues.
options.rationale: This is the final sprint, so reordering the backlog has little left to act on. It also assumes defects to fix when the disagreement is about worth, not correctness.

options.text: Ask the product owner to terminate the project as it is no longer aligned to the expected benefits.
options.rationale: The product owner cannot terminate a project alone, and doing so at the final review discards everything built. It accepts a claim of no value without testing it.

questions.explanation: A dispute about whether something is worth anything is settled against the agreed definition of its worth, not by escalation, rework or abandonment. Meeting the specification and delivering value are separate tests, and only one artefact records the second.
questions.mindset: When people disagree about value, go back to how value was defined.

questions.stem: An agile project is midway through its ten iteration cycles. During the last iteration, the team had to work overtime to accomplish the goal. In the iteration retrospective, the team agreed that they took more time than planned because they did not have the required experience when they executed the assigned tasks for the first time. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the project sponsor for additional team training.
options.rationale: Training takes time to arrange and deliver and may not change what the team can achieve in the next iteration. The team has now done the work once and may already have what it needs.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to approve a change request for more time in future iterations.
options.rationale: Extending future iterations is unnecessary if the team can now complete the work within the planned timeframe. It locks in an allowance for inexperience the team may have already shed.

options.text: Ask the team to re-assess their effort estimates in the iteration planning session.
options.rationale: Teams learn from each iteration, and the place to act on that learning is the next planning session. Re-estimating tests directly whether the experience gained is now enough to finish within the planned timeframe.

options.text: Ask the product owner to reprioritize the product backlog.
options.rationale: Reordering the backlog changes what the team works on rather than how well it can estimate that work. The overrun came from unfamiliarity, which reprioritisation does not touch.

questions.explanation: An overrun caused by doing something for the first time is often self-correcting, so the response is to let the team re-estimate in its next planning cycle and see. Buying more time or arranging training commits to a remedy for a constraint that may no longer exist.
questions.mindset: Let the team test whether it has already learned the lesson before you fix the problem for it.

questions.stem: A newly appointed product owner is not sure how to prioritize product specifications and mentions this challenge to the project manager. What should the project manager do to assist the product owner?

options.text: Prioritize product backlog for the product owner.
options.rationale: Taking over the prioritisation makes a decision the product owner is accountable for and leaves them no more capable next time. It solves today's problem by creating a dependency.

options.text: Coach the product owner on how to prioritize product specifications.
options.rationale: Coaching builds the missing capability while leaving the decision with the person accountable for it. The project manager acts as an impartial bridge-builder rather than deciding matters that belong to others.

options.text: Request that the product owner becomes trained in agile methods.
options.rationale: Referring them to formal training defers help that the project manager could give directly and immediately. It also treats a specific skill gap as a general education problem.

options.text: Ask project team to prioritize product backlog.
options.rationale: The team does not set backlog priority, so this moves the decision to the wrong place entirely. It leaves the product owner's gap unaddressed while confusing accountability.

questions.explanation: When someone lacks a skill their role requires, the response builds that skill rather than substituting for it or outsourcing it, because the accountability stays with them either way. Doing the work for a colleague is the most tempting wrong answer precisely because it produces a correct outcome once.
questions.mindset: Build the capability rather than making the decision for them.

questions.stem: A project manager has developed a schedule for a project involving various departments. The project manager met with each team member to develop a work breakdown structure (WBS). However, after the WBS was finalized, the project manager discovers that some tasks are redundant. What should the project manager have done to avoid this issue?

options.text: Enlisted subject matter experts (SMEs) to provide scheduling guidance.
options.rationale: SME guidance improves the quality of estimates and sequencing but does not reveal that two departments have described the same work. Expertise on scheduling does not detect duplication across contributors.

options.text: Organized group sessions for all team members to review the WBS together.
options.rationale: Joint planning sessions let team members hear each other's approaches, which is what exposes overlap between departments. Reviewing the breakdown together minimises duplicated activity and raises awareness across the group.

options.text: Improved the communication channels with all team members.
options.rationale: Better channels may help generally but the project manager was already meeting everyone individually. The defect came from the one-to-one structure, not from the quality of the connection.

options.text: Prepared a task assignment matrix to represent the WBS.
options.rationale: A matrix records who is responsible for what once the breakdown exists. It formats the result rather than preventing the duplication that got into it.

questions.explanation: Decomposing work through a series of private conversations guarantees that nobody sees the whole, which is how the same activity ends up recorded twice. Planning done jointly surfaces overlap in the moment, and no amount of expertise, formatting or channel improvement substitutes for contributors hearing one another.
questions.mindset: Plan in the same room if you want people to see each other's work.

questions.stem: A company has hired a project manager to implement an adaptive project framework. The project has made some progress, but the team is frustrated because the client does not provide feedback or participate in defining acceptance criteria. What could have caused this situation?

options.text: The development team has no experience in managing an adaptive project.
options.rationale: The team's own experience does not determine whether the client turns up to give feedback. The absence described is on the client's side.

options.text: The client plans to implement the project and does not need to participate.
options.rationale: Intending to implement the result makes a client's involvement more necessary, not less. This reverses the relationship between ownership and engagement.

options.text: The client does not understand the importance of their involvement.
options.rationale: Adaptive work depends on a dynamic, co-creative exchange because requirements carry high uncertainty and change as the product emerges. A client who has not grasped that their ongoing input is the mechanism will not supply it.

options.text: The development team has not produced a complete prototype
options.rationale: Adaptive delivery invites feedback on increments rather than waiting for a complete prototype. Requiring one before engagement misstates how the framework works.

questions.explanation: Adaptive delivery makes the customer part of the production process rather than its audience, so when their input is missing the usual cause is that nobody established why it is structurally required. Explanations that look to the team's skill or the maturity of the product miss that the obligation being unmet is the client's.
questions.mindset: If you need someone's participation, make sure they know why it is not optional.

questions.stem: A virtual team is midway through a sprint of a complex task and is ahead of schedule. During the daily standup, a new team member interrupts and asks everyone to describe what they worked on prior to the current sprint. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Thank the new team member for their interest and direct them to the project documentation.
options.rationale: Pointing someone unfamiliar with the project at documentation they do not know how to navigate is not real help. It closes the request without meeting the need behind it.

options.text: Explain to the new team member that the daily standup is not the best time for this discussion.
options.rationale: Saying so politely protects the focus and brevity the standup depends on without dismissing the person. The project manager can then arrange a separate time to cover prior work and help them get up to speed.

options.text: Request the new team member leave the meeting for interrupting the daily standup.
options.rationale: Ejecting someone for asking a reasonable question is disproportionate and damages team morale. It punishes unfamiliarity with the format rather than correcting it.

options.text: Ask all team members to list their completed tasks prior to the current sprint.
options.rationale: Turning the standup into a history session consumes the whole team's time for one person's benefit. The event is not designed to carry that content.

questions.explanation: A reasonable request made in the wrong forum is redirected rather than granted or refused, so the meeting keeps its purpose and the person still gets an answer. Harsh correction and quiet deflection both resolve the interruption at the cost of the newcomer.
questions.mindset: Protect the meeting's purpose without making the person feel unwelcome.

questions.stem: During a retrospective meeting, some team members expressed that they strongly disagree with how the product owner and scrum master handled some issues related to the scope of the last cycle. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Review the backlog with the product owner to ensure the scope is appropriate.
options.rationale: Examining the backlog treats the disagreement as a scope question when it is about how the issues were handled. It also acts before the project manager understands what happened.

options.text: Collect all available information from the team and address the problem.
options.rationale: Resolving conflict starts with gathering the full picture from the team, studying the problem and setting an appropriate climate for working it through. Including everyone involved is what makes the resolution safe and respectful.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with the specific team members to discuss the issue.
options.rationale: Speaking only to those who complained collects one side of a dispute and can harden positions. A conflict is understood by including everyone involved, not by sequencing private conversations.

options.text: Discuss the team's concerns with the product owner and the scrum master.
options.rationale: Going to the other parties before understanding the concern risks relaying an account the project manager has not verified. It also moves to resolution before the root cause is clear.

questions.explanation: Conflict is worked from a complete understanding of what happened, gathered from everyone involved, before any move toward a remedy. Approaching one side first feels responsive but produces a partial account that shapes everything after it.
questions.mindset: Understand the whole of a disagreement before you begin resolving any of it.

questions.stem: The project scope statement is approved by the project sponsor. The team members would like to modify the work breakdown structure (WBS) without changing the scope and send a request to the project manager. What should the project manager do with this request?

options.text: Determine which changes to implement and inform the team.
options.rationale: Deciding alone and announcing the outcome excludes the people who raised the request and know the work. Unilateral decisions demotivate a team whose views have not been considered.

options.text: Refuse the request and escalate it to the project sponsor.
options.rationale: Escalating a matter that changes no approved scope is non-collaborative and unnecessary. It hands the sponsor a decision the team and project manager can make together.

options.text: Tell the team that they cannot modify the established WBS.
options.rationale: A flat refusal treats the breakdown as fixed when the scope itself is unaffected. It denies the team any say over how its own work is organised.

options.text: Discuss it with the team and make a decision by consensus.
options.rationale: Working it through together empowers the team to own and shape its working environment, which is where the request originated. Team members who can decide how they work perform better, and engaging them signals trust in their judgement.

questions.explanation: Where a proposed change leaves the approved scope untouched, the decision belongs with the people doing the work and is best reached together. Deciding for them, refusing outright or passing it upward each take ownership away from a team that was trying to improve how it works.
questions.mindset: Let the team decide how it organises its own work.

questions.stem: A project team realizes that the product's architecture will not support the growing number of users. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Assign a team member to execute performance testing and ensure the product's performance is acceptable.
options.rationale: Testing confirms a limitation the team has already identified and surfaces it again later rather than resolving it. It spends effort measuring a gap instead of closing it.

options.text: Hire external experts to assess the product architecture and come up with a resolution plan.
options.rationale: Bringing in outside expertise is premature and may be neither budgeted nor approved. The information has not yet reached the person who decides what the team works on.

options.text: Engage with the product owner on the new development and prioritize the solution on the product backlog.
options.rationale: Sharing this with the product owner lets business stakeholders weigh in on value and lets the backlog be reordered to reflect it. That sequence gets company, team and stakeholder concerns addressed before work begins.

options.text: Negotiate with the stakeholders to slow down product development until a viable solution is available.
options.rationale: Slowing development may not be feasible and concedes delivery pace before any solution has been considered. It responds to the problem by stopping rather than by resolving.

questions.explanation: A technical constraint that threatens the product is first routed to whoever decides the order of work, so the response can be weighed for value alongside everything else competing for the team's time. Testing it further, buying expertise or slowing delivery all commit resource before that judgement has been made.
questions.mindset: Surface a serious constraint to the decision-maker before choosing how to attack it.

questions.stem: A customer reviewed a product and requested additional features that were not in the requirements documentation. The work-in-progress (WIP) limits have already been optimized for the teams working on different work components. How should the project manager begin to resolve the customer requirements?

options.text: Build the product according to the previously agreed customer requirements.
options.rationale: Proceeding as though the request had not been made ignores the customer and runs against agile practice. Responding to change is not optional because a requirement was documented earlier.

options.text: Discuss the feasibility and impact of the new features with the product owner.
options.rationale: The product owner is accountable for maximising the product's value and for the end product, so feasibility and impact are assessed with them. That discussion covers the effect on budget and team availability, after which the work can be prioritised into the backlog.

options.text: Breakdown work on additional features with existing component teams.
options.rationale: Decomposing the features starts the work before anyone has agreed to take it on. It also pushes against WIP limits that were deliberately optimised.

options.text: Release increments of the additional features for customer validation.
options.rationale: Producing increments of unapproved features commits team capacity to work that has not been assessed. Validation with the customer comes long after the decision to build.

questions.explanation: A new customer request is neither refused on the strength of earlier documentation nor started on the strength of the customer's enthusiasm; it is assessed with the role accountable for the product's value. Beginning delivery is the subtler error because it looks responsive while bypassing the judgement that should precede it.
questions.mindset: Assess new work with whoever is accountable for the product before touching capacity.

questions.stem: During sprint planning, an agile team and product owner identified that the team should be able to finish five user stories. However, during the sprint, the team worked on more than five stories but did not complete any stories at all. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Clarify priorities with the team.
options.rationale: Taking on extra stories and finishing none points to a gap between the team's understanding of priority and the actual priorities for the sprint. Clarifying that alignment addresses the root cause and refocuses the team on delivering what matters most first.

options.text: Create smaller stories in the future.
options.rationale: Smaller stories may help eventually but the team did not fail on size, it failed on spreading itself across too much work. Resizing without addressing focus leaves the same behaviour in place.

options.text: Review the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: The definition of done is a checklist of criteria for completion and is not why nothing was completed. Revisiting it addresses the standard rather than the scattered effort.

options.text: Update the product release plan.
options.rationale: Adjusting the release plan accepts the shortfall and re-plans around it. It responds to the consequence without touching what produced it.

questions.explanation: A team that starts more work than it agreed and finishes none has a focus problem rather than a sizing or standards problem, so the remedy is to re-establish what matters most first. Resizing the work or re-planning around the shortfall both treat symptoms while leaving the misalignment that caused it intact.
questions.mindset: When everything was started and nothing finished, fix the ordering before the sizing.

questions.stem: A project manager is planning for a complex project that must deliver a high-quality product within the agreed-upon budget. The project stakeholders are eager to see the product launched and are pressuring the team to deliver the product as soon as possible. The project manager must determine the project's estimated duration and address stakeholder expectations. How should the project manager determine a realistic project duration estimate?

options.text: Confirm stakeholder delivery expectations.
options.rationale: What stakeholders want is an input to managing expectations, not a method of estimating. Building a duration from their preferences produces the date they asked for rather than a realistic one.

options.text: Estimate the duration of each project task.
options.rationale: Estimating at task level builds the duration from the work that actually has to be done, which is what makes the resulting timeline realistic. It also exposes roadblocks and dependencies that a top-down figure would hide.

options.text: Analyze industry benchmarks and standards.
options.rationale: Benchmarks compare an organization's performance against peers and competitors rather than measuring this project's work. They give a reference point, not an estimate of these tasks.

options.text: Tell the team to create a detailed release plan.
options.rationale: A release plan sequences and presents work that has already been estimated, giving a false sense of precision when the underlying durations are unknown. The estimate has to exist before the plan can mean anything.

questions.explanation: A credible timeline is assembled from the work itself rather than inherited from what stakeholders hope for, what peers achieve, or how confidently it is presented. Pressure to commit early is precisely when bottom-up estimating matters most, because it is the only one of these that can contradict the expectation.
questions.mindset: Build the date from the work, not from the pressure to name a date.

questions.stem: At a review meeting, the project manager learns about unclear requirements that may impact the project's scheduled completion. The project sponsor still wants to meet the original deadline. How should the project manager approach the issue using agile practices?

options.text: Use iterative delivery and prioritize the requirements based on their importance and impact.
options.rationale: Ordering by importance and impact lets the project keep moving while the unclear areas resolve themselves over successive iterations. It serves the sponsor's deadline without pretending the ambiguity has been removed.

options.text: Inform the sponsor that a change request for scope will be added to the next iteration.
options.rationale: This does nothing about the unclear requirements themselves and defers action to the next cycle. There may not be enough time left for that deferral to work.

options.text: Log unclear scope as an issue and escalate it to the product owner for a decision on unclear requirements.
options.rationale: Logging and escalating hands the ambiguity to someone else instead of adopting a way of working that tolerates it. The project manager has an approach available that does not require a decision first.

options.text: Request that the scrum master clarify the scope before continuing the project.
options.rationale: The scrum master facilitates and does not own scope clarification. Halting until clarity arrives also puts the deadline the sponsor cares about at risk.

questions.explanation: Ambiguity in requirements is not a reason to stop, escalate or defer when the delivery approach allows work to be ordered so that the clearest and most valuable parts proceed while the rest settles. The mistake is treating uncertainty as a blocker to be cleared before work continues.
questions.mindset: Order the work so uncertainty can resolve while you deliver, rather than waiting for it to resolve first.

questions.stem: Due to market changes, a company decided to speed up its product release schedule, moving from yearly cycles to quarterly cycles. The project manager views this as an excellent opportunity to use an agile life cycle, but upper management is not sold on the idea. What should the project manager do to increase the chances of success by using this approach?

options.text: Seek the project sponsor's approval for additional budget and resources.
options.rationale: Asking for more funding before management is convinced of the approach argues from cost rather than from benefit. It also implies the method needs extra resource to work, which weakens the case.

options.text: Review the product backlog to identify some quick wins to present to stakeholders.
options.rationale: Early benefit realisation is one of the strongest arguments for the approach and speaks directly to management's doubt. Demonstrating tangible early value is a motivational strategy, which is what overcomes resistance to change.

options.text: Invite upper management to attend a digital transformation workshop.
options.rationale: A workshop offers general education where the doubt is specific to this approach on this project. Unconvinced executives are unlikely to invest a day before they see a reason to.

options.text: Have the project team work virtually and use the cost savings to speed up delivery.
options.rationale: Changing where the team works is unrelated to whether management accepts the delivery approach. It also pursues speed through savings rather than making the case that was actually asked for.

questions.explanation: Resistance to a new way of working is overcome by showing benefit early rather than by argument, education or resource, because effective change management is motivational rather than forceful. Communicating what the change will deliver, and then proving part of it quickly, is what earns buy-in from people who start unconvinced.
questions.mindset: Convince sceptics by showing them something working, not by explaining why it would.

questions.stem: A project team is in the planning phase of a complex project. The project has an end-date constraint to launch a new product with which they have no previous experience. The project sponsor is requesting a detailed schedule, but the team is unable to predict when tasks will occur throughout the project lifecycle, especially because some of them are dependent on deliverables by other business units. What life cycle methodology should the project manager use in this situation?

options.text: A hybrid life cycle including a prioritized product backlog approved by the sponsor
options.rationale: A hybrid approach combines predictive and adaptive elements, which suits work that carries real uncertainty around requirements but must still land on a fixed date. Prioritising the deliverables in a backlog with the sponsor gives them the visibility they want without demanding predictions the team cannot make.

options.text: A predictive life cycle including a schedule in agreement with all business units
options.rationale: A fully predictive schedule requires the team to commit to timings it has already said it cannot forecast. Agreement between business units does not manufacture the certainty the approach depends on.

options.text: An agile life cycle including a detailed schedule in agreement with all business units
options.rationale: This pairs an adaptive life cycle with the detailed schedule that adaptive working is meant to avoid, which is internally inconsistent. The fixed end date also needs more structure than a purely agile approach supplies.

options.text: An iterative life cycle including task durations and a budget approved by the sponsor
options.rationale: Committing task durations upfront contradicts the very uncertainty that makes an iterative approach attractive here. It asks for the same predictions the team cannot give.

questions.explanation: When requirements are uncertain but a delivery date is fixed, the approach has to carry both properties at once, which is exactly what combining predictive and adaptive elements provides. Distractors typically pair the right life cycle with an artefact that contradicts it, so check the whole option rather than the life cycle it names.
questions.mindset: Fit the approach to both constraints, not just the one that is easiest to satisfy.

questions.stem: A project manager works in an organization using a hybrid project delivery approach. The scope of the project is to implement a new human resources system. The infrastructure will be delivered by another project, and both projects are part of a business transformation program aimed to improve human resources processes. The project schedule needs to be finalized, but the project manager of the other project is unable to provide delivery dates for the infrastructure. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Wait for the infrastructure project to have a schedule and then develop the human resources system project's schedule.
options.rationale: Waiting stalls this project on another's timetable when the programme already provides milestones to plan against. It treats one missing input as though nothing else were available.

options.text: Discuss the situation with the other project manager, agree on a few milestones, and then continue working on the human resources system project's schedule.
options.rationale: Two project managers agreeing milestones between themselves bypasses the programme that sets them. It also excludes the programme manager, who is a key stakeholder in this dependency.

options.text: Develop a schedule based on the information available from the program management team and then progressively align the milestones with the infrastructure project.
options.rationale: Programme milestones are established and must be followed, so the schedule is built against those and refined as the dependency firms up. This keeps both projects aligned to the programme rather than to each other's guesswork.

options.text: Develop a schedule based on the information available and ask the other project manager to align the infrastructure milestones with the human resources project's delivery dates.
options.rationale: Asking the other project to conform to this one's dates inverts the dependency and ignores programme-level priorities. Neither project manager has the standing to subordinate the other.

questions.explanation: A project inside a programme plans against programme-level milestones, which exist precisely so that interdependent projects are not left negotiating timings with each other. Waiting for a sibling project or striking a private agreement with it both route around the governance layer that owns the dependency.
questions.mindset: When projects depend on each other, plan against the level that governs them both.

questions.stem: An agile project team is building a website for a client. The client informs the product owner that their company has decided to release the website one month ahead of schedule, in order to take advantage of a business opportunity. What should the project manager have the team do?

options.text: Commit additional resources to complete work a month in advance.
options.rationale: Adding resource presumes a solution before the team has judged what the new date actually requires. Whether it helps depends on the team's own assessment of risk and action.

options.text: Meet as a group to assess what is possible to complete by the new timelines.
options.rationale: The team is best placed to judge whether earlier delivery is achievable and what would have to give. Assessing together produces a grounded answer for the client rather than a guess in either direction.

options.text: Tell the client it is not possible to release the website this early.
options.rationale: Refusing before any assessment discards a business opportunity on an assumption. The team has not yet looked at what could be delivered by the new date.

options.text: Conduct a retrospective meeting to understand how they could have worked faster.
options.rationale: A retrospective examines past working and does not answer the live question about the new date. It spends the team's time looking backwards while a decision waits.

questions.explanation: A request to move a delivery date is answered by the people who would have to meet it, working out together what is genuinely achievable. Accepting by adding resource and refusing outright are both answers given before that assessment, and they are wrong in the same way despite pointing in opposite directions.
questions.mindset: Let the people doing the work say what is possible before you answer for them.

questions.stem: A team member is unable to work for one week because of sick leave. The team member is currently assigned to a task on the critical path. What is the next step the project manager should take?

options.text: Choose another team member to take over the task immediately.
options.rationale: Substituting someone without a proper handover can do more harm than the absence itself. It also commits a resource before anyone knows whether the schedule can absorb the week.

options.text: Evaluate the possible impacts of a project delay.
options.rationale: Establishing the effect on cost, time and the other constraints is what tells the project manager whether any response is needed. Every sensible option depends on knowing the size of the impact first.

options.text: Refer to the risk response plan to mitigate this issue.
options.rationale: Applying a planned response presumes the impact is already understood and matches what was anticipated. An issue cannot be mitigated before it has been evaluated.

options.text: Convince the team member to proceed with completing the task.
options.rationale: Pressing someone on sick leave to work is neither appropriate nor reliable. It treats a person's health as a schedule variable.

questions.explanation: An absence touching the critical path is assessed for its actual effect before any remedy is applied, because the right response depends entirely on how much float and consequence exist. Reaching for a substitute or a pre-planned response feels decisive but acts on an impact nobody has measured.
questions.mindset: Measure the impact before you choose the remedy, even on the critical path.

questions.stem: An agile project team member is working on a user story that is overdue. This delay is causing the team to miss sprint goals for a specific functionality. The reasons for this delay are unknown to the project manager. What should be project manager do first?

options.text: Discuss the delay with the team member.
options.rationale: The reasons are unknown, and the person doing the work is the direct source of them. Understanding the root cause is what makes any subsequent plan effective, and it gives the team member the chance to explain.

options.text: Request additional resources from the sponsor.
options.rationale: Asking for more people addresses a capacity problem that has not been shown to exist. The cause of the delay is still unknown, so the remedy is a guess.

options.text: Exclude this functionality in the final product.
options.rationale: Dropping functionality is a drastic last resort taken here without any understanding of the delay. Everything possible should be done to complete the story first.

options.text: Replace the project team member with a new developer
options.rationale: Replacing someone before asking why they are behind is both drastic and unfair. It also loses whatever progress and context that person holds.

questions.explanation: When the cause of a delay is unknown, the first move is to ask the person closest to it, because every response worth taking depends on what the answer turns out to be. Adding resource, cutting scope or replacing people are all remedies selected for a problem that has not yet been identified.
questions.mindset: Ask the person doing the work before deciding what is wrong with it.

questions.stem: An organization is trying to adopt agile approaches to execute projects for their customers. During project planning, the product owner proposed that any release to the customer should be approved by the legal department before it is shipped. The development team is disappointed as it may potentially delay releases and the delivery schedule. Since other departments in the organization do not use agile, what should the project manager's role be as a servant leader?

options.text: Advise senior management to introduce agile techniques to all departments to ensure seamless services to customers.
options.rationale: Organisation-wide adoption is a long and complex initiative that will not resolve this project's release problem. It answers a local obstacle with a transformation programme.

options.text: Continue with standardized organizational procedures to ensure compliance with policies and avoid creating problems.
options.rationale: Accepting the existing process unchanged ignores the delay the team has identified and is not proactive. Compliance can be maintained while the process is examined.

options.text: Inform the customer about the organizational procedures and ask them to discuss this with the organization's leadership.
options.rationale: Asking the customer to take up an internal process matter pushes an internal problem outside the organization. It is not the customer's role to negotiate how their supplier works.

options.text: Work with the legal department and other applicable departments to review the processes that support the project delivery.
options.rationale: Reviewing the supporting processes with the departments involved is how legal requirements are met while delay is minimised. Facilitating that collaboration between functions is precisely the servant leader's contribution here.

questions.explanation: Where a project's delivery pace collides with a function that works differently, the resolution is negotiated directly with that function rather than escalated, accepted or exported. Neither wholesale organisational change nor passive compliance addresses the specific interface that is causing the friction.
questions.mindset: Work the interface with the function that owns it rather than changing the organisation or giving up.

questions.stem: A project manager has a new project. The work breakdown structure (WBS) and sequence of activities have been defined, but the team has difficulty estimating the duration of each activity. Which approach should the project manager take to ensure the estimates are reliable?

options.text: Ask each team member to estimate the duration of each activity.
options.rationale: Asking everyone to estimate everything is only effective where every member has the relevant expertise, which is not the case here. Bottom-up estimating is not reliable when the team has already shown it cannot judge these durations.

options.text: Consider the project schedule constraints and estimate the activities accordingly.
options.rationale: Working backwards from constraints produces durations that fit the deadline rather than the work. It manufactures an estimate instead of deriving one.

options.text: Access performance records of similar, past projects and use them as a reference.
options.rationale: Records of comparable past work give an evidence base the team currently lacks. Using actual performance from similar projects as a reference is what makes the resulting estimates reliable.

options.text: Consult other project managers for the duration estimate of each activity.
options.rationale: Other project managers offer opinion where documented performance data is available. Recollection is a weaker basis than the organization's own records.

questions.explanation: When a team cannot estimate from its own knowledge, reliability comes from what comparable work has actually taken, held in the organization's records. Polling colleagues, canvassing the team more widely, or reasoning from the deadline each substitute judgement or convenience for evidence.
questions.mindset: When judgement is thin, reach for recorded evidence rather than more opinions.

questions.stem: During the first few days of executing a six-week project, an impediment is discovered by the project team. The project manager worked with the team to develop and implement a strategy to resolve the issue. Afterward, the project manager discovers that, as a result, the project can now be completed in only three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Work with stakeholders to determine the best course of action.
options.rationale: Alignment between the project and its stakeholders matters, and this discovery is theirs to know about. Being transparent gives them the information they need to decide how the saved time should be used.

options.text: Change the project scope to include additional deliverables.
options.rationale: Adding deliverables introduces risk and is a decision taken without the stakeholders who would receive them. It should only follow a discussion, not precede one.

options.text: Maintain the original six-week timeline and milestone schedule.
options.rationale: Holding to the old schedule conceals a real benefit and wastes resources for three weeks. Stakeholders are denied a decision they are entitled to make.

options.text: Reallocate the team to other projects to maximize efficiency.
options.rationale: Moving the team elsewhere commits the freed capacity before anyone has agreed that is the best use of it. Like adding scope, it introduces risk and should follow discussion.

questions.explanation: Good news that changes the shape of a project is disclosed to stakeholders so they can direct what happens with it, rather than absorbed quietly or spent on the project manager's own judgement. The instinct to put the windfall to use immediately is the error, whichever direction it points.
questions.mindset: Surface a change in the picture to the people entitled to decide what to do with it.

questions.stem: A project team member informs the project manager that all items are complete and the team is ready to move on to the next iteration. The project manager reviews the iteration board and notices incomplete items. The iteration ends today, and the missed items will not be completed on time. What should the project manager have done to ensure that all of the iteration backlog items were completed on time?

options.text: Validated iteration backlog items using the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: The definition of done lists the criteria an item must meet before it counts as ready for customer use. Validating against it regularly through the iteration surfaces incomplete work early instead of on the final day.

options.text: Scheduled longer delivery timelines for project iteration cycles.
options.rationale: Longer iterations may be neither feasible nor practical and do not address why completion was misreported. Extending the timebox postpones the same discovery.

options.text: Requested that the team reports progress during daily standups.
options.rationale: Self-reported progress is what went wrong here, since a team member described incomplete work as finished. More frequent reporting without an agreed standard repeats the error daily.

options.text: Asked team members to demo their work as soon as it was ready.
options.rationale: Demonstrating work once someone judges it ready still relies on that individual judgement. It does not test the item against the agreed completion criteria.

questions.explanation: Disagreement about whether work is finished is prevented by checking it against an agreed, explicit standard during the cycle, not by more reporting or more time. Progress reports and demonstrations both depend on the same individual judgement that produced the false claim of completion.
questions.mindset: Test completion against the agreed standard, not against whoever says it is finished.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a deployment project to replace some equipment that will soon become obsolete. A review of the schedule and cost has revealed that a 5-month delay is likely. How should the project manager address risks from the delay?

options.text: Analyze the business impact in order to reprioritize the deliverables.
options.rationale: Risks from the delay have to be analysed before responses can be planned, and business impact is what determines their importance. That analysis is what lets the deliverables be categorised and reordered sensibly.

options.text: Request to negotiate with the vendors for a longer support period.
options.rationale: Extending vendor support treats one consequence of the delay as though it were the whole risk picture. It is a reaction chosen before any analysis.

options.text: Ask to order new equipment immediately so there will be no support issue.
options.rationale: Ordering equipment commits cost against an unanalysed risk and may not address the delay at all. It acts on urgency rather than on assessment.

options.text: Acknowledge these constraints and take them into account when planning.
options.rationale: Noting the constraints and planning around them accepts the delay without examining what it threatens. Acknowledgement is not a risk response.

questions.explanation: Risks arising from a delay are first analysed for their effect on the organization, because that analysis is what ranks them and shapes any response. Immediate countermeasures and passive acceptance both skip the step that would tell you whether they were the right choice.
questions.mindset: Analyse what a delay threatens before you act on any part of it.

questions.stem: A project is facing a one-month delay, and the project manager realizes that a change request is necessary. The change control board (CCB) will review the change request at their next meeting, which is in two weeks. However, if the implementation of this change is delayed by two weeks, upcoming supply chain disruptions will cause a two-month delay to the project schedule. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Implement the change immediately to avoid the upcoming supply chain disruptions and the two-month delay.
options.rationale: Acting before approval bypasses the change process entirely, however good the reason appears. Urgency does not transfer decision authority to the project manager.

options.text: Revise the change request to incorporate the additional two-month delay due to upcoming supply chain disruptions.
options.rationale: Putting the supply chain consequence into the request gives the board everything it needs to decide with full knowledge of what waiting costs. Communicating the revised request to stakeholders also ensures everyone is prepared for the extended timeline.

options.text: Meet with the sponsor and ask them to contact the CCB and request their immediate approval.
options.rationale: Using the sponsor to press the board for an expedited decision applies pressure in place of information. It seeks to shortcut the established process rather than inform it.

options.text: Request that the CEO approve and implement the change to avoid the potential two-month delay.
options.rationale: Going to the chief executive routes around the body that holds this authority. Seniority is not a substitute for the correct approval route.

questions.explanation: When the cost of waiting for a decision is itself significant, that cost becomes part of what the decision-makers are told, not a justification for going around them. The subtle failure mode is pressuring or escalating past the authority, which looks more responsible than acting unilaterally but undermines the same control.
questions.mindset: If waiting is expensive, put the price of waiting in front of the people deciding.

questions.stem: A company is expanding its product manufacturing to a new country. The date the company will start operating is set and broadly communicated, but the project team is not sure if there is enough time to get all the product features implemented. What should the project manager do to ensure there is enough time to implement the critical features on the committed date?

options.text: Add resources to the project team, as this will increase the velocity and enable the team to deliver more value.
options.rationale: Adding people may not be feasible, is not guaranteed to raise throughput, and introduces complexity of its own. It assumes capacity is the constraint before anything has been sized.

options.text: Collaborate with the project team to estimate the size of the minimum viable product (MVP) functionalities.
options.rationale: Working with the team to size the minimum viable set establishes what the critical features actually require against a fixed date. That estimate is the input every subsequent decision depends on.

options.text: Cut operations documentation because this can be completed after product delivery and operation starts.
options.rationale: Removing documentation to buy time leaves the operation insufficiently supported when it goes live. It sacrifices something needed rather than establishing what is critical.

options.text: Escalate the concern to the executive level and request a new and feasible project due date.
options.rationale: The date is set and broadly communicated, and escalation is a last resort. Asking to move it precedes any attempt to establish what can be achieved by it.

questions.explanation: Against an immovable date the first task is to size the smallest set of functionality that would count as success, because only that tells you whether a problem exists and how large it is. Adding people, cutting corners or moving the date are all responses chosen before that sizing.
questions.mindset: Work out the smallest thing that would succeed before deciding you cannot succeed.

questions.stem: A project manager is required to obtain approval for project requirements before proceeding to the delivery stage. During the project's execution, the project manager realizes that the initial estimates were unrealistic and the project will take much longer to complete. The project manager will have to obtain approval for more realistic project requirements. What should the project manager do to mitigate the problem and keep the project on track while waiting for approval?

options.text: Reprioritize project deliverables to enable phased delivery in increments.
options.rationale: Breaking the work down and reordering it lets the project keep producing tangible results while approval is pending. High-priority components go first, with the rest added as the revised estimates are confirmed.

options.text: Divide the project team into distinct units focusing on different components.
options.rationale: Splitting the team complicates communication, coordination and knowledge sharing without making anything deliverable sooner. It may well have an adverse effect on progress.

options.text: Survey the project team to see if anyone can work overtime to meet the deadline.
options.rationale: Overtime attempts to close an estimating gap through effort, which is neither sustainable nor sufficient when the underlying estimates were wrong. It also does nothing while approval is outstanding.

options.text: Update the schedule baseline so that it is based on realistic estimates.
options.rationale: Baselines are changed through approval, which is precisely what is still being waited for. Updating it now pre-empts the decision.

questions.explanation: While a decision is pending, the way to keep a project moving is to restructure delivery so the most valuable parts complete first, rather than to pre-empt the decision or push harder on the same plan. Waiting is not the same as being stuck, provided the work can be reordered into something deliverable now.
questions.mindset: While you wait for a decision, deliver what does not depend on it.

questions.stem: Part of a project has already been delivered as planned and on schedule. However, unclear requirements for some of the remaining requirements may negatively impact the scheduled completion. How should the project manager approach the issue?

options.text: Prioritize the most important features and clarify the vague requirements.
options.rationale: Ordering by importance protects the deadline as far as possible while the ambiguity is resolved in parallel. It delivers what matters most rather than stalling on what is unclear.

options.text: Initiate a change request for project sponsor approval for a scope change.
options.rationale: Changing scope is considered after other measures have been tried, not as the opening move. Nothing yet establishes that the scope itself needs to change.

options.text: Record the issue and escalate it to the steering committee for a decision.
options.rationale: Escalation to the steering committee is a last resort once other options are exhausted. The project manager has actions available that have not been attempted.

options.text: Acquire additional resources to complete all of the requirements on time.
options.rationale: More people cannot resolve requirements that nobody has yet clarified, and the addition carries budget and timeline consequences. It answers an ambiguity problem with capacity.

questions.explanation: Vague requirements threatening a date are handled by ordering the work so the important and well-understood parts proceed while clarification happens alongside. Changing scope, escalating or adding resource all reach outside the project for a remedy that ordering and clarification can supply from within it.
questions.mindset: Deliver what is clear and important while you resolve what is not.

questions.stem: An agile project manager is overseeing a Kanban project and wants to assess task completion roadblocks for an upcoming major milestone. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Create a performance metric using the work in progress limit.
options.rationale: A metric built on WIP limits shows that flow is constrained without revealing which items are blocked or why. It measures the symptom rather than exposing the causes.

options.text: Ask a trusted team member about the issues the team is facing.
options.rationale: One person's view is unlikely to capture every roadblock and excludes the rest of the team. It gathers a partial picture where a complete one is available.

options.text: Review the blocked items with the team during standup meetings.
options.rationale: The board exists to make bottlenecks and overcommitment visible, and the standup is where the team examines them together. That is where obstacles already encountered or anticipated get named before they threaten the milestone.

options.text: Host a stakeholder meeting to discuss task completion roadblocks.
options.rationale: Stakeholders are not the ones encountering the blockers and cannot identify them. The information sits with the team, not outside it.

questions.explanation: Obstacles to flow are found by examining the work-in-progress board with the whole team at its regular cadence, which is what those tools were built to expose. Metrics, individual conversations and stakeholder forums each look at the problem from further away than the people and the board already sitting in front of you.
questions.mindset: Look for blockers where the work is visible and the whole team is present.

questions.stem: A new project manager is assigned to an ongoing agile project. The project is now starting its second 4-week iteration cycle. The project manager finds there are significant differences of opinion within the project team, leading to major setbacks for the project. What should the project manager do in order to help overcome differences and bring the project back on track?

options.text: Promote conversation among team members in upcoming review meetings to help solve the problem.
options.rationale: Conflict is an inevitable consequence of team interaction and calls for a proactive response from the project manager. Servant leaders promote collaboration and conversation within and between teams, which is what builds the understanding needed to resolve the differences.

options.text: Schedule a team out activity to allow people to know each other better and feel comfortable talking.
options.rationale: A social event may improve familiarity but does not engage with the substance of the disagreement. It leaves the setbacks unaddressed while appearing supportive.

options.text: Allow the team to self-organize before the next iteration to solve the problem.
options.rationale: Standing back from a conflict already causing major setbacks is not proactive involvement. Self-organisation does not mean the project manager withdraws from conflict resolution.

options.text: Reach out to their functional managers so they can talk to the team members and solve the problem.
options.rationale: Delegating the conflict to functional managers removes the project manager from a responsibility they hold. It also brings in outsiders to a dispute inside the team.

questions.explanation: Disagreement within a team is worked through by the project manager actively facilitating conversation, since that is how understanding and cohesion are rebuilt. Social remedies, delegation upward and stepping back all leave the project manager outside a problem they should be helping the team through.
questions.mindset: Facilitate the conversation yourself rather than hoping distance or goodwill will settle it.

questions.stem: A new program manager checks the status of a project. The forecast shows the project is slightly behind schedule. However, in reporting, the project manager stated that the project is on track. The program manager asks the project manager to explain the discrepancy. The project manager explains that the forecast discrepancy is due to a new estimation technique. What should the project manager have done to avoid this discrepancy?

options.text: Asked the program manager to use the old forecasting technique
options.rationale: Requiring a stakeholder to adopt a superseded method solves the mismatch by abandoning the improvement. It also asks the reader of the report to accommodate the reporter.

options.text: Educated the program manager on the new forecasting technique
options.rationale: Explaining the technique does not fix artefacts that still express the old basis of forecasting. The program manager would understand the method while reading figures built on something else.

options.text: Aligned the project artifacts with the new estimation technique and provided them to the program manager
options.rationale: The project manager changed the technique without updating the basis of forecasting, which is what produced two incompatible readings of the same project. Aligning the artefacts and sharing them would have given consistent and accurate information to assess status against.

options.text: Ensured that the program manager has the necessary knowledge to understand estimation techniques
options.rationale: Treating the discrepancy as a gap in the reader's knowledge misplaces the responsibility. The inconsistency lies in the project's own records, not in the audience.

questions.explanation: Changing how something is estimated obliges you to update the artefacts that express the old basis, or the same project will read two ways to two people. Explaining the new method or asking others to adapt leaves the underlying documents contradicting the reporting built on them.
questions.mindset: Change the method and the records together, or the records will argue with you.

questions.stem: A project manager is responsible for a 12-month waterfall project to create a new product. The project is nine months into execution when the customer suggests using a new technology becomes available that would reduce the project costs by 10%. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the configuration management plan to include the new technology as part of the design.
options.rationale: Amending the plan assumes the technology is feasible and that the change will be approved, neither of which has been established. It records an outcome before the evaluation that would produce it.

options.text: Continue working as planned since the new technology was not part of the project management plan.
options.rationale: Dismissing the suggestion because it was not in the original plan ignores a customer proposal that may carry real benefit. Absence from the plan is a reason to evaluate, not a reason to refuse.

options.text: Create a change request to evaluate the feasibility and impact of using the new technology.
options.rationale: A change request gives the suggestion a structured evaluation of how the technology would affect the project. That way the decision rests on a clear understanding of the impacts rather than on the appeal of a saving.

options.text: Ask the development team to implement all remaining components with the new technology.
options.rationale: Directing the team to adopt it commits the project to an unevaluated change three-quarters of the way through. The saving is claimed before the cost of switching has been examined.

questions.explanation: A customer proposal that would alter a running project is neither refused on procedural grounds nor adopted for its headline benefit; it goes into the process built to weigh feasibility against impact. A percentage saving is an argument for evaluation, never a substitute for it.
questions.mindset: An attractive number is a reason to evaluate, not a reason to skip evaluating.

questions.stem: During the development phase of a construction project, key stakeholders approved a project budget. The team identified risks and appropriate risk responses. However, during project execution, an unexpected local health emergency halted and delayed work on the project. This event type was not identified as a risk or listed in the risk register. The team decides that this issue must be mitigated, which would incur additional costs. How should the project manager address this unforeseen budgetary overrun?

options.text: Use the management reserve to cover the cost.
options.rationale: Management reserve sits outside the performance measurement baseline and exists for unforeseen work within the project scope, which is exactly what this emergency is. Because the event was never identified as a risk, this is the fund that applies.

options.text: Identify potential ways to exploit the risk.
options.rationale: Exploiting is a response strategy for opportunities, not for threats, so it does not fit an emergency that has halted work. The scenario also states the issue must be mitigated, meaning the response is already decided.

options.text: Use the contingency reserve to cover the cost.
options.rationale: Contingency covers risks that were identified and analysed in advance, and this event appears nowhere in the risk register. Drawing on it here spends money set aside for known exposures on an unknown one.

options.text: Develop cost and performance baselines.
options.rationale: Baselines already exist, since stakeholders approved the budget during development. Creating them now answers a funding question with a planning activity.

questions.explanation: Which pot of money applies turns entirely on whether the event was identified beforehand: anticipated exposures draw on funds reserved against them, and genuinely unforeseen work draws on the reserve held outside the baseline. Getting this wrong misallocates money that was set aside for a different purpose, which is why the register is the thing to check first.
questions.mindset: Decide which reserve applies by asking whether anyone saw this coming.

questions.stem: An approved project charter stated that an agile approach must be used.
