During a lessons learned session, the client indicates that the team was unable to provide reliable cost estimates for the project, and that more time should be allocated to define the scope during the first iteration. What lesson should be captured in the lessons learned repository?

options.text: The client should be exposed to the agile approach in advance to understand the cost estimating process.
options.rationale: Adaptive environments carry high uncertainty and frequent change, so only high-level cost estimates are expected and they are refined with each iteration. The real lesson is that the client needed to understand this beforehand rather than expecting precision the approach does not produce.

options.text: The agile approach should not be used if the client requires reliable cost estimates.
options.rationale: The charter specified the approach, and an approved charter is followed rather than second-guessed after the fact. It also treats a gap in client understanding as a defect in the method.

options.text: During the first iteration of a project, time should be allocated to define the scope and ensure that reliable cost estimates are performed.
options.rationale: Front-loading scope definition to produce firm estimates works against how costs and scope are managed in this approach, which is iteration by iteration against the overall budget. It adopts the client's suggested remedy without questioning the expectation behind it.

options.text: Client communications should be included in the daily standups.
options.rationale: Standups are short meetings for reviewing task status and project performance, and client communication does not belong in them. It also has nothing to do with the estimating expectation that caused the complaint.

questions.explanation: When a client is dissatisfied with something an approach is designed not to provide, the lesson concerns the expectation rather than the practice, and the remedy is to set that expectation before the work begins. Adopting the complainant's proposed fix is the trap, because it treats the symptom as a diagnosis.
questions.mindset: When someone is disappointed by how a method works, ask whether they understood it going in.

questions.stem: An innovative project is leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to identify chemical compounds for the development of new products. The AI processing phase can vary in duration, ranging from three days to two weeks, and the outcomes are unpredictable. The project's primary objective is to deliver at least one product specification within a fixed two-month timeframe while adhering to a strict budget that cannot be increased. What action should the project manager take to optimize the use of the fixed budget and deliver the highest possible business value?

options.text: Ensure that the specification iterations are limited to 50% of the overall project duration.
options.rationale: Capping iterations by a share of the duration does not address how to get the most value from the remaining budget. It may also be unworkable given how unpredictably the processing phase runs.

options.text: Ensure that the AI processing is limited to 25% of the overall project budget.
options.rationale: Constraining spend on the processing may be neither feasible nor beneficial, since it is the part of the project that generates the findings. An arbitrary cap risks starving the activity everything else depends on.

options.text: Plan an iteration directly after AI processing to analyze and prioritize the development goals.
options.rationale: An iteration placed straight after processing lets the team examine what the results actually are and set priorities from those findings. The remaining budget then goes to the most valuable work rather than to goals fixed before anything was known.

options.text: Plan the specification work as a predictive task with a fixed duration to guarantee value.
options.rationale: A fixed-duration predictive task assumes a predictability the scenario explicitly denies. Committing to a duration does not guarantee value when the inputs to the work are unknown until processing completes.

questions.explanation: Where a phase produces unpredictable results, the way to protect a fixed budget is to build in a decision point immediately after it, so that spending is directed by what was actually found. Arbitrary caps on time or money constrain the work without improving the judgement about where the remaining money should go.
questions.mindset: Put the decision point where the uncertainty resolves, and spend after that.

questions.stem: A project manager is working in the fifth month of an implementation for a construction project. The planner reported that the current schedule performance index (SPI) and cost performance index (CPI) are 0.8 and 0.9, respectively. Which two options will help to accelerate the project? (Choose two)

options.text: Adjust the working procedures to streamline and improve efficiency with the current resources.
options.rationale: Improving efficiency with the resources already assigned accelerates delivery without adding cost, which matters when the cost index is also below one. It attacks the schedule problem from within the existing budget.

options.text: Change the critical path by replacing some critical path activities with activities that have float.
options.rationale: Activities cannot simply be swapped for others because they have float, since the critical path is determined by the work and its dependencies. This misunderstands what float is and what determines the path.

options.text: Increase the number of resources to get more people involved and get activities done faster.
options.rationale: Adding people raises cost on a project whose cost index is already below one, worsening the second problem to address the first. More resources also bring coordination overhead that can slow delivery.

options.text: Rearrange the schedule so that some activities on the critical path can be done concurrently to reduce the project duration.
options.rationale: Running critical path activities in parallel shortens the overall duration without adding resources or cost. It is the schedule compression technique available when the budget cannot absorb more.

options.text: Ask the resources to work overtime to accelerate the project and achieve better results.
options.rationale: Overtime increases cost against an already unfavourable cost index and is not sustainable across the rest of the project. It buys schedule with money the project does not have.

questions.explanation: When both performance indices are below one, acceleration has to come from how the work is organised rather than from buying more of it, because anything that adds cost deepens the other problem. Resourcing and overtime are the instinctive answers and both trade one failing measure for the other.
questions.mindset: When time and money are both short, find the speed in the sequencing.

questions.stem: An entrepreneur has initiated a software development project. The project charter has been approved, and a project manager has been assigned to oversee the project's execution. During development, unforeseen political risks arise, causing an urgent need to expedite the project. The project's sponsor has requested a report on any anticipated delays. Which tool should the project manager use to prepare the report on expected delays?

options.text: Trend analysis
options.rationale: Trend analysis evaluates performance over time and predicts future performance from historical results, which is what a report on anticipated delays requires. It projects the schedule forward from the current rate of progress.

options.text: Root cause analysis
options.rationale: Root cause analysis identifies why a problem occurred rather than what will happen next. The sponsor asked for a forecast, not a diagnosis.

options.text: Quality reports
options.rationale: Quality reports describe how well the work meets its standards and say nothing about schedule projection. They answer a different question about the project's health.

options.text: Milestone list
options.rationale: A milestone list records the significant points in the schedule but does not forecast whether they will be met. It states the plan rather than predicting performance against it.

questions.explanation: A request to know what is coming calls for a technique that extrapolates from performance to date, not one that explains the past or restates the plan. Matching the tool to whether the question is diagnostic, descriptive or predictive is what makes the selection straightforward.
questions.mindset: Choose the tool by whether the question looks backwards, sideways or forwards.

questions.stem: A project manager is appointed to design and develop a strategy for a government organization. The project manager recognizes that the project has a limited amount of detailed information to prepare project estimates. However, several other government organizations have already successfully adopted the same strategy. In this scenario, which type of estimating method should the project manager select?

options.text: Parametric modeling
options.rationale: Parametric estimating applies mathematical relationships to detailed variables, which this project does not have. Without that detail the formulas have nothing reliable to operate on.

options.text: Analogous estimation
options.rationale: Analogous estimating draws on historical data from similar projects to estimate cost, time and resources, and comparable organizations have already done this work. It is the method suited to a project with limited detail but good comparators.

options.text: Three-point estimating
options.rationale: Three-point estimating requires optimistic, pessimistic and most likely values for the activities, which presupposes detail the project lacks. It refines uncertainty rather than compensating for missing information.

options.text: Expert judgment
options.rationale: Expert judgment supports estimating but is not the estimating method itself, and it overlooks the comparable implementations available. Documented experience from similar work is the stronger basis here.

questions.explanation: The estimating technique follows from what information exists: detailed variables allow mathematical models, activity-level detail allows ranged estimates, and comparable completed work allows estimation by analogy. Reading which of those the scenario actually supplies is the whole of the decision.
questions.mindset: Pick the estimating method that matches the information you actually have.

questions.stem: A team is working on a new technology deployment project. This product has never been implemented before so there is no past data or historical records. The team is challenged to provide an initial timeline, budget, and other critical estimations to the client. How should the project manager handle this situation?

options.text: Develop up-front project management plans with a detailed budget.
options.rationale: A detailed budget produced without any data presents precision the project cannot justify. It gives the client false confidence in numbers built on nothing.

options.text: Provide guidance on project cost, time, and quality.
options.rationale: Offering general guidance avoids producing the estimates the client has asked for. It sidesteps the task rather than handling it.

options.text: Develop estimations with the team and explain the assumptions to the client.
options.rationale: Estimates still have to be created despite the absence of historical data, and the team is the source of the judgement behind them. Setting out the assumptions openly lets the client understand what the numbers rest on.

options.text: Encourage the team to perform retrospectives at intervals.
options.rationale: Retrospectives improve how the team works but produce nothing the client can be given now. The immediate need is an estimate, not a review cadence.

questions.explanation: Where no precedent exists, estimates are still owed, and what makes them honest is stating the assumptions they rest on rather than dressing them up or declining to give them. Transparency about the basis is what turns an uncertain number into a usable one.
questions.mindset: When you must estimate without data, show your assumptions rather than hiding the uncertainty.

questions.stem: Due to budgetary constraints, the program manager has requested that project managers prioritize resources over schedule milestones. A project manager reviews the resource histogram and finds that 80% of the project's resources will be used in the last month of the project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request that activities be fast-tracked to make better use of available resources.
options.rationale: Fast-tracking pursues schedule compression when the programme has explicitly asked for resources to take priority over milestones. It optimises the wrong constraint.

options.text: Allow some of the current resources to be available for other projects.
options.rationale: Releasing resources addresses the early months without solving the concentration of demand at the end. The peak that makes the profile unworkable is left in place.

options.text: Suggest the program manager perform an integrated resource leveling among the projects.
options.rationale: Integrated levelling balances resource demand across multiple projects by adjusting activity dates, which is what a spike confined to one month requires. Working with the programme manager also brings in the other projects whose resources could support the earlier months.

options.text: Continue the project execution according to the original plan.
options.rationale: Proceeding unchanged ignores a resource profile the programme has asked to be addressed. A histogram showing four-fifths of demand in the final month is a problem, not a plan.

questions.explanation: A demand profile that spikes cannot be flattened from inside a single project when the resources are shared, so the remedy belongs at the level that can move work across projects. The instruction to favour resources over milestones also settles which constraint to optimise, and compression techniques answer the opposite question.
questions.mindset: Read which constraint you have been told to protect, then solve at the level that can move it.

questions.stem: During a steering committee meeting, a senior executive raised a concern that although the key cost parameters are reported to be on track, the project might not be delivering the work that was originally scheduled. What measurement should the project manager use to address this concern?

options.text: Cost Variance (CV)
options.rationale: Cost variance compares what has been earned against what has been spent, which is the dimension already reported as healthy. It cannot reveal a shortfall in work delivered.

options.text: Earned Value (EV)
options.rationale: Earned value states the worth of work completed but means nothing on its own without a point of comparison. The concern is about a gap, and a single figure does not express one.

options.text: Schedule Variance (SV)
options.rationale: Comparing earned value against planned value produces the schedule variance, which is precisely the difference between work expected and work delivered. That is what exposes a project keeping to cost while falling behind on output.

options.text: Planned Value (PV)
options.rationale: Planned value describes what should have been accomplished by now and is only half of the comparison. Alone it restates the plan rather than measuring performance against it.

questions.explanation: A concern about work delivered versus work scheduled is answered by the measure that sets those two quantities against each other, not by either quantity alone or by a measure of spending. Cost measures cannot detect a delivery shortfall, which is exactly why the executive could see healthy cost reporting and still be right to worry.
questions.mindset: Answer a question about output with a measure that compares output to plan.

questions.stem: An inexperienced project manager requires HR support for a project. The HR manager hired interns and sent them for training. However, the training did not deliver on the competency-based outcomes. The HR manager is not willing to accept the training costs because the training budget is exhausted. What should the project manager do to resolve the situation?

options.text: Prepare clear training requirements for full-time staff and interns.
options.rationale: Clear requirements would have helped before the training was commissioned but do nothing about the gap that now exists. It answers a past failure rather than the present situation.

options.text: Identify the competency gaps and collaborate with the HR manager for options.
options.rationale: Establishing which competencies are actually missing gives both parties something concrete to work from. Collaborating with the HR manager on the options is what moves a funding dispute toward a resolution.

options.text: Communicate training and hiring requirements to the HR manager.
options.rationale: Restating requirements to someone whose budget is exhausted does not produce a way forward. It repeats a demand instead of exploring what is possible.

options.text: Analyze the risk, update the risk register, and inform the HR manager.
options.rationale: Recording the problem as a risk documents it without resolving anything. The gap is present and real, not a future uncertainty.

questions.explanation: A stalemate over who pays is unlocked by establishing precisely what is missing and then working the options jointly with the other party. Restating requirements, documenting the situation or assigning fault all leave both sides where they started.
questions.mindset: Turn a dispute about money into a joint problem by defining exactly what is missing.

questions.stem: A project manager is implementing a phase of an IT project in a location that is prone to security issues. A team member, working at a remote site, notifies the project manager that a permit fee was not received by the local regulatory agency involved; however, the project manager is certain that the fee was paid. The team member reminds the project manager that a test on the critical path is scheduled for that location on the same day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request the team member to provide the payment evidence from the project management office (PMO) and ensure that the hard copy payment receipt is subsequently delivered to the regulatory agency and wait for the feedback.
options.rationale: Routing documents through intermediaries and then waiting introduces exactly the delay the critical path cannot absorb. Passive waiting leaves the test in limbo on the day it is due.

options.text: Request a meeting with the agency officer to present the payment evidence and verify the consequences of a delayed payment to ensure that the test proceeds as planned.
options.rationale: Presenting the evidence directly to the officer removes communication delay and the risk of misunderstanding. Verifying the consequences at the same time protects the project from legal exposure while keeping the test on schedule.

options.text: Instruct the team member to proceed with the test because the penalty for non-compliance with the permit has a negligible cost impact and the test process cannot be altered.
options.rationale: Treating a regulatory penalty as an acceptable cost knowingly accepts non-compliance. The size of the fine is not the measure of whether the project may proceed without a permit.

options.text: Instruct the team member to proceed with the test so as not to allow a lag in the critical path because the test cannot be delayed further and the fee was most certainly paid.
options.rationale: Proceeding on the strength of the project manager's own certainty ignores that the agency has no record of the payment. Schedule pressure does not make an unresolved permit question safe to ignore.

questions.explanation: Where a regulator's records and your own disagree, the resolution is direct engagement with the regulator, which is faster than routing paperwork and safer than proceeding on your own conviction. Schedule pressure explains the temptation to press on but never licenses operating without a permit the authority believes is unpaid.
questions.mindset: Go straight to the authority whose record disagrees with yours, rather than around it or past it.

questions.stem: A project manager has been assigned to a new, multimillion-dollar project that is similar to a project the company executed three years ago. What should the project manager do to create a reliable cost estimate?

options.text: Identify the critical parameters and generate an estimate based on the variation of the parameters.
options.rationale: Working from parameter variation is less accurate than building up from the detailed costs of each work activity. It also discards the actual cost record the earlier project provides.

options.text: Take the original estimate and multiply it by a factor determined by the company's standard for every year.
options.rationale: Escalating an old estimate compounds whatever error that estimate contained and ignores what the work actually cost. An estimate is a weaker starting point than an actual.

options.text: Use the actual cost of the previous project as a reference and compute an estimated cost for each task and roll up.
options.rationale: Building from the detailed costs of each work activity and summing them is the most accurate approach available, and the earlier project supplies real actuals to anchor it. Bottom-up estimating is the logical step once the work has been decomposed and historical data exists.

options.text: Use a commodity exchange for material cost and labor rates for the cost variation and compute a new estimate.
options.rationale: External market rates cover only inputs and miss the project-specific effort that drives most of the cost. It also passes over the company's own record of doing this work.

questions.explanation: Where the work can be decomposed and comparable actuals exist, the most reliable estimate is built activity by activity from real recorded costs and rolled up. Shortcuts that scale a previous estimate or reason from parameters and market rates all inherit error rather than eliminating it.
questions.mindset: Build from what things actually cost, not from what someone once estimated they would.

questions.stem: In the middle of a project, the project manager realizes that a specific set of skills is needed to complete project development. Unfortunately, none of the team members possess the necessary skills. What is the first step the project manager should take to address this issue?

options.text: Reorganize the project team to include people with the necessary knowledge and skills.
options.rationale: Restructuring the team may be neither feasible nor practical and commits to one remedy immediately. It chooses an option before the alternatives have been weighed.

options.text: Review the timeline and budget to consider training, outsourcing, or other alternatives.
options.rationale: Examining what the schedule and budget can absorb is what determines which remedy is actually available. That review is how the project manager decides between training, outsourcing and the other options open to them.

options.text: Organize adequate training for the project team to close the knowledge gap.
options.rationale: Training is one possible answer but may not fit the time remaining or the money available. Selecting it first skips the comparison that would justify it.

options.text: Search for alternative ways to achieve project objectives without the required skills.
options.rationale: Working around a needed capability risks compromising the objectives the project exists to meet. It treats the requirement as negotiable before establishing that it is.

questions.explanation: A capability gap has several possible remedies, and which one is viable depends on the time and money left, so the constraints are examined before a remedy is chosen. Each distractor is a defensible answer selected without the analysis that would show whether the project can afford it.
questions.mindset: Check what your constraints allow before deciding which solution to buy.

questions.stem: An agile team is developing a product with strict budget constraints. The customer is requesting a new independent feature be added to the solution in development. The project manager is concerned that adding the new feature will exceed the budget. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Evaluate the new feature with the customer.
options.rationale: Evaluating it together establishes whether the feature is feasible and whether it meets the customer's need within the budget. That shared understanding is what allows an informed decision, and considering customer needs is fundamental to how this approach works.

options.text: Reject adding the new feature.
options.rationale: Refusing outright decides against the customer before the feature has been examined. The budget concern is a reason to evaluate, not a settled conclusion.

options.text: Add the new feature to the product backlog.
options.rationale: Adding it straight to the backlog accepts the work without testing it against the budget constraint. Prioritisation should follow evaluation, not precede it.

options.text: Reprioritize the product backlog.
options.rationale: Reordering existing items presumes the new feature is coming in and displaces other work on that assumption. Nothing has yet established that the feature is feasible.

questions.explanation: A customer request that strains a constraint is worked through with the customer rather than decided for them in either direction, because they are the ones who can weigh their own need against what it costs. Accepting and refusing are equally premature when nobody has yet examined the request.
questions.mindset: Evaluate a constrained request alongside the person asking, before you answer it.

questions.stem: During a progress meeting, the project team learns that an identified risk materialized. The project manager decides to execute the risk response plan, but the contingency reserve does not cover the total budget for that plan. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to apply the management reserve to cover the remaining cost of the response.
options.rationale: Management reserve is held for unidentified risks, and this one was identified and planned for. The fund does not apply to a risk the project already knew about.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to provide an additional budget to compensate for the cost overage.
options.rationale: Additional budget would itself require a change request, so this skips the step that authorises it. It seeks the money without the mechanism.

options.text: Issue a change request to modify the scope, cost, and schedule baselines to support the new plan.
options.rationale: Implementing the response requires changes to the current plan, and a change request is how the budget is sought, the rescheduling addressed and new activities brought into scope. It is the route that covers all three effects at once.

options.text: Use the contingency reserve and assess options to reduce the budget to cover the remaining work.
options.rationale: Cutting elsewhere to fund the shortfall makes unapproved trade-offs across the project. The shortfall is a change to be authorised, not a gap to be quietly absorbed.

questions.explanation: When a planned response costs more than the money set aside for it, the shortfall is resolved through the formal route that can adjust the baselines, because scope, cost and schedule are all affected. Reaching for another reserve or asking for money directly both look like funding decisions when the situation is actually a change.
questions.mindset: When the response outgrows its reserve, treat it as a change rather than a funding request.

questions.stem: A project has a budgeted cost of $120,000. According to the schedule, 15% of the project should have been completed after one month. After a month, only 12% of the project has actually been completed. What is the scheduled performance index (SPI)?

options.rationale: This does not follow from the figures given under any correct formula. It appears to come from manipulating the percentages rather than dividing earned value by planned value.
Planned value is $18,000 and earned value is $14,400, so dividing earned by planned gives 0.8. Being below one, it shows the project running behind schedule.
This overstates performance and does not result from the values in the scenario. It would require an earned value of $16,200, which the 12% completion does not produce.
This is the result of inverting the ratio and dividing planned value by earned value. An index above one would indicate the project was ahead, which contradicts completing less than planned.

questions.explanation: The index is earned value divided by planned value, each obtained by applying the relevant percentage to the budget, and the order of that division decides whether the answer describes the project or its opposite. A result below one means less has been accomplished than was scheduled, which is the sense check that catches an inverted ratio.
questions.mindset: Check that the number you calculated points the same way as the story.

questions.stem: A construction company is implementing a new strategic project with a fixed budget. While monitoring the project, it was discovered that the overall project cost was increasing. The project manager learns that this is because the team is using more materials than detailed in the original scope. The cause of this discrepancy is that two of the team members are new to the organization and have not been reporting the acquisition of new materials. What should the project manager have done to prevent this situation?

options.text: Documented the risk of a materials cost deviation in the project's risk matrix.
options.rationale: Recording the exposure would have made it visible without stopping it from happening. Documentation is not a control over how people behave.

options.text: Provided training on the material acquisition process and reporting requirements.
options.rationale: The new members did not report acquisitions because they lacked awareness of the proper procedures. Training on the process and the reporting duties ensures everyone understands what is required before they start acquiring materials.

options.text: Created a contingency reserve to cover cost overages associated with materials.
options.rationale: A reserve funds the overrun rather than preventing it, leaving the reporting gap in place. It absorbs the consequence of the problem instead of removing the cause.

options.text: Avoided the inclusion of new engineers on a strategic project with a fixed budget.
options.rationale: Excluding new joiners from significant work is impractical and treats inexperience as disqualifying. The failure was in preparing them, not in including them.

questions.explanation: Where a control is breached because people did not know it existed, prevention lies in making sure they knew, not in funding the consequence or logging the exposure. Reserves and risk entries are the tempting answers on a cost question, and neither changes what anyone does.
questions.mindset: If a process depends on people following it, make sure they were taught it.

questions.stem: During execution, the customer submits a change request to maintain the project's business value, which has been threatened by a recently implemented government regulatory change. The project manager analyzes the change, which will require 50% of the project deliverable to be reworked and will incur additional costs to the customer. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Submit the change request to the CCB as the customer will be comfortable absorbing all additional costs.
options.rationale: Who bears the cost is irrelevant to what the board needs in order to decide. Presenting the customer's willingness in place of an impact analysis withholds the substance of the request.

options.text: Submit the change request to the CCB and advise the panel to consider rejecting the request due to its impact.
options.rationale: Recommending rejection is not part of the project manager's role in submitting a request. The board weighs the impact itself once the facts are before it.

options.text: Submit the change request to the CCB and explain the reason for the request, including a cost-impact analysis.
options.rationale: A change request captures the reasons for the change, its impact on the project and the other relevant facts, and a significant cost impact makes that analysis essential. Supplying it in full is what lets the board review and decide properly.

options.text: Submit the change request to show the change as having no impact, then proceed without notifying the CCB.
options.rationale: Misrepresenting the impact and bypassing the board breaches the code of ethics outright. Omitting material information from a decision-making body is never acceptable.

questions.explanation: A submission to a decision-making body carries the reasons, the full impact and the relevant facts, with nothing shaded, omitted or replaced by a recommendation. Steering the outcome is a lesser failure than misstating it, but both substitute the project manager's preference for the body's judgement.
questions.mindset: Give a decision-making body the whole picture and let it decide.

questions.stem: A project manager has just taken over an ongoing project from another project manager. During a review of the project management plan, the new project manager realizes that the cost variance and schedule variance are largely negative. Several reported issues have not been resolved, vendors have not been paid for work done, and risk mitigation is quickly depleting the budget. Which two actions should the original project manager have taken to avoid this situation? (Choose two)

options.text: Outlined the project's assumptions and documented them in the project charter.
options.rationale: Documented assumptions give every stakeholder a common understanding of the scope, objectives and what the plan depends on. That shared basis is what stops unexamined expectations turning into variances later.

options.text: Added a substantial contingency reserve budget to the project charter.
options.rationale: A larger reserve would cushion the overruns without addressing what produced them. It funds the symptoms rather than preventing them.

options.text: Identified high-level risks and risk responses in the project planning phase.
options.rationale: Identifying risks and their responses during planning is what allows exposures to be addressed before they become issues. The depleted budget and unresolved issues both trace back to that work not having been done.

options.text: Identified appropriate and comprehensive project handoff procedures.
options.rationale: Handoff procedures would have made the transition smoother but none of these problems were caused by the handover. The variances and unpaid vendors predate the new project manager's arrival.

options.text: Ensured that the project governance controls were approved and implemented.
options.rationale: Governance controls set thresholds and escalation paths rather than preventing the specific failures described. They would have surfaced the problems sooner without stopping them arising.

questions.explanation: A project that arrives in trouble across cost, schedule, issues and reserves usually failed at the point where expectations were fixed and exposures were catalogued, because everything downstream inherits those omissions. Remedies that cushion, surface or hand over the damage all operate after the cause has already done its work.
questions.mindset: Write down what you are assuming and what could go wrong, before either becomes a variance.

questions.stem: A project is about to begin and a new regulation has imposed a deadline that will adversely impact the project. Failing to comply with the regulation will result in hefty fines for the organization. The project is key to meeting the organization's annual goals. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Analyze the impact of not initiating the project and share the findings with stakeholders.
options.rationale: The analysis lets stakeholders identify the most time-sensitive activities so resources can be focused where the deadline bites. Sharing the findings is what enables the decisions about compression and priority that follow.

options.text: Delegate tasks associated with higher risk levels to a third party.
options.rationale: Handing high-risk work outside introduces new exposures around quality, communication and control. It also offers no guarantee of finishing faster within the deadline.

options.text: Obtain additional funding to mitigate the need for outside services.
options.rationale: Securing funds is itself time-consuming and may delay progress against a deadline that is already tight. Money does not address the core time constraint.

options.text: Build prototypes and simulations to identify potential issues early.
options.rationale: Prototyping consumes time and resources upfront, which the compressed timeframe may not allow. It invests in early learning at the expense of the deadline itself.

questions.explanation: A regulatory deadline that threatens a project is first quantified and put in front of the people who can act on it, because the shape of the problem determines which responses are worth their cost. Outsourcing, funding and early prototyping all spend time or money before anyone knows where the pressure actually falls.
questions.mindset: Quantify the squeeze and show it to the decision-makers before spending anything on it.

questions.stem: An organization is halfway through a five year project and everything has progressed as scheduled. The latest project assessment indicates that the project will not be in compliance with a recently introduced international regulation. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Proceed with the project because the new regulation is not part of the initial project requirements.
options.rationale: Continuing unchanged guarantees non-compliance when the project completes. A regulation's absence from the original requirements does not exempt the finished product from it.

options.text: Conduct a workshop with the project steering committee to review the new regulation and find a resolution.
options.rationale: The steering committee is the forum where the regulation can be reviewed and a way forward agreed. Working with them is how compliance is secured for a project with years still to run.

options.text: Leverage the contingency reserve to fund the additional tasks required for the new regulation.
options.rationale: Drawing on reserves without change control approval commits funds the project manager cannot unilaterally direct. It also picks a funding answer before the response has been agreed.

options.text: Ask for funds from the management reserve because the new regulation is an unknown risk.
options.rationale: Requesting management reserve likewise requires approval and presumes a solution nobody has yet defined. Labelling the regulation an unknown risk does not authorise the draw.

questions.explanation: A compliance gap discovered mid-project is taken to the governing body to agree a resolution, rather than absorbed, ignored or funded from reserves on the project manager's own authority. Reaching for money first answers how to pay before anyone has decided what is being paid for.
questions.mindset: Agree the response with the governing body before deciding which pot funds it.

questions.stem: A new solution is being deployed in several countries. Country A asked for a change in the solution in order to comply with its own customer market. The project manager for the deployment in country A accepted the change. When the project manager for the deployment in country B received the new version of the solution, the tests performed failed because this version is not consistent with country B's regulations. What should have been done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Prevent the changes from being authorized.
options.rationale: Blocking changes altogether is not how a multi-country deployment is run, since local markets have legitimate requirements. Changes are acceptable provided they are managed properly.

options.text: Ensure that all countries aligned their requirements with country A.
options.rationale: Making one country's requirements the standard cannot work when each has its own regulations to satisfy. Country B's rules do not bend to country A's market.

options.text: Analyze all change requests raised during each country's deployment at a global level prior to implementation.
options.rationale: Where several countries deploy the same solution, an impact analysis has to consider all of them rather than only the one requesting the change. Analysing globally before implementation is what would have caught the conflict with country B's regulations.

options.text: Ensure that any country that requested a change pays for any required changes.
options.rationale: Allocating cost to the requester does nothing to detect the regulatory conflict the change created. Payment is not an impact analysis.

questions.explanation: When one product serves several jurisdictions, the blast radius of any change is all of them, so the assessment has to be made at the level where every deployment is visible. Local approval of a locally sensible change is exactly how a shared solution breaks somewhere else.
questions.mindset: Assess a change everywhere it lands, not only where it was requested.

questions.stem: A compliance issue was found during the course of a project. This caused an inspection of the product by the internal audit team. As a result, the project fell behind schedule. What should the project manager have done initially to avoid this issue?

options.text: Ensured that compliance requirements were documented.
options.rationale: Considering and capturing all potential compliance, regulatory and safety requirements at the outset keeps the project on track even where none appear to apply. Maintaining those requirements is what minimises rework and avoids the inspection delay.

options.text: Created templates to document compliance.
options.rationale: Templates format the recording of requirements after the fact and prevent no non-compliance themselves. An empty template offers nothing to comply with.

options.text: Hired a compliance consultant.
options.rationale: A consultant may advise, but the project manager still has to ensure the requirements are captured. Buying expertise does not discharge that responsibility.

options.text: Engaged stakeholders at the beginning of the project.
options.rationale: Early engagement is good practice but still leaves the requirements themselves to be identified and recorded. Talking to people is a means, not the outcome that was missing.

questions.explanation: Compliance failures are prevented by identifying and recording what the project must satisfy at the start, including on projects that appear to have no obligations. Consultants, stakeholders and templates all support that work without substituting for the documented requirements themselves.
questions.mindset: Write down what you must comply with, even when you think nothing applies.

questions.stem: At the start of a project, the team chose to leverage an agile approach to deliver the project, using user stories to capture requirements. As part of the organization's control framework, the internal compliance department will request a copy of the approved requirements document. What should be done to meet this compliance request?

options.text: Review the project approach with compliance, ensuring they understand how it will meet the control objective.
options.rationale: Bringing compliance into an understanding of the approach shows how the control objective is satisfied by the way the project actually works. That is what reconciles the framework's requirement with iterative delivery.

options.text: Print and assemble all user stories into one package at the end of the project and have the product owner approve them.
options.rationale: Producing a bundled document at the end imitates a waterfall artefact without bringing compliance into any understanding of the approach. It also satisfies the control long after the work it was meant to govern.

options.text: Assign the compliance requirement as a task on the project's Kanban board for the product owner.
options.rationale: Making it a board task deflects accountability to the product owner for explaining how the approach meets compliance. It does not answer the question compliance has actually posed.

options.text: Review the project approach with compliance, indicating that the control objective is not required because the project is using agile.
options.rationale: Adaptive delivery does not presuppose exemption from control objectives. Claiming the requirement does not apply asserts a privilege the approach does not confer.

questions.explanation: A control framework specifies an objective rather than a particular document, so the task is to demonstrate how the chosen way of working satisfies that objective. Manufacturing the expected artefact and claiming exemption are opposite errors, and both skip the conversation that would resolve the matter properly.
questions.mindset: Show how your way of working meets the control, rather than faking the artefact or claiming exemption.

questions.stem: A team member raises a concern that some deliverables may not be compliant with certain regulations. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set up a meeting with the key stakeholders and subject matter experts (SME) to get clarification about the regulations that may impact the project deliverables.
options.rationale: Key stakeholders and subject matter experts are the source of reliable information about which regulations affect the deliverables. Convening them is how the project manager establishes whether the concern is well founded and what it requires.

options.text: Request an official letter from the client to confirm if the regulations apply to the project deliverables.
options.rationale: The client may not be well informed about which regulations govern the deliverables. Seeking a letter also deflects the project manager's own responsibility to establish the position.

options.text: Ask the project management office (PMO) if the project deliverables are subject to the regulations and, if so, how to proceed in order to be compliant.
options.rationale: The PMO typically advises on the overall project life cycle rather than on regulations affecting specific deliverables. It is the wrong source for this particular question.

options.text: Contact the manager of the team member that raised the concern to determine which tasks are needed to stay compliant.
options.rationale: That manager has no particular standing on regulatory matters and was not the one who raised the concern. It passes the question sideways rather than to expertise.

questions.explanation: A question about which rules bind the work is resolved by convening the people who actually know, which means stakeholders with the relevant interest and genuine subject matter expertise. Routing it to a function, a manager or the client substitutes organisational convenience for expertise and leaves the project manager's responsibility undischarged.
questions.mindset: Take a regulatory question to people with the expertise, not to people with a title.

questions.stem: During project execution, the audit team determined that critical regulatory requirements are not being met. What should the project manager have done first to avoid this problem?

options.text: Updated the issue log with regulatory requirements.
options.rationale: The issue log records problems that have arisen rather than obligations the project must plan around. Recording requirements there would not have built them into the work.

options.text: Assessed the internal and external regulatory environments.
options.rationale: Understanding the regulatory requirements for the industry and project type at the outset lets the team build the necessary tasks into the plan and allocate resources to them. That assessment is what prevents the rework a later audit finding creates.

options.text: Had the audit team review the project management plan.
options.rationale: An audit review of the plan checks work the project manager should have done first. It brings assurance to a plan that was never built on a regulatory assessment.

options.text: Included a member of the audit team on the project.
options.rationale: Embedding an auditor provides oversight rather than the initial understanding of what applies. It also confuses the assurance function with the project's own planning duty.

questions.explanation: Regulatory obligations are established at the start so that the tasks and resources needed to satisfy them are inside the plan from the beginning. Bringing in assurance functions or logging requirements elsewhere both act after the planning moment where compliance is actually secured.
questions.mindset: Understand the rules before you build the plan, not after someone checks it.

questions.stem: A project team is installing a fiscal metering system for a crude oil terminal. The project manager has requested a metering system, conducted a factory acceptance test, and delivered meters to the terminal for installation. While onsite, local regulators participated in the factory acceptance tests and declined approvals for the meters due to a breach of statutory procedures. This led to delays in completing testing and had an overall impact on the project cost and schedule. How could the project manager have prevented this situation?

options.text: Referred to lessons learned from previous projects.
options.rationale: Lessons learned are valuable but would not by themselves have secured compliance with the regulators' statutory procedures. It is a general practice offered against a specific obligation.

options.text: Notified stakeholders of the factory acceptance tests for meters.
options.rationale: The regulators evidently knew about the tests, since they attended them. Notification was not what was missing.

options.text: Ensured compliance with the stakeholder requirements.
options.rationale: The regulators are critical stakeholders whose statutory procedures had to be met for the meters to be approved. Complying with those requirements is what would have prevented the refusal and the resulting cost and schedule impact.

options.text: Revised the stakeholder engagement plan.
options.rationale: Adjusting how stakeholders are engaged does not satisfy a statutory procedure that was breached. The failure was in meeting the requirement, not in the engagement approach.

questions.explanation: Where a stakeholder holds approval authority backed by statute, their requirements are binding conditions on the work rather than preferences to be managed. Engagement practices and historical insight are genuinely useful and neither one satisfies a procedure the approver will test you against.
questions.mindset: Treat an approver's requirements as conditions to satisfy, not relationships to manage.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing an agile project that has finalized scope and compliance requirements. During a regular project review, a stakeholder informs the project manager that proposed changes to the country's safety legislation could impact the project's scope. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Focus on completing the activities per the product backlog.
options.rationale: Carrying on with the backlog assumes the project can proceed without regard to external legislative change. It leaves a potential scope impact entirely unexamined.

options.text: Analyze the impact of the legislative changes on the project plan.
options.rationale: Legislative change can significantly affect scope, compliance requirements, timeline and budget, so understanding that impact is what shows how the project must adapt. Changes in the external environment bear directly on value delivery.

options.text: Incorporate the changes in the next sprint based on the proposal.
options.rationale: Implementing on the strength of a proposal that has not become law risks unnecessary disruption. It may also pull the project away from its own goals for a change that never arrives.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to approve the additional budget for the change.
options.rationale: Requesting budget before any analysis is premature, since the change may prove minor or absorbable. The size of the need has not been established.

questions.explanation: A signalled change in the external environment is assessed for its effect before the project either ignores it or acts on it, because proposals do not always become obligations. Both pressing ahead and implementing early commit the project on an assumption about something still undecided.
questions.mindset: Analyse a proposed external change before treating it as either nothing or certain.

questions.stem: A company is developing a new product that needs to implement nonfunctional security requirements. The product owner is concerned about how the team can ensure the implementation of these nonfunctional requirements. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Appoint a security expert as part of the team to review the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: An expert reviewing criteria is not enough on its own to ensure the product is compliant with the security requirements. Review adds a check without making the requirement part of what completion means.

options.text: Send the security requirements to the security department to be implemented.
options.rationale: This hands responsibility for the product's security to another team. The development team is responsible for implementing all requirements, security included.

options.text: Discuss the security requirements during the next sprint meeting.
options.rationale: A discussion is a reasonable start but does not ensure the requirements are met. Awareness in one meeting is not a mechanism for implementation and verification.

options.text: Include the security requirements in the definition of done (DoD).
options.rationale: Putting them in the definition of done makes the team aware of the requirements and embeds them in every item's completion throughout the project. Regular audits and a governance plan can then support the control that establishes.

questions.explanation: A requirement that must hold across everything the team produces is enforced by writing it into the standard for completion, so no item passes without satisfying it. Assigning a reviewer, referring it elsewhere or raising it in a meeting all rely on attention rather than on structure.
questions.mindset: To make a requirement unavoidable, put it in the definition of finished.

questions.stem: A company must launch a global product to respond to a competition threat. As part of an agile approach, the team chooses Region X as the baseline to test the first iteration. While the product meets standards and requirements in Region X, it does not comply with two of the other regions' standards. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ensure that the product meets the standards and requirements in Region X and plan future iterations to address the noncompliance with the standards in the other regions.
options.rationale: Prioritising the region where the product launches first answers the competitive threat while keeping the other markets in view. Later iterations then bring the product into line with the remaining regions' standards, which is how adaptive delivery handles staged compliance.

options.text: Document this as a noncompliance in the quality management plan and correct it in the next iteration.
options.rationale: Recording the gap does not address the fact that the product fails two regions' standards. Documentation substitutes for the action needed to modify the product.

options.text: Re-plan all of the iterations to meet all three regions' standards within the scope of the work.
options.rationale: Re-planning everything to satisfy all three regions at once is not feasible within the scope and would require substantial rework. It also delays the launch the competitive threat demands.

options.text: Connect with customers from each region to reach an agreement on the existing design.
options.rationale: Customers cannot agree away regulatory standards their regions impose. The product still has to be modified to comply.

questions.explanation: Where compliance obligations differ by market and delivery is iterative, the product is brought to standard for the market it enters first and the others are scheduled into later cycles. Attempting everything at once or negotiating with customers both treat a sequencing problem as though it were a scope or relationship problem.
questions.mindset: Comply fully where you are launching, and schedule the rest rather than attempting it all at once.

questions.stem: A functional manager involved in a project complains about the latest quality metrics reports associated with all previous iterations. The team does not think this is a valid complaint. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Fix the reports to accommodate the functional manager's complaints.
options.rationale: Changing the reports before knowing what the objection actually is treats the complaint as automatically correct. It should follow an understanding of the concerns and a judgement that they are valid.

options.text: Speak to the functional manager to understand their specific concerns.
options.rationale: Understanding the specific objection is what tells the project manager whether it is valid and what would need to change. Everything else depends on the answer to that question.

options.text: Review the RACI matrix to identify who is responsible for quality metrics.
options.rationale: Establishing responsibility is useful but is not the first move when the substance of the complaint is unknown. It looks for someone to handle the issue before the issue has been defined.

options.text: Perform a quality audit to validate the applied quality metrics.
options.rationale: An audit is a significant undertaking to launch against an objection nobody has yet articulated. It may also examine something entirely different from what is bothering the manager.

questions.explanation: When one party complains and another dismisses the complaint, the project manager's first task is to find out what is actually being alleged rather than siding with either. Acting on the complaint or investigating it formally both commit effort before the substance is known.
questions.mindset: Find out what someone actually means before deciding whether they are right.

questions.stem: A team is working in a highly regulated industry and the compliance department keeps pushing documentation and process steps that interfere with the team's desired way of working. Team frustration increases with the compliance department, and the team asks the project manager to intervene. What approach should the project manager take?

options.text: Help the team understand that compliance is an important part of the overall success of the project and value creation.
options.rationale: Building the team's understanding of why compliance matters addresses the frustration while keeping the regulatory obligations intact. Focusing on understanding and collaboration serves both the project's goals and its regulatory duties.

options.text: Push back on the compliance department and reduce the number of documents so the team can focus on value creation.
options.rationale: Simply reducing documentation is not sustainable, since the team must still comply with all applicable regulations. It also raises the risk of non-compliance in a highly regulated industry.

options.text: Conduct a daily workshop to assess the compliance, and complete as much compliance work as possible in that timebox.
options.rationale: A daily workshop would disrupt the team's workflow further and deepen the frustration. Compliance activities are better integrated into normal working than separated into standing sessions.

options.text: Invite the compliance team to attend the daily standup meetings to avoid interference and resentment between the two teams.
options.rationale: Daily attendance is not an efficient use of either group's time. Targeted meetings or dedicated channels serve specific compliance concerns better.

questions.explanation: When a team resents an obligation it cannot escape, the useful intervention changes how the team understands the obligation rather than trying to reduce or ritualise it. Advocating for the team against a mandatory requirement feels like leadership and exposes the organization instead.
questions.mindset: When an obligation is not negotiable, work on understanding rather than on resistance.

questions.stem: A project manager is contracted to manage a project for a startup with grants from a foreign source. Midway into this project, the project manager is informed that there is a government regulatory requirement that might affect the project because the customer has foreign funding sources. What should the project manager do since all the necessary approvals for this project have been received?

options.text: Determine the ownership of this project based on the previously approved project charter and continue with the project.
options.rationale: Establishing ownership does not resolve the regulatory question, and continuing unchanged is not acceptable. Prior approvals do not settle an obligation that has since come into view.

options.text: Consult the risk register to determine the likelihood that the project will be accepted by the customer and meet regulatory requirements.
options.rationale: Treating a regulatory requirement as a matter of likelihood disregards that compliance is mandatory. Customer acceptance is a separate question from whether the law applies.

options.text: Confirm that the project is in compliance with all regulations and keep abreast of all legal implications.
options.rationale: Local laws and regulations may have changed, so the position has to be confirmed rather than assumed from earlier approvals. Staying across the legal implications is what allows the project manager to act ethically and inform the client if compliance fails.

options.text: Stop the project, ask for additional funds to obtain work permits, and continue the project without further delays.
options.rationale: Seeking permits presumes what the requirement demands before compliance has even been confirmed. Stopping and funding a specific remedy precedes establishing whether it is the right one.

questions.explanation: Approvals obtained earlier do not immunise a project against obligations that emerge or change later, so the standing position is to verify compliance and keep watching. Reasoning from prior authorisation or from probability both treat a binding requirement as though it were a matter of judgement.
questions.mindset: Past approval is not present compliance; confirm the position as it stands now.

questions.stem: A customer has rejected an interim project deliverable. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Review the reason for the rejection, and check the deliverable against its acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: The reason for rejection has to be established and tested, since it may or may not be valid. Checking the deliverable against its acceptance criteria is how that verification is done.

options.text: Analyze the customer requirements, and rework the deliverable to an acceptable quality.
options.rationale: Reworking assumes the rejection is justified before anyone has checked it against the agreed criteria. The deliverable may already meet what was agreed.

options.text: Create a deliverable improvement plan, and implement it for the remainder of the project.
options.rationale: Committing to a programme of improvement is premature when the single rejection has not been investigated. It generalises from an unexamined case.

options.text: Document the rejection of the deliverable in the Lessons Learned log, and review it with the project delivery team.
options.rationale: Recording a lesson treats the matter as closed while the deliverable is still in dispute. The rejection needs investigating before anything is learned from it.

questions.explanation: A rejection is a claim to be tested against the agreed standard, not a verdict to be acted on, because the deliverable may conform and the objection may not be valid. Rework, improvement plans and lessons all assume the customer is right before the criteria have been consulted.
questions.mindset: Test a rejection against what was agreed before you accept it.

questions.stem: While closing a project, the client finds some defects in the deliverable. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Review the output against the acceptance criteria.
options.rationale: Comparing the output with the acceptance criteria is what establishes the position and shows why the defect was not raised during monitoring and controlling. It is the necessary basis for anything that follows.

options.text: Extend the project until all deliverables are accepted.
options.rationale: Extending the project without approval delays the timeline on the strength of an unexamined claim. The extension may also prove unnecessary.

options.text: Persuade the client to accept the output as is.
options.rationale: Talking the client into accepting defective work compromises quality and the client's interests. It settles the matter without establishing the facts.

options.text: Pay the penalty for the defective item.
options.rationale: Paying a penalty is inappropriate unless the contract with the client contains such a clause. It concedes liability before the defect has been assessed.

questions.explanation: A defect raised late is assessed against the agreed criteria first, which both settles whether it is genuinely a defect and reveals why control activities did not catch it earlier. Extending, conceding or persuading all respond to the claim without testing it.
questions.mindset: When a problem surfaces late, check it against the standard and ask why it surfaced late.

questions.stem: During a final inspection of a new product, the project team discovers a significant defect in one of the key deliverables. This defect poses a security risk to the client, who expects to start using the deliverable in two weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Conduct a quality investigation and initiate corrective action.
options.rationale: Assessing the situation to find the root cause and acting to correct it is what a late-discovered defect posing a security risk demands. Resolving it quickly puts the client's interests, their safety and the project's success first.

options.text: Use the contingency reserve to cover the cost of the defect.
options.rationale: Committing reserve funds is premature when the root cause is still unknown. A response strategy cannot be chosen before the problem is understood.

options.text: Meet with the client to explain the cause of the defect.
options.rationale: Explaining the cause requires knowing it, which means the investigation must come first. The meeting belongs after the issue has been examined and corrective action taken.

options.text: Send the client a letter apologizing for the inconvenience.
options.rationale: An apology substitutes courtesy for action on a defect that poses a security risk. Addressing the problem is the immediate obligation.

questions.explanation: A defect that creates a safety or security exposure is investigated and corrected as the immediate response, with communication and funding decisions following from what the investigation finds. Reaching first for money or for the client conversation both act before anyone knows what is wrong.
questions.mindset: When something is unsafe, find out why and fix it before you talk about it.

questions.stem: During a standup meeting, the project manager discovers that one of the software developers is struggling to complete work because they lack experience with automation testing, potentially affecting the sprint goal. A quality assurance engineer on the team has automation testing experience but is busy preparing a presentation for new employees. What action would increase the chances of achieving the sprint goal?

options.text: Reassign the automation work to the engineer as soon as the presentation is finished.
options.rationale: Waiting for the presentation to finish delays help the sprint goal cannot afford. Taking the work away may also leave the developer feeling their responsibility has been removed.

options.text: Immediately train the software developer on automation testing and then proceed with testing.
options.rationale: Training takes time and will not produce immediate proficiency in something as complex as automation testing. The sprint goal would be jeopardised while the learning happens.

options.text: Ask the quality assurance engineer to assist the software developer as soon as possible.
options.rationale: Timely assistance lets the team draw on the engineer's expertise while the developer keeps ownership of the work. Pairing in this way solves the problem faster than reassignment or training.

options.text: Reschedule the automation testing for when the quality assurance engineer is available.
options.rationale: Moving the testing out introduces delay and puts the sprint goal at risk. It also sidelines the developer rather than supporting them.

questions.explanation: A skills gap discovered mid-sprint is closed by putting existing expertise alongside the person doing the work, which is faster than transferring the task and more effective than training under time pressure. Keeping ownership with the original team member also protects their standing in the team.
questions.mindset: Pair expertise with the person doing the work rather than taking the work away.

questions.stem: A project manager was recently assigned to an investigation project. Due to the complexity of the project, the project manager is unsure if any regulation applies. How should the project manager determine which regulations apply to the project?

options.text: Consult with a manager who has a higher level of authority for this decision.
options.rationale: A more senior manager may not be well informed about which regulations apply to this work. Authority is not the same as regulatory knowledge.

options.text: Contact the project management office (PMO) manager as they are in charge of determining the regulations required for agile projects.
options.rationale: The PMO provides guidance on the methodology to be used rather than on which regulations apply. The premise of the option misstates what that function does.

options.text: Schedule a meeting with key stakeholders, subject matter experts (SMEs), and the project team to better understand if any regulations are applicable.
options.rationale: Consulting the available experts, the project's own resources and stakeholders with knowledge of the topic is expert judgment applied properly. That combination is what establishes whether any regulation bears on the work.

options.text: Request a signed letter from the client to confirm if any regulations apply to any project deliverables.
options.rationale: The client may not be well informed about the applicable regulations. A signed letter also transfers assurance without establishing the facts.

questions.explanation: Determining which rules govern a project is an exercise in expert judgment, drawing on those with genuine knowledge of the domain rather than on organisational seniority or written assurances from a counterparty. Choosing by authority or by paperwork looks decisive and answers a different question entirely.
questions.mindset: Seniority and signatures are not substitutes for expertise.

questions.stem: During a software development project, the team realized that several features failed to comply with quality requirements. After receiving instructions to fix the issues, one team member becomes frustrated, claiming that unclear requirements are causing the issues. Other team members argue that negligent testing is the real cause of these issues. The testers blame poor coding quality. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Support the project team in a retrospective to identify the root cause of the quality issues.
options.rationale: The team is primarily responsible for resolving conflict, and the project manager facilitates when required. A retrospective lets them review how they work, surface threats to performance and cohesion, and build consensus on what is actually causing the failures.

options.text: Remove the most frustrated resource from the team as the confusion is impacting team motivation.
options.rationale: Removing someone for voicing frustration punishes a symptom of a shared problem. It also loses a team member without touching the quality failures.

options.text: Perform a quality review in each stage of the development life cycle to identify quality issues.
options.rationale: Adding review stages imposes process without engaging the team's disagreement about causes. It addresses detection rather than the underlying dispute.

options.text: Discuss the issue with the management team to identify possible solutions to improve quality.
options.rationale: Taking the problem to management bypasses the team that holds the knowledge and the conflict. Solutions arrived at elsewhere will not resolve the mutual blame.

questions.explanation: Where a team fragments into mutual blame, the resolution is a facilitated session in which they examine their own working and reach consensus on the cause together. Removing people, adding process or escalating all decide something about the team without the team, and leave the disagreement intact.
questions.mindset: Bring a team that is blaming each other into one room to find the cause together.

questions.stem: A key member of an agile team was replaced with a less experienced member. One of the stakeholders is concerned that the project will not be delivered on time because of the new team member. What should the project manager do to ensure successful project delivery?

options.text: Add this concern as a risk in the risk log and escalate it to the project management office (PMO).
options.rationale: Logging and escalating records the stakeholder's worry without establishing whether it is justified. The project manager can assess the situation without involving the PMO at all.

options.text: Meet with their functional manager to assess the situation, and obtain guidance on how to proceed.
options.rationale: Seeking guidance from the functional manager defers a judgement the project manager is placed to make. The assessment of project impact belongs with the person running the project.

options.text: Reverse the decision for replacement and bring the former key member back onto the team.
options.rationale: Attempting to undo the replacement may not be possible and assumes the impact is unmanageable. Nothing yet establishes that the new member cannot succeed with support.

options.text: Assess the impact of the replacement and make further resource adjustments where necessary.
options.rationale: An informed decision requires knowing what the change actually costs the project, and adjustments follow from that assessment. Onboarding the new member properly and supporting them is part of making the arrangement work.

questions.explanation: A change in team composition is evaluated for its real effect before anyone reverses it, escalates it or logs it as a threat, because the answer determines whether any action is needed. A stakeholder's concern is a prompt to assess rather than a finding to act on.
questions.mindset: Assess what a change actually costs you before treating it as a problem.

questions.stem: A project manager is assigned to an ongoing project with virtual team members from different countries who are working remotely in different time zones. The project manager notices that team members are not completing project activities on time and are unable to produce the expected deliverables due to irregular communications. How should the project manager resolve this?

options.text: Provide the team with the deliverable list to guide them.
options.rationale: Restating what is expected assumes the team does not know, which the scenario does not suggest. It acts before the underlying difficulty has been identified.

options.text: Engage with the team members to understand their challenges.
options.rationale: Engagement with a dispersed team is how the project manager learns what the members are actually contending with. Once those issues are visible, the project manager can help resolve them.

options.text: Organize time management training for the team.
options.rationale: Training presumes the problem is personal organisation when the scenario points to irregular communication. It applies a remedy to a cause nobody has confirmed.

options.text: Take steps to colocate the team in the same office.
options.rationale: Colocating people across countries is impractical and treats distribution itself as the fault. The difficulty is how communication is working, not where people sit.

questions.explanation: Underperformance in a dispersed team is diagnosed by talking to its members before any remedy is selected, because the visible symptom rarely names the cause. Guidance, training and structural change are all plausible fixes applied to a problem that has not yet been understood.
questions.mindset: Ask a struggling team what is in their way before deciding what to change.

questions.stem: During a one-on-one session, a new team member shared their frustration regarding their inability to successfully complete an assigned task, even after the team member put forth their best effort. What should the project manager do first to address the team member's concerns?

options.text: Encourage the team member to keep working hard on their assignments.
options.rationale: Encouragement tells someone already giving their best effort to continue doing what is not working. It offers sympathy in place of help.

options.text: Identify the root cause for why the team member cannot complete the assigned work and remediate.
options.rationale: Determining why a new team member cannot complete the task is what makes any remedy effective. Applying interpersonal and team building skills to find and fix the cause addresses the frustration properly.

options.text: Authorize additional training for the team member during the next month's educational series opportunities.
