questions.stem: An organization makes an acquisition of a similar product halfway through the development cycle of a potential product. This might create an overlap in the product portfolio. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Assess the feasibility and viability of the project with the product owner.
options.rationale: Assessing the impact of the acquisition and determining next steps with the product owner is what keeps expectations aligned. They are the role accountable for the product's continued worth to the organization.

options.text: Continue to develop the product for the benefit of the organization.
options.rationale: Carrying on may waste effort and time if the organization's intentions have changed. Nothing has established that the product is still wanted.

options.text: Discuss the potential impact of the acquisition with team members.
options.rationale: Discussion with the team is valid but is not the next step. That conversation should follow the one with the product owner, who may join it later for impact analysis.

options.text: Halt the project until a clear path emerges for the product roadmap.
options.rationale: Stopping work is as premature as continuing it when the organization's position is unknown. It wastes time on an assumption rather than establishing the facts.

questions.explanation: When an organisational move casts doubt on whether a product is still wanted, the question goes to whoever owns its value before the team either presses on or stops. Both continuing and halting commit the project on a guess about intentions nobody has checked.
questions.mindset: When the organisation moves under you, ask whether the work is still wanted before deciding anything else.

questions.stem: A project manager has just received news that a new regulation has been adopted and the expectation is that the project will be delivered compliant with this new regulation. This was previously documented as a risk item with a low probability and a moderate impact. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Revisit the risk register and update the rating and response.
options.rationale: The probability has now risen to certainty because the regulation has been adopted, and the impact may have grown too. Updating the rating and response first is what reflects the new information before anything else is decided.

options.text: Update the issue log and apply corrective action.
options.rationale: Corrective action presumes an understanding of the new exposure that the register has not yet been updated to reflect. The assessment precedes the response.

options.text: Revise the project management plan.
options.rationale: Plan revision may become necessary if the regulation demands significant scope change. That follows from the reassessment rather than preceding it.

options.text: Initiate a change request for the updated regulation.
options.rationale: A change request likewise may be needed, but only once the impact on the project has been assessed. Raising one now asks for a decision on an unquantified change.

questions.explanation: When an identified risk actually occurs, the register is updated to reflect its new probability and impact before any plan, log or request is touched, because that reassessment sizes everything downstream. Jumping to the response skips the step that determines which response is proportionate.
questions.mindset: When a risk lands, update what you know about it before deciding what to do.

questions.stem: The project manager of a software development project for a financial institution realizes that team members are unusually delayed on their assigned tasks. The project manager has not experienced this before on previous, similar projects. After further investigation, the project manager determined that the delays were linked to the recent resignation of an experienced team member. What should the project manager have done to avoid this situation?

options.text: Ensured there was a well-defined path to promotion.
options.rationale: A promotion path is not directly related to the exposure created by an experienced member leaving. Retention measures do not remove the dependency on that person's knowledge.

options.text: Provided continuous guidance to project team members.
options.rationale: Ongoing guidance is not enough to mitigate the loss of a key team member. It supports the team without preparing for the gap their departure creates.

options.text: Identified competency risks and developed a mitigation plan.
options.rationale: Identifying competency risks in advance and preparing a mitigation plan is what minimises the impact when someone leaves. It is the proactive step that the other options might sit inside once it has been taken.

options.text: Scheduled periodic training for all project team members.
options.rationale: Periodic training may not produce the specific competencies needed to absorb a departing member's responsibilities. It is a general measure against a specific dependency.

questions.explanation: Dependence on particular people is an exposure to be identified and planned for while they are still present, and the specific remedies belong inside that plan rather than substituting for it. Training, guidance and retention are all things the plan might contain, which is what makes them tempting as answers on their own.
questions.mindset: Name the dependency on a person before that person leaves.

questions.stem: While reviewing progress in the middle of an iteration, the scrum master points out a major risk due to a user story dependency. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Update the product backlog.
options.rationale: Adjusting the backlog does not address the immediate exposure that has been raised. It reorders work without capturing the threat.

options.text: Update the project charter.
options.rationale: The charter is a high-level document that does not typically record risk detail. It is the wrong artefact for this information.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: A newly identified major risk belongs in the risk register, which is where exposures are recorded and tracked. Capturing it there is the immediate next step upon learning of it.

options.text: Update the issue log.
options.rationale: The issue log records problems that have already materialised, and this is a risk arising from a dependency. It should not be reached for before the register.

questions.explanation: Newly identified exposures go to the artefact built to hold them, regardless of the delivery approach in use, because that is what makes them visible and trackable. Confusing the register with the log reverses the distinction between what might happen and what already has.
questions.mindset: A newly spotted threat goes in the register, not the log.

questions.stem: During the design phase, a project manager realizes that the project will benefit from using adaptive tools. The effectiveness of this approach has been proven in past projects inside the organization. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Confirm team capabilities before introducing adaptive tools and artifacts to the project.
options.rationale: Without knowing whether the team can work with adaptive tools, the project manager may compromise aspects of the project unnecessarily. Ensuring the team has the training to perform their roles is part of the project manager's responsibility.

options.text: Contact the project sponsor and request new team members who are familiar with adaptive projects.
options.rationale: Requesting different people assumes the current team cannot adapt, which has not been established. It replaces the team before assessing it.

options.text: Freeze the design stage and look for an external resource to run iterative design at extra cost.
options.rationale: Halting the design and buying external capability is a costly response to an unexamined assumption. The existing team may be perfectly capable.

options.text: Update project documents to include adaptive tools and artifacts and plan the first iterative session.
options.rationale: Implementing the change commits the project before anyone has checked the team can work this way. Success elsewhere does not guarantee success here.

questions.explanation: A practice that worked elsewhere is introduced only after checking that this team can actually work with it, since the tool's track record says nothing about the people who would use it. Buying, replacing or implementing all presume a capability that has never been tested.
questions.mindset: Check the team can use the tool before you introduce it.

questions.stem: Project team members inform their project manager of a challenge they are facing. This challenge will likely impact project timelines. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Determine if the team's challenges impact the critical path.
options.rationale: Examining the critical path is a narrower question than understanding the challenge itself. It should come after the overall impact is understood.

options.text: Initiate a change request to extend the project timeline.
options.rationale: Requesting more time without evaluation is premature and potentially unnecessary. The challenge may prove absorbable.

options.text: Work with the team to assess the impact on the overall project.
options.rationale: Working with the team to understand and evaluate the effect on the project is the necessary first step. Only once the impact is known can a change control procedure be initiated if it is needed.

options.text: Escalate to the project sponsor for proper resolution.
options.rationale: Escalating without proper evaluation is premature and hands the sponsor an unquantified problem. The project manager and team can assess it themselves.

questions.explanation: Any new problem or proposed change is first understood for its effect on the project, with formal routes and escalation following only if the assessment shows they are warranted. Narrowing to one dimension too early is a subtler error than escalating, and both act ahead of the understanding.
questions.mindset: Understand the whole impact before narrowing, requesting or escalating.

questions.stem: Some of the project's materials have been ordered from overseas. The supplier notifies the project team that the materials will not reach the site on time due to a customs clearance delay that will affect the critical path. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Ask the logistics team to arrange an expedited clearance.
options.rationale: Expedited clearance may not be possible, since customs is controlled by regional or governmental bodies. It also acts before the planned response has been consulted.

options.text: Revisit the risk register and implement the respective risk response.
options.rationale: Corrective action for this exposure was identified at the start of the project, so the register is where the planned response sits. It holds the owner, probability, impact, score and planned responses needed to act properly.

options.text: Identify the root cause of the delay and add it to the bid documents.
options.rationale: The cause is already known to be customs clearance, so root cause analysis adds nothing. Bid documents are used to solicit proposals and the supplier has already been chosen.

options.text: Ensure the suppliers cover any additional costs due to the delay.
options.rationale: Cost recovery of this kind is determined when the contract is entered into and may not be available. It also pursues liability rather than delivery.

questions.explanation: When a risk that was planned for materialises, the first move is to consult the plan and execute the response already agreed, rather than improvising a new one. Acting before checking the register discards work the project did precisely so this moment would not require invention.
questions.mindset: If you planned for it, use the plan before you invent a response.

questions.stem: A company is about to start a project in a remote place known for extreme weather. It was agreed to implement the project using a predicted, multiphase approach. Each phase is composed of several iterations. What should the project manager do in the event of extreme weather?

options.text: Pause work until a specialized team arrives to assess the damage that was done to the site.
options.rationale: Pausing may turn out to be the approved response, but that can only be established by consulting the plan. Choosing it directly skips the agreed procedure.

options.text: Consult the initial plans in case of an emergency, then update and follow the corrective procedures.
options.rationale: The risk of extreme weather was acknowledged, so responses were developed and agreed in advance for exactly this event. Consulting those plans and then following the corrective procedures is what puts the prepared response into effect.

options.text: Advise management to reconsider such an investment and the continuity of the project.
options.rationale: Questioning the investment belongs to discussions that should have happened before the project started. Raising it now responds to a known and planned-for risk as though it were a surprise.

options.text: Stop the iteration, run a retrospective, and move to the next phase of the project.
options.rationale: Stopping the iteration may be part of the approved response but cannot be assumed. It also moves the project forward without addressing the event.

questions.explanation: Where a risk was anticipated and responses were agreed, the event triggers the plan rather than fresh judgement, and any of the plausible actions is right only if the plan says so. Reopening the decision to proceed treats a foreseen condition as new information.
questions.mindset: A foreseen event calls for the agreed response, not a fresh decision.

questions.stem: During the testing phase of a project, a team member finds that some requirements were not met. If the project now adds work to meet the requirements, it may cause a large time and cost overrun. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Escalate the issue to top management.
options.rationale: Notifying management before assessing the impact sounds the alarm without being able to describe its size. The assessment has to come first.

options.text: Perform an impact analysis.
options.rationale: Assessing the impact of the unmet requirements is what allows a course of action to be chosen sensibly. It is also the input to updating the risk register and to any communication that follows.

options.text: Call for a stakeholder meeting.
options.rationale: Convening stakeholders is premature when the project manager cannot yet describe the consequences. The meeting would have nothing substantive to consider.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: The impact analysis is an input to updating the register rather than the other way round. Recording an exposure of unknown size adds little.

questions.explanation: Before informing anyone or recording anything, the size of a newly discovered problem is established, because every downstream action depends on knowing it. Raising the alarm first is the most understandable error and leaves the project manager unable to answer the first question they will be asked.
questions.mindset: Know how big it is before you tell anyone about it.

questions.stem: A supplier of a critical component for a construction project notifies the project manager that the component will be significantly late. Because this risk had been identified during project planning, the cost baseline contains an adequate contingency reserve. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Identify a supplier that can provide the component within the amount of the reserve.
options.rationale: Project delivery is the prime focus, so the project manager assesses alternatives that fit within the reserve already set aside for this risk. Once a viable option is identified the case can be put to the sponsor for a decision.

options.text: Order the component from another supplier and submit a change request to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Ordering without regard to the reserve ignores the funding that was deliberately provided for this exposure. It commits spend before establishing that an alternative fits the money available.

options.text: Review the risk response plan and the statement of work for the next steps and a penalty clause for late delivery.
options.rationale: Pursuing a penalty clause for late delivery does not solve the current situation. Seeking compensation amounts to accepting the delay.

options.text: Update the project schedule and the lessons learned repository.
options.rationale: Rescheduling and recording lessons accept the delay rather than working to avoid it. Neither protects the delivery that is the priority.

questions.explanation: When contingency was set aside for precisely this exposure, the response uses it to protect delivery by finding an alternative that fits within it. Options that adjust the schedule or pursue compensation are the shape of accepting a delay, which is what the reserve exists to prevent.
questions.mindset: Money set aside for this risk is there to protect delivery, so spend it on delivery.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project that requires approval from a government agency. The agency is currently drafting legislation that will impact the project's approval process, but it is unclear when the legislation will become law. The project manager is concerned that the legislation may delay the project's key milestones or limit the project's development options. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Apply for an additional contingency to prepare for the anticipated delay in project milestones.
options.rationale: Allocating resources prematurely could create unnecessary cost when there is no clear timeline for the legislation. The project manager cannot yet determine which milestones would be affected or how much contingency would be appropriate.

options.text: Review the project scope and submit a request to exclude activities associated with the legislation.
options.rationale: Excluding those activities may not be feasible and could reduce the quality or effectiveness of the project. It avoids the uncertainty by removing work the project may need.

options.text: Continuously evaluate exposure to the risk to minimize negative impacts on the project and its outcomes.
options.rationale: Continuous evaluation keeps the project manager informed about developments in the legislation and their potential effect. Monitoring closely is what allows mitigation strategies to be developed as the picture becomes clearer.

options.text: Proceed with the project with the understanding that the pending legislation will pass without delay.
options.rationale: Assuming the legislation passes on schedule is risky and may force abrupt adjustments later. A delay or alteration could halt the project or cause overruns.

questions.explanation: Where the timing and content of an external change are both unknown, the correct posture is sustained monitoring rather than a commitment built on any particular assumption about how it resolves. Provisioning, excluding scope and proceeding confidently each fix one guess about something still undecided.
questions.mindset: When you cannot know yet, keep watching rather than betting.

questions.stem: A project manager was just given a new project to handle. She is working on the project documents and, after reading the Project Charter, is compiling the risks as she sees them. Once she completes the list, when should it be reviewed?

options.text: When starting the project and as each risk is closed.
options.rationale: Reviewing only at the start and at closure of individual risks leaves long gaps in which new exposures go unnoticed. Risk identification is not an event tied to those two moments.

options.text: While organizing, preparing, and carrying out the work.
options.rationale: This ties review to particular stages of activity rather than making it continuous. It narrows a process that runs for the whole project.

options.text: During weekly meetings as new risks are identified and added.
options.rationale: A weekly cadence is a reasonable practice but is narrower than the requirement. Review is not confined to one recurring meeting.

options.text: Regularly and throughout the project.
options.rationale: Identifying risks documents individual exposures and sources of overall project risk so the team can respond appropriately. That process is performed throughout the project rather than at fixed points.

questions.explanation: Risk identification is a continuous process rather than a task completed once and revisited at intervals, because new exposures arise at any point. Answers naming a specific cadence or stage are wrong by being narrower than the truth rather than by being bad practice.
questions.mindset: Treat risk identification as something you never finish.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project that is vital to their organization and the local environmental and energy authority. During a team meeting to discuss project risks , the team raised a high risk that an important senior manager is not currently involved with project. What should the project manager do to mitigate this risk?

options.text: Implement regular status reporting.
options.rationale: Status reporting keeps the senior manager informed without securing their involvement. Being kept up to date is not the same as participating.

options.text: Escalate this risk to senior management.
options.rationale: Escalating ensures senior management are aware and can act, since the uninvolved manager is a key stakeholder with major influence over the project. Without their involvement the project is more likely to fail.

options.text: Develop a highly detailed project management plan
options.rationale: A detailed plan is valuable but cannot guarantee that the senior manager becomes involved. Planning does not create participation.

options.text: Invite the senior manager to daily project meetings.
options.rationale: Daily meetings are too frequent for a senior manager and could be disruptive. An unrealistic invitation is unlikely to secure engagement.

questions.explanation: Where the exposure is the absence of someone whose involvement the project depends on, mitigation requires the level of authority that can actually secure that involvement. Reporting, planning and invitations are all things the project manager can do alone, which is exactly why none of them resolves an absence of that kind.
questions.mindset: Some risks can only be mitigated by someone with more authority than you.

questions.stem: A complex project is in the planning phase. The sponsor assigns a newly certified project manager to the project. Upon review of the project charter, the project manager uncovers several factors that could impact the project in unpredictable ways. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Update the project plan with details about schedule and budget forecasts.
options.rationale: Updating forecasts without understanding the exposures, their impact and possible mitigations adds no value. It produces numbers built on unexamined uncertainty.

options.text: Inform the project sponsor about the possible impacts these factors may have on the project.
options.rationale: The sponsor needs the detail of the exposures to understand the project's position properly. Informing them before that work is done gives them an incomplete picture.

options.text: Develop a risk management plan with details about the various factors.
options.rationale: A risk management plan is designed to identify and manage possible uncertain events on a project, which is precisely what these factors are. Developing it is what turns unpredictable influences into something that can be managed.

options.text: Extend the issue log to include a what-if scenario analysis.
options.rationale: The issue log is meant for events that have happened rather than events that may happen. Extending it misuses the artefact for forward-looking analysis.

questions.explanation: Factors that could affect a project in unpredictable ways are handled by building the plan designed for managing uncertainty, before forecasting, reporting or logging anything. Each alternative reaches for an artefact whose purpose is either settled fact or projected certainty.
questions.mindset: Uncertain future events get a plan built for uncertainty.

questions.stem: During a high-risk project, several risks have been materialized and responses have been implemented, However, the project still appears to be in trouble. The project manager is concerned that the risk management rules are not being carried out as specified. What should the project manager do to identify the weaknesses of the risk management process?

options.text: Transfer the risks.
options.rationale: Transferring risks may not be appropriate and does nothing about weaknesses in the process itself. It changes who carries exposures rather than examining how they are managed.

options.text: Update the risk register.
options.rationale: Updating the register is not applicable when it has not yet been determined why the project appears to be in trouble. It records exposures without diagnosing the process.

options.text: Request a risk audit.
options.rationale: Risk audits evaluate whether the risk management rules are being carried out as specified and whether they are adequate. They identify strengths, weaknesses and any barriers to the effectiveness of the process, which is exactly what the concern requires.

options.text: Analyze the risks.
options.rationale: Risk analysis defines the characteristics of a risk and how far it can affect objectives. With no clear indication of why the project is struggling, it does not reveal weaknesses in the process.

questions.explanation: A doubt about whether a process is being followed and whether it works is answered by auditing that process, not by performing more of it. Every alternative here operates on individual exposures, which leaves the question about the machinery itself unexamined.
questions.mindset: When you doubt the process, audit the process rather than working it harder.

questions.stem: Production of a specific machine in a factory was contracted through a foreign supplier. Prior to delivery of the final two components, the supplier informs the project manager that they need to renegotiate prices or the components will not be delivered. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Raise a legal case with the company for breaching the contract.
options.rationale: Legal action is a last resort that destroys the working relationship with a supplier still holding two undelivered components. It should follow attempts to resolve the matter commercially.

options.text: Approach alternative suppliers for the remaining two components.
options.rationale: Sourcing elsewhere for the final two components of a specific machine is likely to be slow and costly. It abandons the existing relationship before trying to preserve it.

options.text: Initiate the response plan for this risk entry based upon the trigger.
options.rationale: Reaching for a planned response assumes the situation cannot be settled directly with the supplier. The pragmatic route has not yet been attempted.

options.text: Work with the supplier to agree on new prices to minimize cost impact.
options.rationale: Negotiating directly is the most pragmatic route and the one most likely to resolve the situation. Maintaining a good relationship matters because this supplier still has to deliver the final two components.

questions.explanation: A supplier demand made late in a contract is first addressed commercially with that supplier, because they still hold what the project needs and the relationship remains an asset. Legal escalation and resourcing elsewhere are both available later and both cost more than a conversation.
questions.mindset: Negotiate first with the party who still has what you need.

questions.stem: A company is expanding, and the project manager is contemplating whether to hire new resources or outsource resources from an approved vendor team. What should the project manager focus on regarding this decision?

options.text: The procurement strategy and standards of the organization.
options.rationale: Strategy and standards frame how procurement is conducted rather than answering whether to hire or outsource. They constrain the decision without deciding it.

options.text: The cost of hiring new resources versus outsourcing resources.
options.rationale: Hiring costs cover salary, benefits, training and overhead, all of which affect the budget significantly, and these vary with the skills, experience and location required. Comparing that total against the expense of outsourcing is the fundamental basis for the decision.

options.text: The organizational resource strengths versus those of the vendor.
options.rationale: Comparing capability is relevant but the vendor team is already approved, which settles the competence question. The open question is the economics.

options.text: The cost of internal resources versus the cost of vendor resources.
options.rationale: This compares existing internal resources rather than the cost of hiring new ones, which is the option actually on the table. It measures the wrong side of the choice.

questions.explanation: A make-or-buy decision turns on the full cost of each route, and the hiring side includes salary, benefits, training and overhead rather than a headline rate. Options that compare capability or restate the choice with the wrong quantity are how a candidate loses a straightforward cost comparison.
questions.mindset: Compare the true total cost of each route, not the headline figure.

questions.stem: An agile project to implement a new automation process in a factory is underway. The project manager needs a vendor to help with the installation. What should the project manager do before the vendor comes to work with the team?

options.text: Delegate all key decisions to the vendor's team so the project manager does not take any risks.
options.rationale: Handing all decisions to the vendor abdicates responsibility rather than managing risk. The project manager remains accountable for the outcome regardless.

options.text: Hold an orientation to ensure both parties share the same understanding of project goals and requirements.
options.rationale: An orientation or kick-off gives all parties the same understanding of goals, requirements, taxonomy, general approach and timelines. Integrating key partners this way, with criteria, expectations and responsibilities set out, is what avoids later issues and impasses.

options.text: Submit the communication matrix so that all team members and vendors are known.
options.rationale: A communication matrix records who contacts whom without building any shared understanding of the work. Knowing names is not alignment on goals.

options.text: Remind the team that the vendor works for them and that the team can make final decisions.
options.rationale: Framing the relationship as one of authority discourages the partnership the installation depends on. It sets a tone that invites friction rather than collaboration.

questions.explanation: A vendor joining a team is integrated as a partner through a session that establishes shared goals, expectations and responsibilities before work begins. Asserting hierarchy in either direction, or exchanging contact details, both skip the alignment that prevents downstream impasses.
questions.mindset: Align a new partner on the work before they start it.

questions.stem: A two-year project was awarded to a company six months ago, but the procurement process has not yet been initiated. What should the project manager do to get the project moving forward?

options.text: Prepare the procurement management plan for the project.
options.rationale: Drafting the plan alone lacks the collaboration the exercise requires. Procurement planning depends on input from the teams who know the work.

options.text: Bring the teams together to draft a procurement management plan.
options.rationale: The procurement plan sets out when the process commences and when deliverables are ordered and delivered, and it belongs at the beginning of the project. Having noticed the lag, the project manager gets the teams collaborating to produce it.

options.text: Track the procurement according to an existing procurement management plan.
options.rationale: An existing plan from elsewhere may not suit this project's needs. Tracking against the wrong plan is worse than having none.

options.text: Escalate the situation to upper-level management.
options.rationale: Escalating a gap the project manager can close themselves is unnecessary. The work required is planning, not authority.

questions.explanation: A missing plan is produced with the teams whose knowledge it depends on, rather than written alone, imported from elsewhere or escalated. Collaboration is what makes the plan match the project, which is the whole reason a borrowed one will not do.
questions.mindset: Draft the plan with the people whose work it describes.

questions.stem: A project manager is meeting with a critical third-party supplier that provides discounted services. During the meeting, the supplier complains that they are dissatisfied with their return on investment (ROI). What should the project manager do to resolve this situation and avoid putting the project at risk?

options.text: Negotiate with the supplier to offer more money until the project until completed.
options.rationale: Offering more money commits to a cost change the project manager cannot authorise alone. It acts before stakeholders have been consulted on any remedy.

options.text: Remind the supplier that the contract is legally binding and they must adhere to the terms.
options.rationale: Asserting the contract against a critical supplier risks the relationship the project depends on. It answers a commercial concern with a legal position.

options.text: Research other third-party suppliers that provide similar services at discounted prices.
options.rationale: Looking elsewhere abandons a critical supplier before any attempt to resolve their concern. Replacement is a drastic response to a complaint raised in a meeting.

options.text: Discuss the issue with stakeholders and come to an agreement on a remediation plan.
options.rationale: No action should be taken before meeting stakeholders and developing a plan with them, since a single change can affect cost, schedule, scope and performance. Changes of this kind may also invoke change control and require approvals from parties outside the project.

questions.explanation: A supplier's commercial grievance is worked through with stakeholders before any commitment is made, because a remedy touching cost or terms is not the project manager's to give. Conceding, refusing or replacing are all unilateral answers to something that needs collective agreement.
questions.mindset: Do not promise a supplier anything the stakeholders have not agreed.

questions.stem: A member of the project team who was hired for six months to complete a specific task has decided to leave the project in the fifth month to pursue another job opportunity. What should the project manager's immediate action be?

options.text: Modify the contract to ensure the team member will complete the packages in the fifth month.
options.rationale: Changing the contract presumes what the existing terms permit and require. The current agreement has not yet been examined.

options.text: Determine what remaining packages might be affected and ensure that adequate resources are available.
options.rationale: Assessing the affected work is necessary but follows from knowing the contractual position. The notice period determines how much time there actually is.

options.text: Confirm the terms of the team member's contract to close their participation appropriately.
options.rationale: Understanding the terms, including the notice period and any outstanding deliverables, determines the appropriate course of action. That is the first step towards a smooth transition with minimal disruption.

options.text: Check the contingency reserve for extra resources to hire a new member to finish these packages.
options.rationale: Funding a replacement precedes establishing what the departing member still owes under contract. The gap may be smaller than assumed.

questions.explanation: When someone engaged under a contract leaves early, the contract itself defines what is still owed and how much notice exists, which sizes every subsequent decision. Planning the replacement or the coverage first means acting without knowing the terms that govern the departure.
questions.mindset: Read the agreement before you plan around someone leaving.

questions.stem: A vendor for a large and complex project has been performing more work than what was originally anticipated in the time and material contract. This type of contract caused the project to be behind schedule and over budget. The contract is about to expire. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Create a request for quotation (RFQ) to formulate a list of new vendors.
options.rationale: Running a new procurement discards a vendor already familiar with a large and complex project. It also takes time the expiring contract does not allow.

options.text: Shift to a master services agreement with appendices for the additional work as required.
options.rationale: A master services agreement covers a wide range of services and simplifies modification, letting additional work be added without renegotiating the whole contract. It also shifts the emphasis towards value delivery rather than hours consumed.

options.text: Consult the lessons learned repository to formulate a list of potential new vendors.
options.rationale: Consulting past records to find replacements likewise abandons the current vendor unnecessarily. The problem lies in the contract structure, not the supplier.

options.text: Try to negotiate a fixed-price contract with the current vendor.
options.rationale: A fixed price requires well-defined scope, which is precisely what this project has not had. It would be difficult to agree and risky for both parties.

questions.explanation: When a contract structure rather than the supplier is producing cost and schedule problems, the remedy is a structure that accommodates evolving work without repeated renegotiation. Replacing the vendor treats a commercial design fault as a performance fault, and a fixed price cannot be set over scope nobody can define.
questions.mindset: When the contract shape is the problem, change the shape rather than the supplier.

questions.stem: The project manager is responsible for a major project that involves working with many vendors. A key project concern is related to the quality and timely delivery of procured products and services as committed by the vendors. What should the project manager do to ensure that the products meet the quality requirements and are delivered on time?

options.text: Raise an item in the risk register to capture potential impacts related to delays in the procurement of products and services, mitigating the risk of suboptimal quality.
options.rationale: Recording the exposure documents the concern without doing anything to secure performance. Visibility is not assurance.

options.text: Conduct procurement performance reviews on a regular basis with all contracted vendors to ensure that products and services are all delivered or will be delivered on time and as per the agreed-upon contract.
options.rationale: Regular performance reviews let the project manager proactively identify and address problems with vendor performance. That is what keeps procurement objectives on track and products arriving on time and to standard.

options.text: Delegate the management of the procurement process and the interaction with all vendors to the organization's procurement department as they have the tools and means to deal with a large number of vendors.
options.rationale: Delegating vendor interaction entirely removes the project manager from performance that directly affects their project. The department's tooling does not transfer the accountability.

options.text: Review vendor management plan with all vendors to ensure they are in agreeance with the plan, mitigating the risk of undelivered and low quality products.
options.rationale: Agreement to a plan at the outset is not the same as performance against it over time. It secures assent rather than delivery.

questions.explanation: Vendor performance is assured by regular structured review against the contract, because that is the only option that detects shortfalls early enough to act. Logging exposures, securing agreement and delegating the relationship all substitute an arrangement for the ongoing inspection that actually catches problems.
questions.mindset: Assurance comes from checking performance repeatedly, not from setting expectations once.

questions.stem: During project closure, the project sponsor requests that a deliverable, developed by a contractor, be transferred to a nonprofit organization at no cost. The procurement documentation states that ownership of the deliverable reverts to the contractor once the procurement contract is finished. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Add "avoid out-of-scope agreements during the closure process" to the lessons learned register.
options.rationale: Recording a lesson is reasonable practice but leaves the sponsor's request unanswered. It notes the difficulty instead of resolving it.

options.text: Initiate a change request and execute the integrated change control process.
options.rationale: Change control governs the project's own baselines rather than the ownership terms of a contractor's agreement. The constraint here is contractual, not a project baseline.

options.text: Consider this transfer as an open issue for the contract department and continue closing the project.
options.rationale: Passing the matter on while closing the project leaves the sponsor's request unresolved and the closure incomplete. It hands over a problem rather than addressing it.

options.text: Review the contract agreement with the contractor to modify the property of the deliverable.
options.rationale: Reviewing the agreement with the contractor is how the ownership terms could be modified to permit the transfer. That route meets the sponsor's request without violating the procurement contract and allows the project to close successfully.

questions.explanation: Where a contract term stands between a stakeholder's request and its fulfilment, the route runs through the counterparty who holds that term, because only they can agree to vary it. Internal change processes cannot alter what an external agreement grants to someone else.
questions.mindset: To change what a contract gives someone, talk to the person it gives it to.

questions.stem: At project initiation, a quote for the required services was requested from a vendor, and the work was estimated at US$100,000. As the project progressed, requirements were updated following the company's procurement process, and a modified quote was received for more than US$250,000. The allocated contingency funds are not sufficient to cover the difference. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Restart the procurement process and select a new vendor.
options.rationale: Starting procurement again consumes time and may not produce a materially better price. The increase followed updated requirements rather than vendor opportunism.

options.text: Review the contract type that will be awarded to the vendor.
options.rationale: Changing the contract type does not close a funding gap of this size. The shortfall is financial rather than structural.

options.text: Proceed with the best offer as per the procurement process.
options.rationale: Proceeding commits to spending the project cannot fund. Following the process correctly does not create the money to pay for the outcome.

options.text: Engage the steering committee and escalate the issue.
options.rationale: The steering committee is best placed to ensure the project is not delayed or derailed by the increased cost. They may provide additional funding or help identify ways to reduce the cost of the services.

questions.explanation: A funding gap beyond the project's reserves is a decision for the governance body, since neither committing to unfunded spend nor reworking the procurement creates the money required. This is the situation where escalation is the correct answer rather than an avoidance of responsibility.
questions.mindset: When the shortfall exceeds what you control, take it to those who control more.

questions.stem: A complex, multimillion-dollar, multi-year product development project requiring unique knowledge is 70% complete. Contract termination is a possibility due to project deliverables and execution being not acceptable. Despite the strained relationship, the vendor is ready for rework at no penalty. What should the project manager do to manage this situation?

options.text: Ask the customer to permit rework as the vendor has unique knowledge of the product.
options.rationale: Asking the customer to accept rework on the strength of the vendor's irreplaceability pressures them without addressing why the work was unacceptable. The standard for acceptance remains undefined.

options.text: Finalize the new definition of done (DoD) with the customer and make the vendor bear the cost of rework.
options.rationale: Setting the standard with only the customer and imposing it on the vendor excludes one party from an agreement that binds them. It builds in the next dispute.

options.text: Facilitate the negotiation of the acceptance criteria between the customer and vendor.
options.rationale: Facilitating between the two is the most collaborative and consensus-building approach available. It ensures the rework is done in a way that meets the needs of both the customer and the vendor.

options.text: Direct the vendor to rework the deliverable since they did not meet the requirements.
options.rationale: Directing rework without agreed criteria repeats the conditions that produced unacceptable deliverables. The vendor would be working to the same unclear standard.

questions.explanation: Rework that has any chance of being accepted requires both parties to agree in advance what acceptable means, which is why the project manager facilitates rather than instructs. Setting the standard with one side and imposing it on the other guarantees the same disagreement a second time.
questions.mindset: Get both sides to agree the standard before anyone rebuilds to it.

questions.stem: A project manager walked into a project office and found a team member and a supplier representative engaged in a disagreement over a clause in the supply agreement. The project manager invites the supplier for a negotiation with the project team to resolve the conflict. Applying the principles of negotiation, for what should the project manager and team aim?

options.text: Give up the project objective for a win-lose outcome.
options.rationale: Abandoning the project objective defeats the purpose of the negotiation entirely. Conceding the goal is not a negotiating position.

options.text: Achieve the project objective for a win-lose outcome.
options.rationale: Winning at the supplier's expense damages a relationship the project still depends on. A defeated counterparty performs accordingly.

options.text: Achieve the project objective for a win-win outcome.
options.rationale: The ultimate goal is to achieve the project objective, and negotiation with a supplier should aim at a win-win. Combining both is what makes the outcome sustainable.

options.text: Achieve the project objective no matter what the outcome.
options.rationale: Pursuing the objective regardless of the consequences disregards the relationship and any wider impact. The cost of the win is left out of the calculation.

questions.explanation: Negotiation with a supplier holds two things at once: the project's objective must be met, and the counterparty must come out of it willing to continue performing. Options that sacrifice either the goal or the relationship are each half an answer.
questions.mindset: Win the point without defeating the person you still depend on.

questions.stem: One of the project vendors is late in providing a related product solution, which is affecting the release due dates. What should the project manager do to help the agile team manage this impediment?

options.text: Work with the vendor to understand the alternatives.
options.rationale: The project manager takes ownership of the impediment and works with the vendor to identify alternatives that could mitigate the delay. Doing so also builds the full understanding of the scope and impact that any further action depends on.

options.text: Review and update the release date with the team.
options.rationale: Moving the release date accepts the delay before exploring whether it can be mitigated. It acts without understanding the issue fully.

options.text: Have the technical lead escalate the issue to the functional manager.
options.rationale: Escalating through the technical lead passes on an impediment the project manager should own. It also acts before the situation is understood.

options.text: Have the team members and experts work together on a solution.
options.rationale: Internal problem-solving proceeds without the vendor who holds the delayed solution. The alternatives available depend on what the vendor can actually offer.

questions.explanation: An impediment originating with a supplier is owned by the project manager and explored with that supplier, since they know which alternatives exist. Rescheduling, escalating or solving internally all proceed without the party whose constraint created the problem.
questions.mindset: Own the blocker and explore it with whoever created it.

questions.stem: In order to reduce procurement time during a bidding process, a project manager decided to contract the additional work to a current contractor. The other bidders are complaining about this decision because they think that the process lacked transparency and fairness. What should the project manager have done to prevent this?

options.text: Invited all potential bidders to a meeting.
options.rationale: A meeting does not make an award transparent if the procedure itself was bypassed. Contact is not the same as process.

options.text: Awarded the contract without negotiation.
options.rationale: Removing negotiation does nothing to address the fairness of how the contractor was selected. The complaint concerns the selection, not the terms.

options.text: Followed the company's bidding procedure.
options.rationale: Complete transparency in bidding is only possible if the company's procedure is followed. Doing so ensures the process is fair and consistent and that all parties have an equal opportunity.

options.text: Shared the project objectives with all bidders.
options.rationale: Sharing objectives informs bidders without giving them a fair route to compete. Information does not substitute for procedure.

questions.explanation: Fairness in competitive procurement comes from following the established procedure, since that is what gives every party an equal and demonstrable opportunity. Gestures toward openness such as meetings or shared information cannot repair an award made outside the process.
questions.mindset: Fairness is the procedure, not the courtesies around it.

questions.stem: During the execution of repair work, the root cause of the damage was discovered to be failures that occurred during the construction phase. The same contractor who performed the construction work is performing the repairs. Because of this, the CEO wants to negotiate with the contractor for a reduced price. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Negotiate with the contractor to cancel the repair work and pay compensation for the previous work.
options.rationale: Cancelling the repairs leaves the damage unaddressed while pursuing compensation. It prioritises recovery over the outcome the project needs.

options.text: Negotiate the repair work with the contractor based on a shared risk-reward relationship.
options.rationale: Since the same contractor performed the construction phase in which the failures occurred, a collaborative approach is required. A shared risk-reward arrangement means both parties share in the risks and rewards and incentivises the contractor to complete the repairs efficiently and effectively.

options.text: Proceed with the contractor without mentioning the issue since the previous work is already closed.
options.rationale: Staying silent about a known cause of the damage forgoes any legitimate commercial adjustment. Closure of the earlier work does not make the finding irrelevant.

options.text: Proceed with the contractor and subtract the amount paid for supervision of the previous work.
options.rationale: Unilaterally deducting sums is a punitive move made without agreement. It invites dispute rather than securing effective repairs.

questions.explanation: Where a supplier caused the problem they are now fixing, the commercial answer aligns both parties' interests in the outcome rather than punishing or ignoring the history. Deduction and silence are opposite errors, one damaging the relationship and the other surrendering the position entirely.
questions.mindset: Align interests in the fix rather than litigating the fault.

questions.stem: A client has contracted a company to manage a large project in an agile environment with many subcontractors. The client is giving direct orders to the subcontractors, rather than to the contractor's project manager. This has created conflict within the team. What should the project manager do to prevent this situation from occurring again?

options.text: Keep the team informed about client expectations.
options.rationale: Informing the team is useful but will not stop the client issuing direct orders. It prepares people for the behaviour rather than ending it.

options.text: Invite the client to the team planning meeting.
options.rationale: Greater involvement does not address the specific behaviour causing the conflict. It may even create more opportunities for direct instruction.

options.text: Tell the team to avoid conflicts with the client.
options.rationale: Instructing the team to absorb the friction leaves the cause untouched. It asks people to tolerate a problem rather than removing it.

options.text: Ask the client not to give direct orders to the subcontractors.
options.rationale: Asking the client directly is the most direct and effective way to address the behaviour causing the conflict. Prevention requires speaking to the person whose actions create the problem.

questions.explanation: Behaviour by a stakeholder that disrupts a team is addressed with that stakeholder, however senior or commercially important they are. Managing the team's response to it, or increasing their involvement, both work around a conversation that has to happen.
questions.mindset: Raise the behaviour with the person doing it, even when they are the client.

questions.stem: During the testing phase of a technical project, the project manager discovers some issues with the final product and subsequently learns that after negotiations, important product features were excluded from the contract's scope in an effort to minimize costs for the client. What should the project manager do to resolve the issue?

options.text: Escalate the issue to the sponsor to make a decision to redefine the scope and solve the problem.
options.rationale: Escalating hands the sponsor a problem the project manager can address with the client directly. The negotiation belongs with the party whose product it is.

options.text: Work with the client to negotiate and ensure the inclusion of the missing crucial features in the project.
options.rationale: The project manager has found a deficiency in scope and must remedy it, which means informing the client and negotiating how to deliver the product with the important features. That is the proactive and collaborative route to resolution.

options.text: Continue with the project as planned and register the contract scope issue in the issue log.
options.rationale: Logging the deficiency and continuing delivers a product known to be missing crucial features. Documentation is not a remedy.

options.text: Review the lessons learned to find a solution for contract negotiation and scope issues.
options.rationale: Consulting past lessons does not address a live deficiency in this product. It studies the problem rather than resolving it.

questions.explanation: A scope deficiency discovered during delivery is taken to the client and renegotiated, because they are the party who accepted the exclusion and who will receive the result. Escalating, logging or researching all defer a conversation that is the only route to a working product.
questions.mindset: Take a scope gap back to whoever agreed the scope.

questions.stem: A project manager is overseeing a procurement project for a company that has a dedicated procurement management team that handles all contracts. The quarterly report identifies six contracts that do not align with the company's objectives. What will be the most suitable action for the project manager to take?

options.text: Keep the six contracts despite their misalignment.
options.rationale: Retaining misaligned contracts ignores the finding and wastes resources. It could actively harm the company's overall goals.

options.text: Suggest terminating all contracts that are misaligned.
options.rationale: Recommending termination of the contracts that do not align with the company's objectives is the appropriate action. Keeping them would waste resources and potentially damage the organization's goals.

options.text: Ask the project sponsor to revise the contracts.
options.rationale: The procurement management team handles all contracts, so directing this to the sponsor targets the wrong party. It also proposes revision where alignment is the issue.

options.text: Request that the customer revise the contracts.
options.rationale: The customer is not the party responsible for contracts the company holds. Asking them to revise misplaces the responsibility entirely.

questions.explanation: Where another function owns contracts, the project manager's contribution is a clear recommendation rather than a direct instruction or a request routed to the wrong party. Recognising who holds the decision is what separates a useful recommendation from a misdirected one.
questions.mindset: Recommend to whoever owns the decision, and recommend clearly.

questions.stem: The development of a final project schedule is delayed due to the inability to negotiate an agreement with one of the vendors needed for successful project delivery. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Circulate meeting minutes and discuss the agreed and outstanding clauses with the project team and customer.
options.rationale: Circulating minutes documents the impasse without moving it forward. Discussion internally does not resolve a negotiation with the vendor.

options.text: Meet with the vendor to discuss a path forward and identify an alternative vendor if necessary.
options.rationale: It is in the project's best interest to come to terms with the vendor, so the conversation continues first. If agreement proves impossible, the project manager then looks for alternatives.

options.text: Meet with the project sponsor and seek their support in replacing the vendor due to the inability to negotiate an agreement.
options.rationale: Seeking sponsor support to replace the vendor is premature. It may become necessary in extreme cases but not before further negotiation.

options.text: Communicate the project needs and influence the vendor to accept the terms as soon as possible for successful project delivery.
options.rationale: Pressing the vendor to accept the existing terms repeats the approach that has already stalled. Influence without movement on either side is not negotiation.

questions.explanation: A stalled negotiation is pursued further with the counterparty while a fallback is prepared, rather than escalated or resolved by pressure. Holding both the continued conversation and the alternative in view is what keeps the project moving without burning the relationship prematurely.
questions.mindset: Keep negotiating while quietly readying an alternative.

questions.stem: A project manager has received quotes from two vendors for the same parts. Vendor A has informed the project manager that they fulfilled a similar order two months ago at a price that was 2% under the original planned cost. Vendor B has a history of on-time delivery but has announced a price increase. How should the project manager evaluate this situation?

options.text: Review the agreements and procurement documentation for Vendor B to force them to keep the original pricing.
options.rationale: Attempting to compel a vendor to hold pricing is adversarial and may have no contractual basis. It also evaluates nothing about which supplier is preferable.

options.text: Evaluate the contract clauses to reduce the orders from Vendor B, and buy them from Vendor A to improve project indicators.
options.rationale: Shifting volume to the cheaper vendor decides on price before performance has been examined. Improving indicators is not a basis for source selection.

options.text: Use the metrics from Vendor A to request better pricing from Vendor B, keeping both providers as a risk mitigation strategy.
options.rationale: Using one quote as leverage over the other is a price tactic rather than an evaluation. It still rests on cost without reviewing past performance.

options.text: Review the work performance information of both vendors against their contracts to find the preferred supplier.
options.rationale: Reviewing both vendors' work performance information against their contracts is how a preferred supplier is properly identified. Past performance must be reviewed before turning to an alternative source, and the decision should rest on a variety of factors rather than price alone.

questions.explanation: Choosing between suppliers rests on documented performance against their contracts rather than on the most recent price signal, because delivery reliability carries cost that quotes do not show. Every option built around the price comparison is a negotiating move dressed as an evaluation.
questions.mindset: Judge suppliers on what they have actually delivered, not on what they are quoting today.

questions.stem: A project manager has created the stakeholder list and is deciding how to distribute information effectively to the customer. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Meet with all the stakeholders face-to-face on a weekly basis.
options.rationale: Weekly face-to-face contact with everyone may not be practical, and the method and frequency will not suit every stakeholder. It fixes one approach before anyone's requirements are known.

options.text: Send updates to all stakeholders, including the customer.
options.rationale: Uniform updates ignore that different stakeholders need different information at different intervals. Broadcasting is not distribution designed around requirements.

options.text: Perform a stakeholder analysis and prepare a communications management plan.
options.rationale: Analysis identifies all the stakeholders along with their communication requirements, which is what the plan is then built from. That sequence produces distribution designed around actual needs rather than assumption.

options.text: Review historical data sent to other customers and follow the same practices.
options.rationale: Historical practice can guide the project manager but does not identify this project's stakeholders or their preferences. Those still have to be established for this project.

questions.explanation: Effective distribution of information is designed from an understanding of who needs what, which means analysis precedes any decision about channel or frequency. Copying past practice or defaulting to uniform contact both fix the method before the requirements are known.
questions.mindset: Find out what people need before deciding how to send it to them.

questions.stem: A project manager has recently been assigned to an existing multinational project and is not familiar with the key stakeholders. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Request a meeting with the resource manager.
options.rationale: A resource manager has authority over particular resources and will not know all the project's stakeholders. They are the wrong source for a complete picture.

options.text: Review and update the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: The register holds the details of the project's stakeholders, their roles and their attitude toward risk. Reviewing and updating it is how the new project manager learns the landscape and begins building rapport.

options.text: Ask for the opinion or expert judgment of the sponsor.
options.rationale: The sponsor's judgment will not give the project manager a systematic understanding of the stakeholder community. It offers one perspective where a record exists.

options.text: Identify the communications tool and update the plan.
options.rationale: Selecting tools and updating the plan does nothing to familiarise the project manager with who the stakeholders are. It acts on information they do not yet have.

questions.explanation: When taking over a project, the existing record of who matters and how they regard the work is the fastest route into the landscape. Asking individuals or adjusting communication mechanics both substitute activity for consulting the artefact built to answer the question.
questions.mindset: Read the record before you start asking around.

questions.stem: The product owner has asked the project manager and the agile team to demonstrate the completed functionality to key project stakeholders. The project is in its early days and has only completed three iterations of functionality. This is the first time the stakeholders will be exposed to an agile project. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Reinforce with the product owner that it is their role to communicate and manage the stakeholder groups directly.
options.rationale: Pushing the responsibility to the product owner avoids preparing stakeholders who are new to this way of working. The project manager has a part to play in setting the context.

options.text: Set expectations with the stakeholders regarding what agile is, the approach, and that they will be seeing a small amount of functionality.
options.rationale: Because it is the stakeholders' first exposure, they need to understand the approach and that delivery comes in small increments that build on each other. Setting that context is what makes the small amount of functionality intelligible rather than disappointing.

options.text: Demonstrate the completed functionality to the stakeholders, along with the user requirements and solution prototypes available.
options.rationale: Demonstrating without context leaves stakeholders to judge three iterations against expectations formed elsewhere. Adding requirements and prototypes increases the material without supplying the framing.

options.text: Protect the team from distractions by providing a link to the user acceptance test (UAT) environment so the stakeholders can view the functionality directly.
options.rationale: Sending stakeholders to an environment unattended removes any opportunity to explain what they are seeing. It treats their first exposure as an interruption to be deflected.

questions.explanation: Before showing partial work to an audience unfamiliar with incremental delivery, establish how the approach works and what they should expect to see. Presenting the increment without that framing invites them to measure it against a finished product they were never going to get.
questions.mindset: Frame what people are about to see before you show it to them.

questions.stem: A company has started doing agile projects. The project sponsor is frustrated and does not understand the new requirements gathering process, which seems to be incomplete and moving too fast. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Help the project sponsor understand the different tools and techniques available and why this one was selected.
options.rationale: Each practitioner is empowered to train and mentor stakeholders so they understand the process and can participate effectively. Explaining the options and the reasoning behind the choice is what converts frustration into informed involvement.

options.text: Update the stakeholder register to identify the project sponsor as a potential impediment.
options.rationale: A sponsor cannot be treated as an impediment on an agile project without breaking the fundamental trust model. Recording them that way damages the relationship rather than the confusion.

options.text: Let the team know that the sponsor is unhappy and switch from iterative planning to predictive planning.
options.rationale: Dictating a change of process without buy-in from the team doing the work runs against self-organisation and servant leadership. It also abandons the approach rather than explaining it.

options.text: Pause the project work until the scrum master has a chance to review the complete backlog with the sponsor.
options.rationale: Pausing implies the entire backlog must be approved in advance, which would create a waterfall project without agility or thoroughness. It breaks the process to accommodate a misunderstanding of it.

questions.explanation: A senior stakeholder's frustration with an unfamiliar process is met by teaching them how it works and why it was chosen, not by abandoning it or labelling them an obstacle. Practitioners carry a responsibility to bring stakeholders into the way of working rather than shielding it from them.
questions.mindset: Teach the stakeholder the process rather than bending the process to their confusion.

questions.stem: A company used to deliver technical services to customers using external labor. When a new project manager arrived, the team hired specialized personnel to reduce costs by delivering an in-house service. Some of the stakeholders are frustrated that the resources are taking too much time to deliver the service. What should the project manager do to address the concern?

options.text: Review the communication plan with the frustrated stakeholders.
options.rationale: Reviewing how communication happens does not clarify the project timeline that is causing the frustration. It addresses the channel rather than the concern.

options.text: Increase stakeholders' understanding of the project approach.
options.rationale: Interacting with stakeholders to explain the approach and the plan is what addresses their concerns and reduces frustration. Understanding why delivery looks different in-house is the thing they are missing.

options.text: Rehire the external contractor who provided the service previously.
options.rationale: Returning to the previous arrangement may reproduce the very delays that frustrated stakeholders before. It reverses a cost decision without examining the complaint.

options.text: Develop a glide path and communicate the ramp-up plan to stakeholders
options.rationale: A ramp-up plan does not address the stakeholders' concern about the delay they are experiencing now. It offers a schedule where an explanation is needed.

questions.explanation: Frustration arising from a change in how work is delivered is addressed by explaining the approach and what it entails, since the expectation gap is the actual problem. Reversing the decision or offering plans and processes leaves stakeholders without the understanding that would settle the concern.
questions.mindset: When people are frustrated by a change, explain the change.

questions.stem: A project manager is leading a project where a low-level stakeholder has just been promoted to a new position and has now become a high-level stakeholder. What should the project manager update to ensure the proper involvement of this stakeholder to the project?

options.text: Communications management plan
options.rationale: The communications plan governs how information flows rather than how a stakeholder is engaged with. It does not address their changed importance to the project.

options.text: Stakeholder engagement plan
options.rationale: The engagement plan is updated to reflect changes in the stakeholder community, including when the importance of a particular stakeholder to the project's success changes. A promotion of this kind is exactly that situation.

options.text: Resource management plan
options.rationale: The resource management plan concerns the people and materials the work requires. It has no bearing on how a stakeholder is involved.

options.text: Risk management plan
options.rationale: The risk management plan sets out how uncertainty is handled rather than how stakeholders are engaged. It does not benefit this scenario.

questions.explanation: When someone's importance to a project's success changes, the artefact that describes how each stakeholder is worked with is the one updated. Changes to the stakeholder community route there rather than to plans governing information flow, resources or uncertainty.
questions.mindset: When a stakeholder's standing changes, revisit how you plan to engage them.

questions.stem: A company is implementing a new computerized system. During project execution, the leader of a department that is critical to project completion raises a concern that the department's requirements are completely missing from the approved project management plan. What should the project manager have done to avoid this issue?

options.text: Managed the expectations of all relevant stakeholders.
options.rationale: Managing expectations does not help when the requirements are missing altogether. It is reasonable for the department head to expect their needs to be recorded in an approved plan.

options.text: Sought expert judgment in the project scope design.
options.rationale: Expert judgment on scope design would not surface requirements from a department that was never consulted. The gap came from who was excluded, not from insufficient expertise.

options.text: Involved all relevant stakeholders in the project planning.
options.rationale: The department leader is a stakeholder who should have been included in planning activities. Had they been involved, the team would have understood their requirements and how to engage them.

options.text: Developed a change management plan to approve changes.
options.rationale: A change management plan would only help once the issue was known, and the project manager was unaware until the concern was raised. It handles changes rather than preventing omissions.

questions.explanation: Requirements go missing from a plan when the people who hold them were not in the planning, so the preventive measure is inclusion rather than better technique or process. An approved plan that omits a critical department's needs is evidence of who was in the room, not of how well the room worked.
questions.mindset: If someone's requirements matter, they belong in the planning.

questions.stem: A key stakeholder is upset about the new features in the current iteration for the product. The key stakeholder was unavailable during the last review and did not have the opportunity to provide input. What should the project manager have done to prevent the stakeholder from being upset?

options.text: Waited until all stakeholders approved the change before implementing
options.rationale: Waiting for universal approval causes unnecessary delay and does not avoid disagreement. It makes every absent stakeholder a blocker.

options.text: Ensured that updated project information is always accessible to all stakeholders
options.rationale: Stakeholders need updated project information to be accessible to them, and that transparency is what keeps everyone aligned about the product outcome. Accessibility does not depend on anyone attending a particular session.

options.text: Met individually with every stakeholder to avoid disagreement
options.rationale: Individual meetings do not avoid disagreement and consume considerable time. They also create the same dependency on availability.

options.text: Scheduled meetings only when all stakeholders could be present
options.rationale: Requiring full attendance before meeting causes unnecessary delays. Availability would dictate the project's pace.

questions.explanation: Alignment that depends on attendance fails whenever someone cannot attend, so the durable answer makes current information continuously available instead. Options built around gathering everyone or securing universal agreement hand the schedule to whoever is least available.
questions.mindset: Make the information reachable so alignment does not depend on attendance.

questions.stem: A project can gain downstream marketing benefits if additional equipment is included in the project scope. However, this equipment is still in an early development phase and will not be ready to meet the project timelines. A member of the project steering committee is in favor of its inclusion. How should the project manager proceed?

options.text: Prepare a scope change request to include the additional equipment because it is beneficial to the marketing team.
options.rationale: Raising a change request acts on one committee member's preference before the committee has reached a position. Consensus has not been achieved.

options.text: Provide a clear rationale for its exclusion based on the business case and its impact on the project timelines.
options.rationale: Arguing for exclusion likewise pre-empts a decision that belongs to the committee. The project manager would be settling a matter outside their authority.

options.text: Conduct a survey among steering committee members to assess their individual project requirements for a consensus decision.
options.rationale: The steering committee provides direction and makes decisions outside the project team's authority, so its consensus is needed before proceeding. Surveying the members also surfaces potential conflicts, concerns and impacts associated with introducing the new equipment.

options.text: Request the project sponsor to escalate the issue to the steering committee member to avoid delaying project approval.
options.rationale: Using the sponsor to press an individual member treats a governance question as a matter of influence. It also bypasses the committee as a body.
