questions.explanation: Where a decision sits above the project team's authority, the project manager's task is to secure a position from the governing body rather than to advocate for or against the proposal. Arguing either side is equally out of place when the decision is not yours to make.
questions.mindset: When the decision belongs to a body, gather its position rather than taking a side.

questions.stem: An external stakeholder has a significant impact on the project, as they have the ability to approve or reject changes to the project scope, timeline, and budget. What approach should the project manager take with this stakeholder?

options.text: Communicate with the stakeholder according to the stakeholder engagement and communications management plans.
options.rationale: Managing engagement this way ensures the stakeholder understands the project's goals, objectives, benefits and risks, and how their contribution supports success. It also keeps them informed of progress, able to give feedback and able to raise concerns.

options.text: Request feedback from the stakeholder so that the project meets the stakeholder's expectations and can be delivered as planned.
options.rationale: Seeking feedback alone is narrower than managing the relationship comprehensively. It captures one element of engagement rather than the whole approach.

options.text: Add the stakeholder to the risk register and quantify the level of impact that the stakeholder could have on the project goals.
options.rationale: Treating a person with approval authority as a risk entry records the exposure without engaging them. It analyses rather than builds the relationship.

options.text: Inform the stakeholder of the key project benefits and keep them updated on the project's progress and milestone achievements.
options.rationale: One-way updating is less comprehensive than planned engagement and gives the stakeholder no route to raise concerns. It informs without involving.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder with authority over the project's constraints is managed through the planned engagement approach, which covers understanding, feedback and the raising of concerns together. Answers offering one strand of that, or treating the person as an exposure to be quantified, each fall short of the whole relationship.
questions.mindset: Work the planned approach with important stakeholders rather than one strand of it.

questions.stem: A project manager is working on a project charter and discovers that two key stakeholders are transferring to other departments and replacements have not been identified yet. What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Put the project on hold until the replacements are identified.
options.rationale: Holding the project may be neither necessary nor feasible and causes delay of its own. It responds before the effect of the departures is known.

options.text: Involve senior management to resolve the challenge.
options.rationale: Senior management should be brought in after an impact analysis, so they understand the risks and impacts involved. Going to them first hands over an unquantified problem.

options.text: Obtain support from the project sponsor to continue the project.
options.rationale: Seeking backing to continue presumes the departures are absorbable without having checked. It may prove unnecessary or insufficient.

options.text: Perform an impact analysis of the possible delays.
options.rationale: The analysis establishes the potential effect of the stakeholders leaving and identifies the risks that come with it. From there the project manager can determine the best course of action and communicate the findings to the right parties.

questions.explanation: Departures of key stakeholders are assessed for consequence before the project is paused, escalated or reassured, because the response and the audience both depend on the size of the effect. Escalation with findings in hand is useful; escalation without them transfers a question rather than a problem.
questions.mindset: Quantify the effect before choosing who needs to hear about it.

questions.stem: During project execution, a key stakeholder is replaced with a new team member who has approval authority. The new member states that the project deliverables are not aligned with the design and does not approve them. However, a few weeks later the project manager learns that the new team member had not been informed of changes during execution. What should the project manager have done to avoid this miscommunication?

options.text: Organized a meeting with the sponsor before the execution began.
options.rationale: A meeting with the sponsor before execution is good practice but would not have prevented this miscommunication. The gap arose when the stakeholder changed partway through.

options.text: Updated the stakeholder register to include the new team member.
options.rationale: Updating the register would have made the project manager aware of all the stakeholders and ensured regular communication with the new member. That is what would have kept them informed of the changes made during execution.

options.text: Asked the previous stakeholder to hold a meeting with the new team member before leaving.
options.rationale: A handover meeting is good practice but is not always possible, for instance where someone leaves suddenly. It relies on the departing person's availability.

options.text: Updated the project charter during the execution phase to include all the changes.
options.rationale: The charter authorises the project and defines its scope, goals and success criteria, and is not typically updated during execution. It is the wrong artefact for tracking stakeholder changes.

questions.explanation: When people in key roles change mid-project, updating the record of who the stakeholders are is what keeps them inside the flow of information. Handover conversations help when they happen, and they depend on circumstances that cannot be relied on.
questions.mindset: Keep the list of who matters current, or people drop out of the loop unnoticed.

questions.stem: A five-year highway construction project is in its third year of execution when the project manager receives a complaint from a local community group. The group is upset because they noticed that the path of the highway changed and now runs closer to their homes. This conflict has disrupted construction and put the project in danger. What should the project manager have done to avoid this issue?

options.text: Created a contingency plan to mitigate the impact of community opposition.
options.rationale: A contingency plan prepares for opposition rather than preventing it. It is reactive where the question asks what would have avoided the conflict.

options.text: Established an internal review board to integrate quality assurance activities.
options.rationale: Quality assurance matters in construction but does not address the community's grievance. The complaint concerns the route and how they learned of it.

options.text: Held community meetings to keep stakeholders informed of progress and changes.
options.rationale: Open and transparent planning that engages internal and external stakeholders is vital, and community meetings would have surfaced the route change before it was discovered. That engagement builds trust and maintains a positive relationship.

options.text: Ensured that the project planning was confidential and well-documented.
options.rationale: Confidentiality would have deepened the mistrust and misunderstanding that caused the conflict. Keeping affected people uninformed is the opposite of the remedy.

questions.explanation: External groups affected by a project are engaged openly and continuously, because a change discovered rather than communicated converts a neighbour into an opponent. Planning for opposition or working more privately both accept the information gap that produced the conflict.
questions.mindset: Tell the people affected before they find out for themselves.

questions.stem: During a kick-off meeting with the project sponsor and various project members, it became clear that it was not necessary for some participants to be present. In addition, one required expert was not aware of the meeting and was not present at the meeting. What should the project manager have done to prevent this from happening?

options.text: Established a fixed communication platform to provide updates on the project to all stakeholders.
options.rationale: A platform for updates does not establish who needs to participate and when. It distributes information rather than managing involvement.

options.text: Managed stakeholder engagement by involving the stakeholders in the appropriate phases of the project.
options.rationale: Managing engagement brings awareness to stakeholders of when their participation is required and when it is optional. That is what would have brought the missing expert and spared the unnecessary attendees.

options.text: Developed the project charter including the roles and responsibilities of all the stakeholders.
options.rationale: Recording roles in the charter does not ensure people know which sessions they should attend. Documentation is not engagement.

options.text: Created a responsibility matrix to notify stakeholders of the meetings they are required to attend.
options.rationale: A responsibility matrix assigns accountability for work rather than managing participation across the project. It does not address engagement in the appropriate phases.

questions.explanation: Getting the right people into the right sessions follows from actively managing engagement across the project's phases, so participants know when they are needed and when they are not. Charters, matrices and platforms all record or distribute without establishing that awareness.
questions.mindset: Manage when people are needed, rather than documenting that they exist.

questions.stem: During project implementation, a stakeholder is questioning the purpose of the project and wants to pause the project to assess a new process that may affect the final deliverable. What is one of the first things the project manager should do?

options.text: Use a power/interest grid to determine the stakeholder's influence on the execution of the project.
options.rationale: The grid groups stakeholders by authority, level of concern about outcomes and ability to cause changes to planning or execution. Understanding the stakeholder's power and interest is what lets the project manager develop a strategy for addressing their concerns.

options.text: Consult with the project sponsor to determine the next steps and the potential new process.
options.rationale: Consulting the sponsor comes after assessing the stakeholder's influence and concerns. It escalates before the situation has been analysed.

options.text: Postpone any changes to a future project in order to fulfill the deliverables in the current project.
options.rationale: Deferring the matter decides against the stakeholder without assessing their standing or their point. It closes the question rather than analysing it.

options.text: Revisit the acceptance criteria with the stakeholder to ensure the quality level is appropriate.
options.rationale: Reviewing acceptance criteria addresses quality when the stakeholder is questioning the project's purpose. It answers a different concern.

questions.explanation: A challenge from a stakeholder is first understood in terms of how much authority and influence they actually hold, since that shapes what response is warranted. Acting on the substance before assessing the source risks either over-reacting to a marginal voice or dismissing a decisive one.
questions.mindset: Work out who is objecting and what weight they carry before deciding how to answer.

questions.stem: The project manager of an agile project notices that many stakeholders are skipping iteration planning and review meetings. Some stakeholders admit that they do not see the value of the meetings and prefer not to participate. The project is in danger of falling behind schedule due to the lack of stakeholder participation. What should the project manager do first to address this issue?

options.text: Review and update the communications management plan.
options.rationale: Revising the plan is a reasonable long-term measure but does not address the immediate lack of participation. The project is already at risk of slipping.

options.text: Identify gaps and mentor stakeholders on the iterative approach.
options.rationale: Stakeholders saying they do not see the value indicates they lack a proper understanding of the iterative approach and why these meetings matter. Identifying those gaps and mentoring addresses the cause, which the schedule risk makes urgent.

options.text: Record the iteration review and share it with stakeholders.
options.rationale: Recordings let stakeholders observe without participating, which is what the meetings need from them. It accommodates the absence rather than ending it.

options.text: Build a RACI matrix and develop a training plan for stakeholders.
options.rationale: A matrix and training plan may help in the longer term but are slow relative to the immediate schedule risk. They are structures where a direct intervention is needed.

questions.explanation: When people opt out because they do not see the point, the remedy addresses the understanding rather than the logistics, and the urgency comes from what the absence is costing. Recording sessions or building structures each accept non-participation instead of resolving why it is happening.
questions.mindset: When people do not see the value, show them the value rather than working around them.

questions.stem: A company is creating a new application for its users. The agile team completed the initiating stage and is performing iterations to complete planning and execution. However, a stakeholder wants to change the order of the deliverables to demonstrate new aspects of the app to stakeholders. How should the project manager address this situation?

options.text: Include the stakeholder in sprint planning to ensure the right priorities are assigned.
options.rationale: Sprint planning is where work evolves and adapts to stakeholder feedback, so bringing the stakeholder into it addresses their request properly. It ensures the right priorities are assigned while keeping the project on track.

options.text: Use key performance indicators (KPIs) to verify that the project is progressing on schedule.
options.rationale: Confirming schedule performance does not respond to the request about the order of deliverables. It measures something the stakeholder has not questioned.

options.text: Ask the stakeholder for a change request and submit it to the change control board (CCB).
options.rationale: Agile projects do not typically route reordering through traditional change control. Imposing that process treats adaptation as an exception.

options.text: Explain to the stakeholder that modifying the schedule now will increase the delivery risk.
options.rationale: Warning about risk may sometimes be necessary but forecloses a request the approach is built to accommodate. Working with the stakeholder toward a solution serves the project better.

questions.explanation: Reordering work in an adaptive environment is handled through the planning event designed for exactly that, by bringing the requester into it. Routing it through formal change control or refusing on risk grounds both treat evolving priorities as a disruption rather than as the expected case.
questions.mindset: Adaptation belongs in the planning event, not in an exception process.

questions.stem: An organizational transformation project has two workstreams running in parallel between corporate headquarters and an overseas office. Before kick-off, the project manager is scheduled to meet the overseas office leader. What should the focus of the meeting be?

options.text: Informing the overseas office leader of the project's strategic value, key deliverables, and their expected involvement.
options.rationale: Because the meeting precedes kickoff, it is the moment to set expectations with all parties involved. Covering strategic value, deliverables and expected involvement leaves the leader informed, prepared to contribute and aligned with everyone else.

options.text: Reaching an agreement on the choice of procurement strategies to be employed by the overseas office.
options.rationale: Procurement strategy is detail that belongs after the project has been kicked off. It presumes a shared understanding that this meeting exists to create.

options.text: Assisting the overseas office leader in communicating with the corporate headquarters staff about the project.
options.rationale: Facilitating their communication with headquarters is an activity for once the project is under way. The leader has not yet been briefed on the project itself.

options.text: Identifying and assigning a subject matter expert (SME) to represent the project at the overseas office.
options.rationale: Assigning representation is a step that follows kickoff. It allocates a role before the leader understands what the project is for.

questions.explanation: A meeting held before a project formally starts is used to establish why the work matters, what it will produce and what is expected of the person, because everything operational depends on that foundation. Options naming specific downstream activities are all things that become possible only after this conversation.
questions.mindset: Use the meeting before the start to establish why, what and who.

questions.stem: While gathering requirements for the project scope, the project manager realizes that some of the stakeholder requirements have a conflict. What should the project manager do to define a clear scope?

options.text: Assist affected stakeholders in reaching a consensus.
options.rationale: The project manager has to be proactive in reaching consensus between the team and stakeholders, with all parties involved. Using the necessary communication techniques is what makes requirements clear and agreed.

options.text: Follow the recommendation of the technical consultant.
options.rationale: A consultant's recommendation resolves the conflict without involving the parties who hold the requirements. Their agreement is what makes the scope stick.

options.text: Escalate to the project sponsor to make a decision.
options.rationale: Escalating removes the resolution from the stakeholders whose requirements are in conflict. A decision imposed from above does not produce their agreement.

options.text: Conduct a meeting with the disagreeing parties only.
options.rationale: Meeting only the parties in dispute leaves out others whose requirements bear on the scope. Resolution needs all affected parties involved.

questions.explanation: Conflicting requirements are reconciled by bringing the affected parties to agreement, because a scope nobody has agreed to will be disputed later regardless of who decided it. Expert recommendations and escalated decisions both settle the question without producing the consent that makes scope durable.
questions.mindset: A scope everyone agreed to holds; a scope someone decided does not.

questions.stem: An experienced project manager is mentoring a new project manager assigned to their first project. As the new project manager prepares for the project, they are overwhelmed by the number of stakeholders identified by the team. What should the experienced project manager tell the new project manager to do next?

options.text: Perform a stakeholder analysis to determine the relative importance.
options.rationale: Once stakeholders are identified, the next step is to understand and analyse them, examining each one's position on and perspective of the project. Stakeholder analysis gathers quantitative and qualitative information systematically to determine whose interests should be taken into account.

options.text: Categorize key stakeholders using a workbook register.
options.rationale: Categorising relies on the insight that analysis produces and should therefore follow it. Sorting before understanding produces arbitrary groupings.

options.text: Update the communications management plan with stakeholder preferences.
options.rationale: Recording preferences presumes an understanding of the stakeholders that has not yet been developed. The plan depends on the analysis.

options.text: Prioritize stakeholders based on the stakeholder register.
options.rationale: Prioritising from the register alone lacks the foundational insight that analysis provides. The register lists who they are, not what weight each carries.

questions.explanation: Identification produces a list, and everything useful that follows depends on systematically analysing that list to establish whose interests carry weight. Categorising, prioritising and planning communications are all downstream activities that rest on insight the analysis has yet to supply.
questions.mindset: A long list becomes manageable through analysis, not through sorting it.
